la-ts051.x: Listen to an announcement from an economics professor.
sc: W: Hello, everyone. This is Professor Alvarez with a quick update for Introduction to Economics.

W: Because the lecture hall will be used for a department event on Thursday, our midterm exam will not be held in class. Instead, I will post the exam online on Wednesday evening, and you will have forty-eight hours to submit your answers.
W: The exam is open book, but you must work alone. I will be checking answers for similarity, so please write everything in your own words.
W: If you have a disability accommodation or a problem with your internet connection, email me by Tuesday, and we will find another way for you to take it.
W: Thursday's class is cancelled, and we will meet again next Tuesday.

la-ts052.x: Listen to a phone message from a research assistant.
sc: W: Hi, this is Mei Lin from the Sleep and Memory Lab, calling for people who signed up as volunteers last month.

W: We are starting a new study in two weeks, and we need adults between eighteen and thirty-five who normally sleep at least seven hours a night. The study has two visits. On the first visit, you will learn a list of word pairs. You will come back the next morning to be tested on them.
W: Each visit lasts about forty minutes, and participants receive twenty-five dollars in total.
W: Please call me back at extension four five one two, or reply to the email I sent today, to choose your time slots. Spaces are limited, so the sooner, the better.

la-ts053.x: Listen to an announcement at a museum.
sc: W: Welcome to the Harbor Maritime Museum. Before you begin your visit, we would like to share a few notes.

W: The main gallery, with the old sailing ships, is open all day. However, the lower level, which shows the tools of early navigators, is closed this week while we install new lighting. It will reopen on Monday.

W: Guided tours leave from the front desk at eleven and two. They last forty-five minutes and are included in your ticket. If you prefer to explore on your own, free audio guides are available in four languages.
W: Finally, please remember that flash photography is not allowed near the old maps, because bright light can damage them. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

la-ts054.x: Listen to a fire drill announcement in an office building.
sc: W: Attention, everyone. This is a notice from the Building Safety Office about Wednesday's fire drill.

W: The alarm will sound at ten fifteen. When you hear it, stop what you are doing, leave your computer on, and walk to the nearest stairwell. Please do not use the elevators, even if you are on the top floor.
W: Once outside, gather in the parking area behind the building and wait for your floor warden to take attendance. Wardens will be wearing orange vests.

W: The drill will last about fifteen minutes. Staff who work from home on Wednesday do not need to take part, but they should read the safety checklist we emailed last week. Thank you for your cooperation.

la-ts055.x: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship.
sc: W: Good afternoon. This is the Financial Aid Office with a reminder about the Global Citizens Scholarship.
W: The scholarship gives two thousand dollars to second-year students who have shown strong leadership in a community project. Applications are due by five p.m. on the fifteenth of March.
W: Your application must include a one-page essay and a letter from someone who has seen your project first-hand. Please note that a letter from a family member will not be accepted.

W: Last year, several students missed the deadline because they waited to ask for letters. We strongly suggest that you contact your references this week. Forms are available at the front counter and on our website.

la-ts056.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a university housing office.
sc: M: Hello, this is Daniel from the Student Housing Office, calling for Priya Nair.

M: I'm calling about your request to move to a quieter room. A single room has opened up in Birch Hall, on the second floor, and I wanted to offer it to you before I contact the next person on the list.
M: The room costs about eighty dollars more per month than your current one, but it has its own desk and a window facing the garden.

M: If you want it, please come to our office before noon on Friday and sign the new agreement. After that time, I will have to offer the room to someone else. You can also call me back at five five five, oh one four two. Thanks, and have a good day.

la-ts057.x: Listen to an announcement at a conference.
sc: W: Good morning, and welcome to the third day of the Regional Teaching Conference. I have a few updates about today's schedule.

W: The session on classroom technology has been moved from the Ballroom to Room C, because a larger group than expected has registered for the keynote speech in the Ballroom. The start time is the same, ten thirty.
W: Lunch will be served in the Garden Court from twelve until one thirty. Vegetarian meals are marked with a green card, so please look for them if you need one.
W: The shuttle to the hotels will leave from the main entrance at five, not five thirty as printed in your program. A later shuttle will leave at seven. Thank you, and enjoy your day.

la-ts058.x: Listen to an announcement about campus construction.
sc: M: Good afternoon. This is the Facilities Department with news about the work on the east side of campus.
M: Starting Monday, crews will begin replacing the pipes beneath Maple Walk, the path between the library and the Engineering Building. The walkway will be closed for about three weeks.

M: Students can still reach both buildings. Follow the yellow signs along Lake Road, which adds roughly five minutes to the walk. The library's main doors will stay open, but the side entrance facing Maple Walk will be locked.
M: We know that noise may be a problem for people studying nearby, so the loudest work will be done only between nine and eleven in the morning. We thank you for your patience.

la-ts059.x: Listen to an announcement about a school sports event.
sc: W: Hello, athletes and fans. This is Coach Rivera with news about Saturday's swimming meet.
W: Because of a problem with the heating system in our own pool, the meet will take place at Lakeside College instead. Warm-ups begin at eight thirty, and the first race is at nine thirty.
W: The college is about a thirty-minute drive away. A bus will leave from the gym parking lot at seven forty-five, and team members are expected to ride it, even if a parent is willing to drive them.
W: Spectators are welcome and tickets are free, but seating is limited, so please arrive early. Swimmers, remember to pack a towel, two swim caps, and your own water bottle. See you on Saturday.

la-ts060.x: Listen to an announcement from a history professor.
sc: W: Before we finish for today, I'd like to say a few words about your research paper in this course.

W: Some of you have asked about choosing a topic outside the period we have studied. You can, but only if you first email me a short proposal, three or four sentences, explaining why the topic fits the themes of the course.
W: I should also mention that the library has reserved a shelf of books on trade routes. These are meant for everyone, so please do not take more than two at a time, and return them within a week.
W: The first draft is due in three weeks. A draft need not be perfect, but it should show a clear argument. I will return comments within seven days.

la-ts061.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a professor to a student.
sc: M: Hi Kwame, this is Professor Lindqvist returning your call about the geology field report.

M: I looked at the outline you sent, and the structure is good. My only concern is the section on rock samples. You describe where you found each sample, but you don't yet explain what the samples tell us about the history of the valley, and that is the main goal of the assignment.
M: I'd suggest you spend some time in my office hours this week. Bring your notes and the photographs from the trip, and we can go through them together.
M: I'm in my office on Wednesday from two to four, or Thursday morning by appointment. Let me know which works for you. Talk soon.

la-ts062.x: Listen to an announcement about a research study.
sc: W: Hello, everyone. I'm Dr. Hassan, and I'm looking for volunteers for a study on how people choose what to eat in a cafeteria.

W: The study takes place in the Student Center, and you need no preparation. You will simply have lunch as you normally would, while a small camera above the food stations records which foods you look at and select.
W: No one will see the recordings except the research team, and your name will not be attached to them. After lunch, you will answer five short questions about your choices.
W: Volunteers receive a free meal and a coupon for a coffee. If you can join us on Tuesday or Thursday between noon and one, please speak to the assistant at the table outside this room.

la-ts063.x: Listen to a notice from a guided tour company.
sc: W: Thank you for choosing Old Town Walking Tours. Before we begin, here are a few details about this morning's tour.

W: We will walk about three kilometers over two hours, mostly on flat streets, with a short stop at the market square. If anyone prefers a slower pace, please tell me now, and I will arrange for a second guide to walk with you at the back.
W: Our route passes the old clock tower, which was built in the fifteenth century. Normally we climb to the top, but the stairs are being repaired, so we will view it from the square instead.
W: Please keep your belongings close in crowded areas. Restrooms are available at the market, and we will meet here again at noon.

la-ts064.x: Listen to a safety announcement in a chemistry laboratory.
sc: M: Before you start your experiments today, I need your attention for a short safety reminder.

M: Last week, someone left a bottle of solvent open on the shared bench. Nobody was hurt, but the smell filled the room, and we had to open all the windows. From now on, every bottle must be closed and returned to the cabinet as soon as you finish with it.
M: Also, goggles must be worn at all times, even if you are only writing notes at your bench. Regular glasses are not a substitute.
M: If you spill anything, don't try to wipe it up with paper towels. Raise your hand, and one of the assistants will bring the right equipment. Thank you, and good luck with today's work.

la-ts065.x: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship program.
sc: W: Hello, students. This message is from the Office of International Programs.

W: Applications are now open for the Horizon Exchange Scholarship, which pays for one semester of study abroad. To apply, you need a grade point average of three point two or higher and at least two semesters left at this university.
W: The application has two parts. The online form is due on the first of April. Finalists will then be interviewed in the second week of April, and decisions will be sent by email on the thirtieth.

W: An information session will be held next Wednesday at four in the Global Lounge. You do not need to register for it, but we would encourage you to bring your questions. Past winners will be there to share their experiences.

la-ts066.x: Listen to an announcement from an art history professor.
sc: W: Good morning, everyone. Before we look at today's slides, I have news about our class trip to the City Gallery.

W: The visit is next Friday, and we will meet at the gallery entrance at ten, not in our classroom. The gallery is offering us a private talk with one of its curators about the paintings from the nineteenth century, which we have been studying.

W: Admission is free for our group, but you must show your student card at the door. If you cannot attend because of another class, send me an email, and I will give you a short written assignment on the same paintings instead.
W: Please wear comfortable shoes, since we will be standing for most of the hour.

la-ts067.x: Listen to an announcement at a research conference.
sc: M: Good evening, delegates. Here is some information about tomorrow's poster session.

M: The session takes place in the Exhibition Hall from four to six. If you are presenting, you may begin setting up your poster at three. Pins will be provided at each board, so you don't need to bring your own.
M: Please look at the number on your name badge. That number is the board you have been given. Please don't move to a different board, even if it seems to have more space.

M: Judges will walk through the hall at about four thirty, so stay near your poster during that time. Light refreshments will be served at the back of the hall, and we ask that no food or drink be carried near the posters.

la-ts068.x: Listen to an announcement about parking on campus.
sc: W: Attention, students and staff who drive to campus. This is an update from the Parking Office.

W: Starting next Monday, Lot B, the large lot next to the gym, will be closed for resurfacing. The work should take two weeks. During this time, drivers with a Lot B permit may park in Lot D without paying any extra fee.
W: Lot D is a ten-minute walk from the main buildings, so a free shuttle will run every fifteen minutes from seven in the morning until six at night. The shuttle stop is at the corner of Pine Street.
W: Please note that cars left in Lot B after Sunday night will be moved at the owner's expense. Thank you.

la-ts069.x: Listen to an announcement about an intramural sports event.
sc: W: Hello, everyone. This is the Recreation Center with details about the intramural soccer tournament.
W: Registration closes this Friday at five. Each team needs between eight and twelve players, and at least three players on every team must be first-year students. That rule is new this year.
W: Games will be played on Saturdays in October, and the schedule will be posted on our website next week. The team with the most points at the end of the month will win a trophy and a pizza party.
W: If you want to play but don't have a team, come to the front desk, and we will help match you with other players. Teams without enough players by Friday will be dropped from the tournament.

la-ts070.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a library.
sc: M: Hello, this is Marcus from the Lakeside College Library, calling for Yuki Tanaka.
M: On Tuesday, you reserved a study room for Thursday afternoon, but unfortunately, there is a problem. The air conditioning in that room has stopped working, and the repair will not be done by then.

M: We have two choices for you. You could take our larger room on the third floor at the same time, though it has no screen for presentations. Or you could keep the original room if you don't mind the heat, and we would provide a fan.
M: Please call us back at extension two two one eight, or stop by the front desk before Wednesday evening, and tell us which you prefer. Thanks for your understanding.

la-ts071.x: Listen to an announcement from a linguistics professor.
sc: M: Hi, everyone. Two quick things before you leave today.

M: First, the recording project. Each pair needs to record a ten-minute conversation in natural speech. I know some of you have worried that your recording will sound too formal. Please try to forget the microphone, talk about something you care about, and don't prepare a script.

M: Second, our guest. Next week, instead of my usual lecture, Dr. Ivanova from the Language Technology Institute will talk about how computers learn to recognize accents. Her visit was arranged only yesterday, so it isn't on the syllabus.
M: There will be a short quiz on her talk the following Monday, so take careful notes. I'll post the recording project instructions online tonight.

la-ts072.x: Listen to a phone message asking for volunteers for a survey.
sc: W: Hello, this is Amara from the Parks and Recreation Department. I'm calling members of our neighborhood group about a survey this weekend.

W: We are counting how many people use Riverside Park, and at what times of day. We need volunteers to stand at the four park entrances for two hours each and mark a tally sheet every time someone walks or cycles in.
W: No special skills are needed, but because it may be cool by the water, we recommend a warm jacket. We will provide clipboards, pens, and snacks.

W: The shifts are Saturday and Sunday mornings and afternoons. If you can help, please text your name and your preferred shift to five five five, oh one nine nine. Thank you so much for supporting your park.

la-ts073.x: Listen to an announcement at a planetarium.
sc: W: Welcome to the Starfield Planetarium. We are pleased to have you with us this afternoon.

W: In a few minutes, our program, Journey Through the Solar System, will begin in the main dome. The show lasts thirty-five minutes. Latecomers cannot be admitted after the lights go down, because sudden light from the doorway affects everyone's view of the stars.
W: If you have a child under five, you may prefer our short show, Little Stars, which is shown in the smaller theater at one thirty and three. It has softer music and shorter scenes.
W: Please turn your phones off or set them to silent. And remember that our gift shop closes thirty minutes before the last show.

la-ts074.x: Listen to an announcement about a campus safety service.
sc: M: Good evening, this is Campus Security with a reminder about the night walking escort service.

M: If you are on campus after nine p.m. and feel uncomfortable walking alone, you can request an escort. Just call the number on the back of your student card, or press the blue button on any of the emergency phones near the paths.

M: A trained student officer will meet you where you are, usually within ten minutes, and walk with you to your residence hall or to the parking lot. The service is free and is available every night until two in the morning.
M: Last term, officers accompanied more than five hundred students. You do not need a special reason to use it. We would rather you call than walk alone.

la-ts075.x: Listen to an announcement about a research grant for undergraduates.
sc: W: Hello, everyone. This is Dr. Osei from the Undergraduate Research Office.

W: We are now accepting proposals for the Summer Research Grant. This grant gives up to three thousand dollars to students who want to carry out a research project of their own with a faculty mentor, between June and August.
W: Before you apply, you must find a professor willing to be your mentor. Without a signed mentor form, your application will not be considered, so start that conversation soon.

W: Proposals should be two pages long and explain not only what you plan to study but also why it matters. The deadline is the twentieth of February. We will hold a workshop on proposal writing on the sixth, in Room one fourteen of the library.

la-ts076.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a computer science teaching assistant.
sc: W: Hi everyone, this is Sofia, the teaching assistant for Computer Science one fifty. I'm leaving this message for all students in Thursday's lab section.

W: Our lab this week has a different format. Instead of working on the programming exercise in the computer room, we will meet in Room two eleven for a code review. Each of you should bring a printed copy of your last assignment, and you will explain your solution to a classmate.
W: The point is not to find mistakes but to practice describing your thinking clearly. It will not be graded, but attendance will be recorded.
W: If you have not submitted your last assignment yet, please do it today, so that you have something to discuss. Thanks, and see you Thursday.

la-ts077.x: Listen to an announcement at a conference registration desk.
sc: M: Welcome to the International Business Forum. If you are listening to this message, you are probably in line for registration, so let me explain how it works.

M: There are two lines. People whose last names begin with A through L should use the left desk, and everyone else should use the right desk. Please have your confirmation email ready, either on your phone or printed.
M: After you register, you will receive a badge, a program, and a meal ticket. Your badge is required to enter all sessions, so please wear it at all times.
M: If you ordered a conference T-shirt, you can collect it from the table by the stairs, not at the registration desk. Thank you for your patience.

la-ts078.x: Listen to an announcement about renovations in a residence hall.
sc: W: Hello, residents of Cedar Hall. This message comes from the Residence Life Office.

W: Beginning next week, the north elevator will be out of service for about a month while it is being modernized. The south elevator will remain open, but we expect longer waiting times in the morning and evening.

W: If you live on the first or second floor, please use the stairs, so people living on higher floors or with mobility needs can use the elevator more easily. Residents who cannot use stairs can contact the front desk to arrange a room on the ground floor temporarily.
W: We also ask you not to move large furniture during the work. The elevator will return before the end of the month.

la-ts079.x: Listen to an announcement about a community fun run.
sc: W: Hello, runners and walkers. This is Hye-jin from the City Fitness Club, with the final details for Sunday's charity fun run.

W: The five-kilometer course starts at the clock tower and finishes at Memorial Field. Roads along the route will be closed from seven thirty, so please do not try to drive near the course. The run begins at eight.

W: You can collect your race number at the club until Saturday at six. If you are late, you can still pick it up on Sunday, but only from half past six until seven fifteen, and queues are likely to be long.
W: Every runner will receive a medal, and all the money raised goes to the children's hospital. We hope the weather stays dry.

la-ts080.x: Listen to a tour announcement at a botanical garden.
sc: M: Good morning, and welcome to the Greenfield Botanical Garden. I'll be your guide on today's walk.

M: We will start in the tropical greenhouse, where the air is warm and humid, so you might want to take off your jackets. After about twenty minutes, we'll move outside to the herb garden, where you are welcome to touch and smell the plants.
M: Please remember that some plants in the garden are rare, and a few can irritate the skin, so only touch those that have a green tag. The ones with a red tag are for looking only.
M: The walk ends at the garden cafe, around eleven fifteen. Anyone who has to leave early may do so, but let me know first.

la-ts081.x: Listen to an announcement from a sociology professor.
sc: W: Before I let you go, a note about the survey assignment. most groups have chosen to ask classmates about their social media habits. That's convenient, but it's also why I'm going to be strict about one thing.

W: A sample drawn only from this course won't tell you anything about students at the university as a whole. We'll discuss that on Monday, and I'll expect your reports to address it directly, whether or not you fix it.

W: Anyone willing to go beyond the classroom is welcome to use the lounge in the student union on Wednesday afternoon. The union lets us approach people there, provided we ask permission first and stay under an hour.
W: Of course, this is optional. But I would think carefully before dismissing it.

la-ts082.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a volunteer coordinator.
sc: M: Hello, this is Tomas from the Riverside Language Exchange, returning your message about volunteering as a conversation partner.

M: I appreciate your offer, and your experience teaching would certainly be an asset. However, I should be upfront about one thing. Our sessions are usually held in the evening, and most volunteers commit to a whole semester, because the learners build trust with one particular partner over time.

M: If your schedule makes that difficult, I could add you to our short-notice list instead. Those volunteers cover for absent partners, so there are fewer hours, but it can lead to a regular placement in the next term.
M: Give me a call back at your convenience, and we can talk through which arrangement suits you best.

la-ts083.x: Listen to a talk by a museum guide at the start of a tour.
sc: W: Thank you for joining me. Since several of you asked about the glass cases, let me explain why this wing looks the way it does.

W: These manuscripts are over six hundred years old, and light is their greatest enemy. That is why the room is so dim, and why we rotate the displays every three months. A page that you see today may not be available when you return in the spring.
W: You'll notice that a few pages are shown only as high-quality copies. The originals are in storage, and come out only for researchers.
W: Many visitors say the copies let them look more closely, since they can be enlarged on the screens at the end of the hall.

la-ts084.x: Listen to a safety announcement before an evacuation drill.
sc: M: Good morning, everyone. As you know, we will be practicing our evacuation procedure at half past ten. I would like to address a few common mistakes we noticed in the previous drill.

M: First, many people stopped to collect their coats and bags. In a real situation, those seconds matter, and it is better to leave everything behind. Second, a number of staff held the doors open for others after the alarm, which blocks the safe closing of fire doors. Close every door behind you.
M: Finally, please resist the temptation to gather at the building entrance. Those who stand there prevent others from leaving, and make it harder for firefighters to arrive.
M: Move to the field, past the white line, and wait for instructions. Thank you.

la-ts085.x: Listen to an announcement about scholarship requirements.
sc: W: Good afternoon. This message is for students who currently hold the Merit Scholarship.

W: Renewal for next year is not automatic. To keep your award, you must complete at least thirty credits and maintain a grade point average of three point oh. Students who fall short by even a small margin will receive a letter, and the committee will review their situation individually.

W: I want to be clear that this is not a formality. In the past two years, a fifth of recipients lost their funding, and most of them could have appealed. The deadline for appeals is the first Friday of the next semester, and late appeals are not considered.
W: If you are uncertain about where you stand, the advising office can calculate your figures with you.

la-ts086.x: Listen to an announcement from a biology professor.
sc: M: A reminder about next week's field trip to the wetlands. The bus leaves at seven, and I know that's early, but the tide determines our schedule, not me.
M: The best time to observe the birds is when the water is low, and that happens before nine. If we arrive later, the mud flats will be covered, and there will be little to see except water.
M: Bring boots, because the ground will be wet, and bring your field guides. The binoculars belong to the department, so I'll hand them out on arrival and expect them back.
M: Anyone who cannot make the early departure should speak to me today. Please don't simply arrive at eight, expecting to join us.

la-ts087.x: Listen to a phone message about a psychology experiment.
sc: W: Hello, this is Dr. Ng's lab calling for Lucas Moreau. Thank you for completing our online screening questionnaire.

W: Based on your answers, you qualify for the next stage of our study on attention. I should mention that the study involves wearing a small headband that measures brain activity. It is painless and harmless, but some people find it uncomfortable around the forehead, so we like to mention it beforehand.
W: The session lasts an hour and pays thirty dollars. If you are still interested, please do not drink coffee or energy drinks for four hours before you arrive. Caffeine can change the readings.
W: To book a time, reply to this number by text, and we'll send you directions.

la-ts088.x: Listen to a notice about changes at a science museum.
sc: W: Visitors, please note that the Hall of Origins will be closed for the next two weeks. We know many of you came to see it.

W: While the hall is closed, we have opened a temporary display in the lobby, which includes a few of the smaller fossils, though not the large skeleton at the entrance. Tickets for this week and next are half price, and your ticket will also be valid for a return visit within six months.
W: If you have purchased a ticket for a guided tour of the Hall of Origins, you will receive a refund at the front desk, or you may exchange it for a tour of the Planet Gallery.
W: Thank you for your understanding.

la-ts089.x: Listen to an announcement about a graduate scholarship.
sc: M: This is a message for those considering the Hartwell Fellowship. The committee has asked me to clarify a few points that cause confusion.

M: The fellowship supports one year of study, but it is not a general scholarship. Applicants must propose a project that connects two academic fields, such as economics and public health. A strong grade record alone will not be enough.

M: Letters of recommendation must come from professors who know your work, not from friends or employers, however impressive their titles. The application closes on the first of November, and no extension is possible, since the committee meets the following week.
M: We recommend that you begin the proposal now, even if the plan is not final.

la-ts090.x: Listen to an announcement at an academic conference.
sc: W: Good morning, and thank you for your patience. We have had a last-minute change in the program that I'd like to explain.

W: Dr. Fernandez, who was due to give the opening talk on urban planning this morning, is stuck at the airport because her flight was delayed. She expects to arrive by lunchtime. Rather than cancel, we have swapped her talk with the one scheduled for two o'clock.

W: That means the panel on water systems now begins at half past ten in this room. If you planned to attend Dr. Fernandez's talk this morning, you might consider the workshop in Room B, which is on a similar subject.
W: Printed programs are not updated, but the corrected schedule is on the screen outside.

la-ts091.x: Listen to an announcement about construction near the library.
sc: W: Many of you have noticed the fence going up around the plaza. Let me explain what is happening and, more importantly, what it means for your exam preparation.

W: The plaza is being rebuilt, and the drilling will occur on weekdays from eight until four. The library says that the ground floor will be the most affected, while the fourth floor, which is the quietest, should hardly notice it.

W: The library will extend its opening hours to midnight through the exam period. The study rooms in the Humanities Building have also been opened to all students, though they have to be booked online.
W: The work is expected to continue until the end of the term, so please plan accordingly.

la-ts092.x: Listen to an announcement about tickets for a basketball game.
sc: M: This is the athletics office with information about tickets for Friday's championship game. Demand has been far greater than we expected.

M: Because the arena holds only three thousand people, student tickets will be distributed by lottery. To enter, log in to the athletics page before noon tomorrow. Results will be emailed at three, and winners will have until five to confirm, or the ticket passes to someone else.
M: Each winner may claim one extra ticket for a guest, but the guest must be a current student. This rule is meant to prevent resale.
M: Students who do not win may still watch on the big screen in the Student Center, where seating is first come, first served.

la-ts093.x: Listen to a recorded message from a language center.
sc: W: Thank you for calling the Westbridge Language Center. Our office is currently closed, but here is information that may answer your question.

W: If you are calling about the placement test, please note that it is no longer given in person. You can take it online at any time, and it takes about forty minutes. You must finish it at least three days before your intended start date, so that we can place you in the right class.
W: Many callers ask about refunds. Tuition is refundable only until the end of the first week, and registration fees are not refundable at all.
W: Our office reopens at nine tomorrow morning. For urgent questions, you may leave a message after the tone.

la-ts094.x: Listen to a talk by a guide at an observatory.
sc: M: Welcome, everyone. Before we step into the dome, I'd like to set expectations, since I've seen visitors leave disappointed in the past.

M: Tonight, the sky is partly clear, and the telescope will point at Saturn. Through the eyepiece, you will see a small, sharp image of the planet and its rings. It will not look like the colorful photographs you've seen online, which are made by combining many exposures.
M: There is a line, and it moves slowly, because everybody gets about a minute at the eyepiece. If clouds appear, we may have to switch to the star cluster, which is less dramatic but more reliable.
M: Please use only red flashlights in the dome, because white light ruins everyone's night vision.

la-ts095.x: Listen to a message from a professor about office hours.
sc: W: This is Professor Mbeki. I'm sending this message to everyone in my statistics seminar, because I've noticed a pattern.

W: Over the past two weeks, almost all the students who came to my office hours did so on the day before an assignment was due. That is exactly when I can help least, since I'm usually busy answering the same question for ten people at once.
W: From now on, I'll hold extra hours on Mondays, at least three days before each deadline. If you bring a draft or a specific problem, we can accomplish a great deal in twenty minutes.
W: I'm not saying you shouldn't ask for help at the last minute. I'm saying it will be less useful.

la-ts096.x: Listen to a voicemail message from an academic advisor.
sc: M: Hi Aisha, it's Mr. Brandt from the advising office, following up on our conversation yesterday.

M: The good news is that the prerequisite is offered in the summer, and most students who go this route finish without delay. The registration for summer courses closes on the twenty-fifth, though, so you can't afford to wait.
M: I'm in the office until five. Come by, or call, so we can work out the details.

la-ts097.x: Listen to a notice about dining services during construction.
sc: W: As many of you know, the Central Dining Hall will close next Monday for renovation. I'd like to describe what will replace it, since the changes aren't all that obvious.
W: Three food trucks will park outside the Student Center from eleven until two on weekdays. Meal plan swipes will be accepted there, but each swipe covers only a main dish, not a drink.
W: The two smaller cafes, which usually sell only snacks, will serve hot lunches, though their menus will be limited. They are expected to be crowded, so we suggest avoiding noon.
W: The dining hall should reopen in January. Updated menus are on the dining services website.

la-ts098.x: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship essay.
sc: W: Good afternoon. A few of you have asked about the essay for the Founders' Scholarship, so I'd like to make a short comment.

W: The prompt asks you to describe a challenge you have faced. Past winners were not necessarily those who had faced the biggest challenges. The committee tells us that the essays which impressed them most were honest about what the writer learned, and what they would do differently.
W: A common weakness is to spend the whole essay describing the difficulty and then end with a single sentence of lesson. Try to give the reflection at least as much space as the story.
W: Essays are limited to six hundred words, and are due by Friday the ninth.

la-ts099.x: Listen to a message inviting students to join a study about commuting.
sc: M: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel from the Transportation Research Group. We are looking for students who travel to campus by bike or on foot.

M: Our interest is in how weather affects commuting choices. If you take part, we'll ask you to keep a short travel diary for two weeks, noting how you came to campus each day and why. We'll also invite you to a thirty-minute interview afterward.
M: We aren't looking for people who always cycle in all weather, nor for those who never do. We want the ones whose habits change depending on conditions.
M: If that sounds like you, send a short email to the address on our website. Participation earns a gift card.

la-ts100.x: Listen to a safety announcement about bicycles on campus.
sc: M: Attention, cyclists. The campus police have asked me to share a few words about bike safety, especially since the new bike lane opened on Oak Avenue.

M: Many of you have welcomed the lane, and it has certainly made the ride easier. However, there have been several near misses where cyclists crossed the lane at the bus stop without looking, and where pedestrians stepped into the lane without realizing it was there.
M: The solution is simple: slow down near bus stops and crossings, and ring your bell before passing anyone.
M: Also, remember that locks are free at the campus police office, and any bike left unlocked overnight will be tagged and may be removed.

la-ps001.x: Listen to an announcement at the campus gym.
sc: W: Good evening, members of the Campus Gym. I have some news about next week.
W: The swimming pool will be closed on Monday and Tuesday because workers are cleaning the water. The pool will open again on Wednesday at six in the morning.

W: The weight room and the running track will be open as usual. On Tuesday, we will also have a free yoga class at seven in the evening in Room two. Bring your own mat, or ask for one at the front desk.
W: Thank you, and enjoy your workout.

la-ps002.x: Listen to an announcement in a school cafeteria.
sc: M: Hello, everyone. This is Mr. Lopez from the cafeteria. I have a short message about lunch.

M: We will also stop selling soda. Instead, you can buy fruit juice or bottled water for one dollar.
M: If you have an idea for the menu, please write it on a card and put it in the box near the door. Thank you.

la-ps003.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a tutoring center.
sc: W: Hello, this is Rosa from the Tutoring Center, calling for Hamza.

W: Please bring your math book and the homework you want to work on. If you can't come at three, please call me back at five five five, oh one two three. Or you can send an email to the center.
W: I hope to hear from you soon. Goodbye.

la-ps004.x: Listen to an announcement at a bookstore.
sc: W: Welcome to the University Bookstore. Please listen to some news about our special sale.
W: This week, all notebooks and pens are twenty percent cheaper. If you buy three notebooks, you will get a free pen. The sale ends on Sunday.
W: We also have a table of used textbooks near the door. These books cost half the price of new books, but they go quickly, so come early.
W: If you pay with a student card, you can get a small discount on everything. The store is open from nine to six every day. Thank you for shopping with us.

la-ps005.x: Listen to an announcement from an environmental science professor.
sc: W: Hello, everyone. I have some changes to share about the stream study project.

W: We were going to collect water samples this Saturday, but the forecast shows heavy rain, and the stream will be too high to enter safely. We will collect the samples next Saturday instead, at the same time and place.
W: This delay actually helps us. Since we will have a week of data about rainfall, we can compare the samples to the amount of rain. So please keep a record of the rain in your own neighborhood.
W: You can use a simple cup and a ruler. Bring your record to class on Monday, and we will combine everyone's numbers.

la-ps006.x: Listen to a phone message asking for research volunteers.
sc: M: Hi, this is Kenji from the Language Learning Lab. We are looking for students who speak Spanish as their first language.

M: Our study looks at how people learn English pronunciation. If you join, you will listen to short English sentences through headphones and repeat them into a microphone. Then we will ask you to read a short story aloud.
M: The session takes about forty-five minutes and is held in the Humanities Building. We pay fifteen dollars in cash at the end.
M: We have openings every weekday afternoon next week. Please reply to this message with the day you prefer, and I'll confirm the time.

la-ps007.x: Listen to a notice on a museum tour.
sc: W: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining the Heritage House tour. This house was built in eighteen ninety and was once the home of a wealthy merchant family.
W: The tour lasts about an hour. We will begin in the kitchen, then visit the dining room and the library on the ground floor, and finish in the bedrooms upstairs.
W: Please do not touch the furniture or the wallpaper, as they are very old. Photographs are allowed, but without flash. The upstairs rooms are narrow, so groups will go up in two parts.
W: If you need a rest, there are benches in the garden. Questions are welcome at any time.

la-ps008.x: Listen to a safety announcement for a science laboratory.
sc: M: Welcome to the first meeting of Chemistry Lab. Before we begin, I need to explain the safety rules.

M: First, wear goggles and a lab coat at all times. Long hair must be tied back, and open shoes are not allowed. If your clothes are not suitable, you will be asked to leave and come back for the next session.
M: Second, never taste or smell chemicals directly. If you need to smell something, wave the air toward your face with your hand.
M: Finally, if an accident happens, tell me immediately. Do not try to hide it, even if it seems small. A quick report keeps everyone safe.

la-ps009.x: Listen to an announcement from an economics professor.
sc: M: Before we end, a word about the group presentations. I've seen the proposals, and most of you chose famous companies. That's understandable, but it's not what I had hoped for.

M: A company everyone knows is a company everyone has opinions about, which makes it difficult to say anything new. I'd encourage you to consider a small local business, because there you can interview the owner and collect your own data.
M: I won't force anyone to change. Groups that stay with a famous company can do so, but I'll expect a clearer argument from them, since the information is so easy to find.
M: Send me your final choice by Friday, and I'll confirm it.

la-ps010.x: Listen to a message from a museum volunteer coordinator.
sc: W: Hello, this is Elena from the Natural History Museum, calling about your volunteer application.
W: We were pleased to read about your experience as a teaching assistant. Our difficulty is that our weekend positions, which are the ones most students prefer, are already filled for this season.

W: What we do have are openings on weekday mornings, working with school groups. The hours are less convenient, but the work is more interesting, since you would lead the activity tables yourself rather than only directing visitors.
W: If you think you could manage that, please tell me by Wednesday, and we can set up an orientation.

la-ps011.x: Listen to an announcement about a campus bridge renovation.
sc: M: This is a notice for everyone who crosses the footbridge between the science and arts buildings. Some of you may have thought it would stay open during the renovation. I'm sorry to say that won't be possible.
M: The bridge will be closed from the fifteenth of May to the end of August. The old surface needs to be removed entirely, and the workers can't do that safely with people walking above.
M: A path along the river will be marked as an alternative. It adds about ten minutes, so those with classes in both buildings should allow extra time in the fall.
M: On a positive note, the new bridge will be wider and will include a space for bicycles.

la-ps012.x: Listen to a talk by a tour leader before a cave visit.
sc: W: Before we go underground, here is what to expect. The cave stays at about twelve degrees all year, so it will feel cold in summer and mild in winter. Most of you are dressed correctly, but a few might regret leaving sweaters in the bus.

W: The passage is narrow in places, and the ceiling is low. Anyone who is nervous in enclosed spaces should speak to me now, not halfway through. There is no shame in that, and our visitor center has a model of the cave with a film.
W: I'll also ask you to stay behind me. The stones are slippery, and the formations take thousands of years to grow, so even a gentle touch can leave a permanent mark.

la-ts001.x: Listen to an announcement in a biology class.
sc: W: Good morning, everyone. This is an announcement for students in Biology one oh one.

W: The lab will still start at ten o'clock, and the topic stays the same. You will study plant cells under the microscope.
W: Please bring your lab notebook and wear closed shoes. If you cannot find the new room, ask at the front desk of the Science Building.

la-ts002.x: Listen to an announcement about library hours.

M: If you need to return a book while we are closed, please use the blue box outside the main door. Thank you, and have a good week.

la-ts003.x: Listen to a voicemail message from a dentist's office.

la-ts004.x: Listen to an announcement about a campus event.

la-ts005.x: Listen to an announcement in a residence hall.

la-ts006.x: Listen to an announcement about a final exam.

la-ts021.x: Listen to an announcement in a history class.

M: Also, please move any boxes away from the radiators so the worker can reach them. Thank you for your help, and have a pleasant day.

lt-ts031.x: Listen to part of a talk in a chemistry class.
sc: W: Today I want to talk about catalysts, which are substances that speed up a chemical reaction without being used up by it.

W: To understand how they work, think about activation energy. Even when a reaction releases energy overall, the molecules first need a certain amount of energy to get started. You can picture it as a hill that the reactants have to climb before they can roll down the other side.

W: A catalyst doesn't make the hill disappear, and it doesn't change how much energy is released at the end. What it does is offer a different path, one with a lower hill. So at the same temperature, many more molecules have enough energy to react, and the reaction goes faster.

W: Here's an everyday example. Hydrogen peroxide, the kind people keep in a medicine cabinet, breaks down into water and oxygen very slowly on its own. But if you put it on a cut, it fizzes right away. That's because an enzyme in your blood and tissue called catalase acts as a catalyst.

W: And because a catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged, a small amount can be used again and again. That's one reason industry relies on catalysts so heavily. Most large-scale chemical production depends on them at some stage.
W: Next time, we'll look at why enzymes are so selective about which reactions they speed up.

lt-ts032.x: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.
sc: M: Let's turn to the tiny pores on the surface of a leaf, called stomata. A single leaf can have thousands of them, and in many plants they're found mostly on the underside.

M: Stomata solve a problem that every land plant faces. To make food through photosynthesis, a plant has to take in carbon dioxide from the air. But whenever a pore opens to let carbon dioxide in, water vapor escapes through it. So every opening is a kind of trade: carbon in, water out.

M: Each pore is surrounded by two guard cells, shaped a bit like a pair of beans. When the plant has plenty of water, the guard cells fill up, swell and bend apart, and the pore opens. When water is scarce, they lose pressure, go limp, and the pore closes.
M: That's why many plants close their stomata in the hottest part of a dry afternoon. They're giving up some photosynthesis to avoid wilting.

M: Some desert plants, cacti for example, go even further. They keep their stomata shut during the day and open them at night, when it's cooler and the air is more humid, so they lose far less water. They store the carbon dioxide overnight and use it for photosynthesis once the sun comes up.
M: It's a clever arrangement, though it does come at a cost. These plants tend to grow quite slowly.

lt-ts033.x: Listen to part of a lecture in an economic history class.
sc: W: In July of nineteen forty-four, representatives from forty-four countries met at a hotel in Bretton Woods, a small town in New Hampshire. Their goal was to design a stable system for international money. Many of them remembered the nineteen thirties, when countries kept lowering the value of their currencies to sell more goods abroad, and trade between nations shrank.

W: The plan they agreed on worked like this. Each country fixed the value of its currency to the US dollar, and the dollar itself was tied to gold, at thirty-five dollars an ounce. Foreign governments could, in principle, swap their dollars for American gold at that price.
W: The conference also created two institutions: the International Monetary Fund, which could lend to countries having trouble keeping their exchange rate fixed, and what we now call the World Bank.

W: For about twenty-five years, the system gave businesses predictable exchange rates. But there was a weakness built into it. As the world economy grew, more and more dollars circulated abroad, far more than the gold the United States held. Other countries started to doubt that every dollar could really be exchanged for gold.
W: In nineteen seventy-one, the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold, and within a couple of years the major currencies were floating, meaning their values were set by markets.
W: So the Bretton Woods system didn't last, but its institutions did. Both are still operating today.

lt-ts034.x: Listen to part of a talk in a sociology class.
sc: M: Today's topic is an idea from the sociologist Mark Granovetter, who published a famous paper in nineteen seventy-three called The Strength of Weak Ties.

M: First, some terms. Your strong ties are the people you're close to, like family and best friends. Weak ties are acquaintances, people you know but don't see very often, like a former classmate or someone from an old job.

M: Now, you'd probably expect your close friends to be the most helpful people in your life, and in many ways they are. But Granovetter interviewed people who had recently changed jobs, and he found that many of them had heard about the new job through a weak tie, not a strong one.

M: Why would that be? Think about who your close friends are. They tend to know each other, go to the same places and hear the same news. So the information they have is mostly information you already have. An acquaintance, on the other hand, moves in a different circle. They're a bridge to people and news you'd never reach otherwise.
M: So the strength of a weak tie isn't emotional. It's about access to new information.
M: This idea has been very influential. It's shaped research on how new ideas and products spread through a community, and we'll come back to it later in the course.

lt-ts035.x: Listen to part of a talk in an architecture class.
sc: W: When you walk into a Gothic cathedral, the first thing most people notice is the light. Huge windows of stained glass fill the walls. But that light was really an engineering problem, and today I want to explain how builders solved it.

W: A stone roof, or vault, is extremely heavy. And its weight doesn't just press straight down. It also pushes outward, against the tops of the walls. If nothing resists that sideways push, the walls lean out and the vault falls in.
W: Earlier Romanesque churches dealt with this the simple way: very thick walls with small windows. Cut a big hole in a wall like that, and you weaken it exactly where it needs to be strong.

W: Gothic builders, starting in France in the twelfth century, moved much of the support outside the building. A flying buttress is a stone arm, a kind of half arch, that reaches from the upper wall out to a massive pier standing apart from the church. The arm catches the outward push of the vault and carries it down through the pier into the ground.
W: Once the walls no longer had to carry all that load, they could be thinner and opened up with glass. In a sense, the windows were possible because the support had been moved outdoors.
W: Some people find buttresses ugly, like scaffolding nobody bothered to take down. I'd say they're honest. They show you exactly how the building stands up.

lt-ts036.x: Listen to part of a talk in a film studies class.
sc: M: In film editing there's a famous principle named after Lev Kuleshov, a Russian filmmaker and teacher who was working around nineteen twenty.

M: As the story is usually told, Kuleshov took a close-up of a well-known actor with a completely neutral face. He then cut that same shot together with different images. In one version, the face was followed by a bowl of soup. In another, by a child playing.

M: Audiences who saw these short sequences reportedly praised the actor's performance. They said he looked hungry when he faced the soup and tender when he looked at the child. But it was the identical shot every time. The emotion wasn't in the face. Viewers created it from the combination.

M: Now, I should be careful here. Kuleshov's original film hasn't survived, so we can't check exactly what he did, and modern attempts to repeat the experiment have had mixed results. The effect seems real, but it's probably weaker than the legend suggests.
M: Still, the lesson changed filmmaking. It showed that meaning in cinema comes not only from what's inside a shot, but from how shots are placed next to each other.
M: Editors use this all the time. A reaction shot of someone's face can make an ordinary line of dialogue seem funny or threatening, depending on what comes right before it.

lt-ts037.x: Listen to part of a talk in an education class.
sc: W: Today let's look at a classroom method called the jigsaw technique. It was developed in the early nineteen seventies by the psychologist Elliot Aronson and his colleagues, in schools in Austin, Texas.

W: The schools had recently been integrated, and classrooms brought together students from different backgrounds for the first time. Teachers noticed a lot of tension, and Aronson thought part of the problem was the classroom itself. Students competed for the teacher's attention, so one student's success often felt like another's loss.

W: Here's how jigsaw works. Say the lesson is about a famous person's life. The class is split into groups of five or six, and each student in a group gets one part of the story, say, childhood or early career. Next, students with the same part meet in an expert group to master it. Then everyone goes back to their home group and teaches their piece.

W: Notice what this does. No one can understand the whole lesson without listening to every member. Even a shy student, or someone the others usually ignore, suddenly holds information the group needs.
W: Studies of jigsaw classrooms reported that students came to like each other more, and that their learning was at least as good as in traditional lessons.
W: It does take careful planning, though. The teacher has to divide the material into fair pieces and prepare all of it in advance.

lt-ts038.x: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.
sc: M: Today's method is dendrochronology, or tree-ring dating. It's one of the most precise dating tools archaeologists have.

M: In places with clear seasons, a tree adds one growth ring each year. And the rings aren't all the same width. In many regions, a year with plenty of rain produces a wide ring, and a dry year produces a narrow one. So trees growing in the same area at the same time record the same pattern, something like a barcode of wide and narrow rings.

M: Here's the clever part. Start with a living tree, where you know the exact year of every ring. Now take an old wooden beam. If the beam's last rings match the pattern in the tree's earliest rings, you can line the two up and extend your record back in time. Repeat this with older and older pieces of wood, and you build a continuous calendar going back centuries, in some places thousands of years.

M: The method was developed in the American Southwest in the early twentieth century by an astronomer, A. E. Douglass. He was originally interested in climate, but his records ended up dating ancient villages in the region.

M: There's one limit to keep in mind. Tree rings tell you when a tree was cut down, not necessarily when a building went up. People sometimes reused old beams. So archaeologists date many beams from a site before drawing conclusions.

lt-ts039.x: Listen to part of a talk in an oceanography class.
sc: W: Most ocean currents you've heard of, the ones near the surface, are pushed along mainly by wind. But there's another, much slower circulation that reaches all the way down to the sea floor. It's called thermohaline circulation. Thermo for heat, haline for salt.
W: The key idea is density. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. And dense water sinks.

W: So let's go to the North Atlantic, near Greenland. Surface water arriving from the south loses heat to the cold air and gets colder. On top of that, when sea ice forms, the ice is mostly fresh. The salt is left behind in the water around it. Now you have water that is both cold and salty, and it sinks, thousands of meters down.

W: That deep water then creeps southward along the bottom of the ocean, and over a very long time it spreads into other ocean basins and slowly rises back toward the surface. Estimates vary, but a full trip around this system may take something like a thousand years.
W: People sometimes call it a conveyor belt. That's a useful picture, as long as you remember that the real system is much messier, with lots of branches and swirls.
W: Why does it matter? Because the water moving north near the surface carries heat with it, it helps keep parts of the North Atlantic region milder than they would otherwise be.

lt-ts040.x: Listen to part of a talk in a zoology class.
sc: M: Today we're looking at one of the fastest color changers in the animal world, the cuttlefish. It's a relative of the octopus and the squid, and it can change the color and pattern of its skin in well under a second.

M: How does it do that? The skin is packed with tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, in colors like yellow, red and brown. Each sac is surrounded by a ring of small muscles, and those muscles are controlled directly by nerves from the brain.

M: When the muscles contract, they pull the sac open, a bit like stretching a balloon flat, and the color spreads out. When they relax, the sac shrinks back to a tiny dot you can barely see. Because nerves and muscles are doing the work, the change is extremely fast. Compare that to a chameleon, which changes color far more slowly.

M: Underneath the chromatophores are other layers of cells that reflect light, producing shimmering blues and greens or a bright white. Cuttlefish can even raise small bumps on their skin to copy the texture of rocks or seaweed.

M: Now here's the puzzle. Behavioral tests suggest that cuttlefish are colorblind. Their eyes seem to have only one type of light receptor. Yet they match their surroundings remarkably well. How they manage it is still an open question, and honestly, it's one of my favorite mysteries in biology.

lt-ts041.x: Listen to part of a talk in a meteorology class.
sc: W: If you've ever spent a summer day at the beach, you may have noticed that around midday or early afternoon a cool wind starts blowing in from the water. That's a sea breeze, and it's a nice small-scale example of how pressure differences create wind.

W: It starts with the fact that land and water heat up differently. On a sunny morning, the land warms quickly. Water warms much more slowly. It takes a lot of energy to raise its temperature, and the heat gets mixed down into deeper layers.

W: So by late morning, the air over the land is noticeably warmer. Warm air expands and rises, and that leaves slightly lower pressure near the ground over land. Over the sea, the air is cooler and denser, so the pressure there is higher. Air moves from higher pressure toward lower pressure, and there's your breeze, flowing from the sea onto the land.
W: At night, the whole thing runs in reverse. The land cools off faster than the water, so the air flows from the land out to sea. We call that a land breeze, and it's usually weaker.

W: Sea breezes can do more than cool people on the beach. Where the cool sea air pushes in under the warm air inland, it forces that warm air upward, and that can set off afternoon thunderstorms. Florida is a classic place to see this on many summer days.

lt-ts042.x: Listen to part of a talk in a chemistry class.
sc: M: Let's talk about buffers, and let's use the most important example there is, your own blood.

M: Blood has to stay within a very narrow pH range, about seven point three five to seven point four five, so just slightly basic. Move much outside that range and enzymes and other proteins stop working properly. Yet your cells are constantly producing acids as they work. So something has to absorb those changes.

M: That something is a buffer: a mixture of a weak acid and a related base that together resist changes in pH. In blood, the main pair is carbonic acid and bicarbonate. If extra acid enters the blood, bicarbonate picks up the hydrogen ions and becomes carbonic acid. If the blood becomes too basic, carbonic acid releases hydrogen ions. Either way, the pH barely moves.

M: What makes this system especially effective is that it's connected to your lungs. Carbonic acid can break down into water and carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide you can simply breathe out. So when acid builds up, say during hard exercise, you breathe faster and get rid of more of it.
M: The kidneys help too, by removing acid and holding on to bicarbonate, but they're slower. They work over hours or days, while breathing adjusts within minutes.
M: So a buffer isn't a single chemical. It's a balanced partnership, and in the body it's backed up by organs.

lt-ts043.x: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.
sc: W: When we picture a plant taking up water and nutrients, we usually think of roots. But for most land plants, that picture is incomplete. Roughly eighty percent or more of plant species form partnerships with fungi in the soil. These partnerships are called mycorrhizae, which literally means fungus roots.

W: Here's how the deal works. The fungus grows extremely thin threads, much finer than the finest roots, and they spread through a huge volume of soil. They're very good at collecting water and minerals, especially phosphorus, which tends to stay locked in place and is hard for roots to reach. The fungus passes these nutrients on to the plant.

W: In return, the plant gives the fungus sugars it makes through photosynthesis. The fungus can't make its own food, so this is how it survives. And it's not a small payment. A plant may send a significant share of its sugars underground.

W: This relationship is very old. Some of the earliest fossils of land plants, around four hundred million years old, already show fungi living in their tissues. Some researchers think plants might not have managed to move onto land without these partners.

W: You may have heard the phrase wood wide web, the idea that trees use fungal networks to share food and even warn each other. Fungal networks connecting trees do exist, but some of the bigger claims go beyond the evidence. I'd treat them with caution for now.

lt-ts044.x: Listen to part of a lecture in an economic history class.
sc: M: Today let's go to eleventh-century China, to the region of Sichuan, because that's where the world's first government-issued paper money appeared.

M: Why there? Sichuan used iron coins, and iron coins weren't worth much individually, so they were terribly heavy for large purchases. Picture a merchant needing a cart full of coins just to buy a load of silk. Not very practical.

M: So merchants started leaving their coins with trusted deposit shops, and in exchange they got paper receipts. These receipts, called jiaozi, could be passed from person to person, and people began to treat the paper itself as money.

M: The problem was that some shops issued more receipts than they had coins to back them up, and when they couldn't pay, people lost their savings. So in the early ten twenties, the government stepped in and took over issuing the notes itself, with official limits on how many could be printed.

M: It worked for a while. Later, though, governments in China, facing heavy expenses, printed more and more notes, and their value fell sharply. That's an early example of what we'd now call inflation.
M: When the traveler Marco Polo visited China in the thirteenth century, he wrote about paper money with real amazement. In Europe at that time, money still meant metal coins.

lt-ts045.x: Listen to part of a talk in a sociology class.
sc: W: When people hear the word bureaucracy today, they usually think of long lines, endless forms and rules that make no sense. But for the German sociologist Max Weber, writing in the early twentieth century, bureaucracy was a serious subject, and in many ways an impressive one.

W: Weber described what he called an ideal type of bureaucracy. Now, ideal here doesn't mean perfect or desirable. It means a simplified model that captures the key features, so we can compare real organizations against it.

W: And what are those features? There's a clear hierarchy, where everyone knows who reports to whom. Work is divided into specialized jobs. Decisions follow written rules, and everything is recorded. People are hired and promoted for their qualifications, not because they're someone's cousin. And the rules apply to everyone in the same way.

W: Compare that with older forms of organization, where positions often went to relatives or favorites, and decisions could depend on a ruler's mood. Weber argued that bureaucracy was more efficient, more predictable and fairer than those systems.

W: But he was also worried. He feared that as more and more of life became organized this way, people might end up trapped by rules and efficiency, a situation that's often translated into English as an iron cage.
W: So Weber was neither simply a fan nor simply a critic of bureaucracy.

lt-ts046.x: Listen to part of a talk in an architecture class.
sc: M: Let's look at one of the most remarkable buildings to survive from ancient Rome, the Pantheon. The version we see today was completed in the second century, under the emperor Hadrian, and its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, about forty-three meters across.

M: Unreinforced means there's no steel inside. Modern concrete structures depend on steel bars to resist cracking. The Romans had nothing like that, so how has this dome stayed up for nearly nineteen hundred years?
M: Part of the answer is the material. Roman concrete was made with lime and volcanic ash, which produced a strong, durable binder. But the more interesting part is how the builders managed weight.

M: Near the bottom of the dome, they used heavy stone in the concrete mix. As they went higher, they switched to lighter and lighter materials, ending with a light volcanic rock called pumice near the top. The dome is also much thicker at its base than at its crown. And the inside surface is covered with sunken square panels, called coffers, which remove even more weight.

M: Then, at the very top, there's no concrete at all, just an open circle, the oculus, about eight or nine meters wide, letting in light. Leaving out the center of a dome, where extra weight would cause the most trouble, is actually a smart structural choice.
M: The result is a structure that's heavy where it needs strength and light where weight would be a problem.

lt-ts047.x: Listen to part of a talk in a film history class.
sc: W: In nineteen twenty-seven, audiences watching The Jazz Singer heard something new: the actor Al Jolson singing and speaking in sync with his image on the screen. The film was actually mostly silent, with title cards, but those few minutes of synchronized songs and talk caused a sensation. Within just a few years, most Hollywood studios had switched to sound.
W: You might assume this was pure progress. In some ways, though, early sound films took a step backward.

W: Think about the cameras. They were noisy machines, and the new microphones picked up every whirring sound. The solution was to put the camera and its operator inside a soundproof booth. That worked for the sound, but a camera in a heavy box can barely move. Many late silent films had used elegant camera movement, and suddenly that was gone.

W: Microphones created problems too. They were often hidden in flower vases or lamps on the set, and actors had to stay near them and speak carefully. So a lot of early talkies feel stiff and stagey, almost like filmed plays.

W: The fix came within a few years. Engineers built quieter, insulated cases for cameras, and microphones were mounted on long poles, called booms, that could follow the actors. Movement returned to the screen.
W: So the story of sound isn't a straight line. It's a big leap forward that briefly made filmmaking lose skills it had already mastered.

lt-ts048.x: Listen to part of a talk in an education class.
sc: M: Let's talk about Maria Montessori, who was one of the first women to qualify as a doctor in Italy. In nineteen oh seven, she opened a school for young children in a poor neighborhood of Rome, and the approach she developed there is now used in thousands of schools around the world.

M: What made it different? First, the classroom itself. In those days, children often sat in rows at fixed desks. Montessori brought in small, light furniture that children could move themselves, and shelves low enough for them to reach materials on their own.

M: Second, the materials. Many of them are designed so that the child can tell if a mistake has been made. A good example is a wooden block with holes of different sizes and a set of cylinders. Each cylinder fits only one hole. If a child puts one in the wrong place, there'll be a cylinder left over at the end. The child sees the error and tries again, without an adult pointing it out.
M: Third, the role of the teacher. Instead of lecturing the whole class, the teacher observes, introduces materials to individual children, and lets them choose what to work on.

M: Montessori based these ideas on careful observation. She watched how children actually behaved, and she noticed they could concentrate for long periods on tasks they'd chosen themselves. Modern research on her method has produced mixed results, but some studies have found real benefits.

lt-ts049.x: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.
sc: W: Today I want to introduce one of the most basic ideas in archaeology. It actually came from geology, from a seventeenth-century scientist named Nicolaus Steno. It's called the law of superposition.

W: The idea is simple. When layers of soil or rock build up, each new layer is laid down on top of the ones already there. So, as long as nothing has disturbed them, the deeper a layer is, the older it is.

W: For archaeologists, that's extremely useful. Think of a site where people lived for centuries. Floors, ashes from fires, broken pots, all of these get buried, and new layers form on top. When we dig down carefully, we're moving backward in time.
W: Notice, though, that this gives us relative dates, not exact ones. It tells us that one layer is older than another, but not by how many years. For that, we need other methods.

W: And there's a catch: as long as nothing has disturbed them. People dig pits, wells and foundations. Animals burrow. A pit dug in a later period can carry newer objects deep down into older layers. If you don't notice the edges of that pit, you could badly misdate what you find.
W: That's why excavators record every layer so carefully as they dig. Excavation destroys the very layers we're studying. Once a site is dug, there's no going back to check.

lt-ts050.x: Listen to part of a talk in an oceanography class.
sc: M: Today we're looking at coastal upwelling, which explains why some of the richest fishing waters on Earth are found off coasts like Peru and California.

M: Here's the setup. Along these coasts, winds often blow parallel to the shore, toward the equator. You'd think the wind would just push the surface water along the coast. But because of Earth's rotation, the moving surface water is turned to one side, and it ends up flowing away from the shore, out to sea.
M: Now, that water has to be replaced by something. So cold water rises up from below to take its place. That's upwelling.

M: Why does that matter so much? Deep water is full of nutrients, things like nitrates and phosphates, from dead organisms that sank and broke down. Near the surface, where there's sunlight, those nutrients feed huge blooms of tiny drifting plants called phytoplankton. Those feed small animals, which feed fish like anchovies, and so on up the food chain.
M: Upwelling zones cover only a tiny part of the ocean's surface, but they produce a remarkably large share of the world's fish catch.

M: They're also sensitive. During an El Nino event, the winds off South America weaken and warm water spreads east. Upwelling off Peru weakens, fewer nutrients reach the surface, and the anchovy catch can fall dramatically. For local fishing communities, that's a serious problem.

lt-ts051.x: Listen to part of a talk in a zoology class.
sc: W: Here's a puzzle. A duck can stand on ice for a long time, or paddle in nearly freezing water, and yet it doesn't lose a dangerous amount of body heat through its feet. Its feet have no feathers, so how does it manage that?

W: The answer is a system called countercurrent heat exchange. In the duck's legs, the arteries carrying warm blood down to the feet run right alongside the veins carrying cold blood back up to the body. The two flows move in opposite directions, which is where the name countercurrent comes from.

W: As the warm blood flows down, it passes its heat to the cold blood flowing up next to it. So by the time it reaches the feet, it's already quite cool, and there's little heat left to lose to the ice. Meanwhile, the returning blood has been warmed back up before it reaches the body's core.

W: The key is the opposite direction. If both flows ran the same way, they'd quickly reach the same in-between temperature and the exchange would stop. Running them in opposite directions keeps a temperature difference all along the way, so heat keeps moving.
W: The feet stay cold, just above freezing, but that's fine. The tissues there are adapted to low temperatures.

W: You'll find the same arrangement in many animals: in the flippers of dolphins, in the legs of wading birds, and even in some fast-swimming fish, which use it to keep their muscles warmer than the surrounding water.

lt-ts052.x: Listen to part of a talk in a meteorology class.
sc: M: People are often surprised that hail is most common in late spring and summer, not winter. It's ice, after all. But hail doesn't depend on cold weather at the ground. It depends on thunderstorms, and especially on their updrafts, the powerful currents of rising air inside them.

M: Here's how a hailstone grows. High up in a thunderstorm cloud, temperatures are well below freezing, but many of the water droplets there are still liquid. We call that supercooled water. When a small ice particle is carried up through this region, the supercooled droplets freeze onto it the moment they touch it. Layer by layer, it grows.

M: And it can keep growing as long as the updraft holds it up. In some storms, a stone moves up and down through different parts of the cloud several times. That's why, if you cut a large hailstone in half, you often see rings, a bit like an onion. Some layers are clear and some are cloudy white, depending on how quickly the water froze.
M: Eventually, the stone gets too heavy for the rising air to support, and it falls.

M: So the size of hail tells you something about the storm. Small, pea-sized hail can form in fairly ordinary storms. But stones the size of golf balls or larger need extremely strong updrafts. That's one reason forecasters watch updraft strength so closely.

lt-ts053.x: Listen to part of a talk in a chemistry class.
sc: W: Why does toast taste so different from plain bread? Or a seared steak from a boiled one? Much of the answer is a set of chemical reactions named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described them in the early nineteen hundreds.

W: The Maillard reaction happens between amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and certain sugars. When food containing both is heated, they react and produce brown colors and literally hundreds of new flavor and aroma molecules. That's the smell of baking bread, roasting coffee, or onions frying in a pan.

W: Temperature matters a great deal. The reaction is slow at low temperatures, and it speeds up dramatically once the surface of the food gets well above the boiling point of water, roughly a hundred and forty degrees Celsius and higher.

W: And that explains something cooks have always known. Boiled meat doesn't brown. As long as water is present, the surface can't get much hotter than a hundred degrees. That's also why cooks pat meat dry before searing it. The surface moisture has to evaporate before browning can really begin.

W: People often confuse this with caramelization, but they're not the same. Caramelization involves sugar alone breaking down under heat. The Maillard reaction needs the building blocks of protein as well.
W: So the next time you brown something in a pan, you're running a small chemistry experiment.

lt-ts054.x: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.
sc: M: If you've kept a plant on a windowsill, you've probably noticed it leaning toward the glass. Plants bend toward light, and this is called phototropism. What's interesting is how scientists figured out the mechanism, because some of the first important experiments were done by Charles Darwin, with help from his son Francis.

M: In the late eighteen hundreds, the Darwins worked with young grass seedlings, which grow a pointed shoot. When light came from one side, the shoots bent toward it. But the bend happened a little below the tip. So the Darwins tried covering different parts.

M: When they covered just the tip with a small cap that blocked light, the seedling didn't bend. When they left the tip uncovered and shaded the part lower down, where the bending actually happens, it still bent. So the tip was sensing the light, but a lower region was doing the bending. The Darwins concluded that some kind of influence must travel down from the tip.
