M: They didn't know what that influence was. In the nineteen twenties, other researchers identified a chemical messenger, a plant hormone now called auxin.

M: Here's what auxin does. When light comes from one side, auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot. Cells on that side grow longer than cells on the lit side, and the uneven growth bends the shoot toward the light.
M: It's a nice example of a careful experiment answering one question and opening up another.

lt-ts055.x: Listen to part of a lecture in an economic history class.
sc: W: Today we're going to look at an unusual kind of economic power, the Hanseatic League, which shaped trade in northern Europe from roughly the thirteenth to the sixteenth century.

W: The first thing to understand is that the Hansa wasn't a country. It had no king and no permanent government. It was a loose network of merchant groups and trading towns, eventually many dozens of them, with the port of Lubeck as its leading city. Representatives met from time to time to agree on common rules, but attendance was irregular, and decisions weren't always followed.

W: So what held it together? Mainly shared interests. Merchants traveling alone faced pirates, unfamiliar laws and local rulers who might seize their goods. By acting together, Hanseatic merchants could win trading privileges, such as lower taxes, and protect each other.

W: They also set up permanent trading posts abroad, in places like London, Bruges, Bergen in Norway and Novgorod in Russia. In Bergen, for instance, Hanseatic merchants bought dried fish from the north and supplied grain in return.
W: The goods themselves were mostly everyday bulk items: grain, timber, salt, fish, furs, wax and cloth. Not glamorous, but essential.

W: By the sixteenth century, the League was in decline. Stronger national states, competition from Dutch and English traders, and the growth of Atlantic trade all reduced its importance. A network built on shared interests was hard to hold together once those interests began to differ.

lt-ts056.x: Listen to part of a talk in a sociology class.
sc: M: In the nineteen twenties, sociologists at the University of Chicago treated their own city as a giant laboratory. Chicago had grown incredibly fast, and they wanted to understand how a modern city organizes itself.

M: One of the best-known results is Ernest Burgess's concentric zone model, from nineteen twenty-five. Burgess pictured the city as a series of rings, like a target. At the center is the business district, with offices and department stores. Around it is what he called the zone in transition, with factories and older, crowded housing, often the first stop for newly arrived immigrants. Farther out come zones of working-class homes, then middle-class neighborhoods, and finally a commuter zone at the edge.

M: Burgess borrowed ideas from ecology, the study of how living things compete for space. As the center expands, he argued, it pushes into the next ring. Groups who can afford to move outward do so, and new groups take their place. He compared this to the way one plant community gradually replaces another in a field.

M: The model was hugely influential, partly because it was so simple. But critics soon pointed out problems. It was based on one city, and Chicago itself, sitting on a lake, forms more of a half circle. Other cities grew along railway lines or around several centers, not neatly in rings.
M: Still, even its critics used it as a starting point. Later models were largely built by asking where Burgess went wrong.

lt-ts057.x: Listen to part of a talk in an architecture class.
sc: W: Today let's look at a building feature that kept people cool long before air conditioning: the windcatcher. Some of the most famous examples are in the desert city of Yazd, in Iran, where tall towers rise above the rooftops.

W: A windcatcher is basically a tower with openings near the top. Why put the openings up high? Because wind near the ground is slowed down by buildings and walls. A few meters up, the air moves faster, and it's often cleaner and less dusty too.

W: When the wind blows, it enters the openings facing it and is directed down a shaft into the rooms below. That moving air pushes warmer indoor air out through windows or doorways. So you get a steady breeze through the house.

W: But here's the clever part. Even on a still day, the tower can work. The sun heats the air inside the tower, that warm air rises and escapes from the top, and that draws air through the house below. It's the same principle as a chimney.

W: Some buildings went further, by sending the incoming air over a pool of water or through an underground channel first. As some of the water evaporates, it cools the air before it reaches the rooms.
W: These ideas aren't just history. Modern architects are studying windcatchers again, because they cool buildings without using any electricity.

lt-ts058.x: Listen to part of a talk in a film studies class.
sc: M: In most films, the camera keeps only part of the image sharp. A face in the foreground is crisp, and the background is a soft blur. That's a choice, and it tells you where to look. Today I want to talk about a technique that does the opposite, called deep focus.

M: In deep focus, objects close to the camera, in the middle, and far in the background are all sharp at the same time. The most famous example is Citizen Kane, from nineteen forty-one, directed by Orson Welles and shot by the cinematographer Gregg Toland.

M: Getting that look wasn't easy. Toland used wide-angle lenses, very bright lighting and a small lens opening, which increases the range of distances that stay in focus. He wasn't the first to use deep focus, but he pushed it further than almost anyone before him.

M: Think of the scene where the young Charles Kane is playing outside in the snow. We see him through a window, far in the background, while in the foreground the adults sign papers that will change his life. Both are sharp, and nothing is cut. We understand that his future is being decided without him, all in one shot.

M: The French critic Andre Bazin admired this approach. He argued that deep focus respects the viewer, because instead of an editor deciding what you notice, you're free to look around the frame and make connections yourself.
M: Of course, not every director agreed that this freedom was always a good thing.

lt-ts059.x: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.
sc: W: When archaeologists want to know what a landscape looked like thousands of years ago, one of their best sources is something you can't even see without a microscope: pollen.

W: Pollen grains have an extremely tough outer wall. In places where there's little oxygen, like the mud at the bottom of a lake or a peat bog, they can survive for thousands of years. And each kind of plant produces pollen with its own shape. Under a microscope, an expert can tell oak from pine, or wild grasses from cereal crops.

W: So researchers drill a long tube, called a core, down into the lake bed or the bog. The layers at the bottom are the oldest, and the ones at the top are the most recent. By counting pollen types in each layer, they can track how the plant life around the site changed over time.

W: Here's the kind of thing they find. In many parts of Europe, cores show a point where tree pollen drops sharply while pollen from grasses and cereal crops goes up. That pattern is usually read as people clearing forest to plant fields. So pollen can reveal the spread of farming even where no farm buildings have survived.

W: One complication: wind-pollinated plants, like pine, release huge amounts of pollen, while plants pollinated by insects release very little. So a simple count would exaggerate some plants and miss others. Researchers have to correct for that before they draw a picture of the past landscape.

lt-ts060.x: Listen to part of a talk in a zoology class.
sc: M: When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it often flies back to the hive and recruits its nestmates. But how does it tell them where to go? The answer came largely from the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who later shared a Nobel Prize for this work.

M: Von Frisch found that the returning bee performs what's called the waggle dance. On the vertical surface of the honeycomb, the bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side. Then it circles back and repeats the run, again and again, tracing something like a figure eight.

M: The direction of that straight run is the key. Inside the dark hive, straight up on the comb stands for the direction of the sun. So if the bee runs straight up, the flowers are toward the sun. If it runs at an angle forty degrees to the right of vertical, the flowers are forty degrees to the right of the sun.
M: And distance? That's coded in how long the waggling run lasts. A longer run means the food is farther away.

M: Some scientists were skeptical at first. Maybe the other bees just followed the smell of flowers on the dancer's body. But later studies, including ones that tracked recruited bees with radar, showed that they really do fly in the direction the dance indicates.
M: So the bees translate a direction relative to the sun into a direction relative to gravity. That is remarkable for an insect brain.

lt-ts061.x: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
sc: W: Today I want to look at a question neuroscientists still argue about: do adult human brains keep making new neurons? For most of the twentieth century, the textbook answer was no. You were born with all the neurons you'd ever have.

W: That view began to crack in the nineteen sixties, when researchers found new neurons forming in the hippocampus of adult rats, and later in songbirds and monkeys. The hippocampus, remember, is important for forming new memories.
W: Then, in the late nineteen nineties, a study of human brain tissue found signs of new cells in the adult hippocampus too. Many people took that as settling the matter.

W: But it didn't. In two thousand eighteen, one team examined human brain samples and reported that new neurons became extremely rare after childhood. That same year, another group looked at similar tissue and concluded that healthy older adults still produce them.

W: So how can two careful teams reach opposite conclusions? Part of the answer seems to be method. The markers used to spot young neurons can fade quickly after death, so how long the tissue waited before it was preserved may change what you see.

W: Some of my colleagues treat the question as closed, in one direction or the other. I'd say that's a bit premature. This is a measurement problem as much as a biological one, and until the methods improve, I'd keep both possibilities on the table.

lt-ts062.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: M: Let's turn to a puzzle about spiral galaxies. If most of a galaxy's mass sits in its bright center, then stars far out near the edge should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune moves around the Sun much more slowly than Mercury does.

M: In the nineteen seventies, Vera Rubin and her colleagues measured how fast stars and gas were moving in the outer parts of galaxies. The speeds didn't drop off. The outer regions were moving about as fast as the inner ones.

M: The most popular explanation is dark matter: a large halo of matter we can't see, which adds extra gravity. Most astronomers accept it, partly because it also helps explain other observations, like the way galaxy clusters bend light.

M: There's a rival idea, though, called modified Newtonian dynamics. It says there's no hidden matter at all. Instead, gravity itself behaves a little differently when accelerations are extremely small, as they are at the edges of galaxies.

M: To be fair to that idea, it predicts the rotation of many individual galaxies remarkably well, sometimes better than dark matter models do. Where it struggles is on larger scales, with clusters of galaxies and the early universe.

M: And here's the awkward part for dark matter: decades of experiments built to detect its particles directly have found nothing so far. So the majority view is strong, but it isn't finished business.

lt-ts063.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: W: The idea we're discussing today is linguistic relativity, the claim that the language you speak shapes the way you think. It's often linked to Benjamin Lee Whorf, who wrote about it in the nineteen thirties.

W: In its strong form, the claim is that language determines thought, so if your language lacks a word for something, you can't really think about it. Very few researchers accept that version today. People clearly grasp new concepts before they have words for them.
W: Whorf's own evidence also took a beating. He argued that the Hopi language had no way of talking about time, but later linguists showed that it has plenty of ways to do exactly that.

W: So is the whole idea dead? Not quite. A weaker version says language can nudge thinking, especially habits of attention. Take color. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and in experiments Russian speakers are slightly faster at telling those shades apart than English speakers are.
W: Notice how small that effect is, though. Russian speakers aren't seeing different colors. They're a fraction of a second quicker on one kind of task.
W: You'll find the strong version in popular articles all the time, usually under a dramatic headline. I'd just ask you to check which version the evidence actually supports before you repeat it.

lt-ts064.x: Listen to part of a talk in a philosophy of science class.
sc: M: Last week we asked what makes a theory scientific. Today, Karl Popper's answer. Popper said a theory is scientific if it's falsifiable, meaning it makes predictions that some possible observation could prove wrong.

M: His favorite example was Einstein. General relativity predicted that starlight would bend by a specific amount as it passed the Sun. In nineteen nineteen, astronomers checked during a solar eclipse. The theory could have failed. It didn't, and for Popper, that risk was exactly what made it science.

M: Critics, though, pointed out a problem. When a prediction fails, it's never just one theory on trial. You're also relying on your instruments, your background assumptions, and so on. So a failed prediction doesn't tell you which piece is wrong.

M: History gives a nice case. In the eighteen forties, Uranus wasn't moving the way Newton's laws said it should. Astronomers didn't throw out Newton. They assumed an unseen planet was pulling on it, calculated where it should be, and found Neptune.

M: So rescuing a theory can be perfectly good science. Then again, the same move failed with Mercury's orbit. A hidden planet was proposed there too, it was never found, and the real answer turned out to be Einstein's relativity.
M: Popper's idea is still useful as a rule of thumb, I think. But as a strict test of what counts as science, well, it's harder to apply than it first sounds.

lt-ts065.x: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
sc: W: Today's topic is a hypothesis that ecology students meet early and then, increasingly, see questioned. It's called the intermediate disturbance hypothesis. A disturbance, in this sense, is anything that clears space: a storm, a fire, a flood, heavy grazing.

W: The idea goes like this. If disturbances are rare, a few strong competitors gradually take over and push everyone else out. If they're constant, only the hardiest, fastest-growing species survive. So the greatest variety of species should appear somewhere in the middle.

W: Classic support came from rocky shores. In one well-known study, boulders that waves overturned now and then held more kinds of seaweed than boulders that were rarely moved or rolled over all the time.

W: It's an elegant picture, and it found its way into conservation planning. But when researchers pulled together hundreds of studies, the predicted hump-shaped pattern showed up in only a minority of them. Often diversity simply rose, fell, or showed no clear pattern.

W: Some ecologists went further and argued that the hypothesis has a logic problem: disturbance on its own shouldn't let competitors live side by side in the long run unless other conditions are also met.
W: Its defenders say it still describes certain systems well. That may be so. But a rule that holds only some of the time is, let's say, a local story rather than a law of nature.

lt-ts066.x: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
sc: M: So, can you beat the stock market? The efficient market hypothesis, which became influential in the nineteen sixties and seventies, says, in its basic form, not reliably. The reasoning is that prices already reflect the information available to investors.

M: Think of it this way. If a company's good news were public and the price hadn't moved yet, traders would rush to buy, and the price would jump almost instantly. So by the time you read the news, the opportunity is gone.
M: There's real evidence behind this. Most professionally managed funds, once you subtract their fees, do worse over the long run than a simple fund that just tracks the whole market.

M: But behavioral economists have challenged the idea that markets are fully rational. They point to bubbles, like the rise and crash of internet company shares around the year two thousand, when prices drifted far above any sensible estimate of value. They also point to investors who hold on to losing shares too long and sell winners too early.
M: Defenders reply that spotting a bubble afterward is easy. Spotting it in advance, and profiting from that, is another matter entirely.

M: Interestingly, leading figures on both sides shared the Nobel Prize in economics in the same year, two thousand thirteen. Which tells you, perhaps, that the profession hasn't quite made up its mind.

lt-ts067.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: W: In two thousand one, the painter David Hockney proposed something that upset a lot of art historians. Looking at European paintings from the early fourteen hundreds onward, he noticed a sudden jump in realism: folds of fabric, reflections on metal, the exact patterns of a carpet.
W: His explanation, developed with the physicist Charles Falco, was that some artists were using optical devices, curved mirrors or lenses, to project an image onto a surface and then paint from it.
W: The thesis has a certain appeal. Lenses and mirrors did exist at the time, and some details in these paintings, they argued, show the slight distortions you'd expect if a lens had been refocused.

W: Critics raised several objections. Almost no written record from the period describes artists working this way, which is odd for a method supposedly used so widely. Others tested the setups and found that images from early mirrors would have been dim and small, hard to work from.

W: And some critics took offense at what the thesis seemed to imply, that these painters' skill was a kind of trick. Hockney said that was never his point. A projected image, he argued, still has to be painted, and that takes enormous skill.

W: Personally, I find the question more interesting than any final answer. Even if the thesis turns out to be wrong, it's made a lot of people look much harder at how these paintings were actually made.

lt-ts068.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: M: Around seven hundred million years ago, something strange happened to Earth's climate. Geologists have found deposits left by glaciers in rocks that, at the time, sat near the equator. We know their position from magnetic signals in the rocks, which record the latitude where they formed.

M: The boldest explanation is the snowball Earth hypothesis: the whole planet froze over, oceans included, from the poles to the tropics. Once ice covers enough of the surface, it reflects so much sunlight that the cooling feeds on itself.

M: But then how did Earth escape? The proposed answer is volcanoes. They kept releasing carbon dioxide, and with the oceans frozen, very little of that gas was being removed. Over millions of years it built up, until the greenhouse effect melted the ice.
M: Supporters point to unusual layers of carbonate rock lying directly on top of the glacial deposits, which fit a sudden, very warm aftermath.

M: Critics prefer what's called a slushball Earth, where a band of open water stayed near the equator. Their main argument is biological. Many simple organisms that needed sunlight survived this period, and it's hard to see how, if every ocean was sealed under thick ice.

M: Snowball supporters have answers: small patches of open water, thin ice in places. But notice that each answer moves the snowball a little closer to the slushball. The two camps may end up meeting somewhere in the middle.

lt-ts069.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: W: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists argued about where modern humans came from. There were two main camps, and I want to walk you through how the argument was, well, partly resolved.

W: The first camp held the multiregional model. Early human populations spread out of Africa long ago and then evolved into modern humans in several regions at once, in Africa, Europe and Asia, with enough interbreeding between regions to keep them one species.

W: The second camp held the recent African origin model, often called Out of Africa. Modern humans evolved in Africa alone and then spread across the world, replacing older groups like the Neanderthals without mixing with them.

W: In the late nineteen eighties, genetic studies seemed to settle things in favor of Out of Africa. Living Africans show more genetic variety than any other population, which is what you'd expect from the oldest population, the one the others branched off from.

W: Then, in two thousand ten, scientists published a draft of the Neanderthal genome. And it turned out that most people whose ancestors come from outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA, roughly one to two percent.
W: So there was mixing after all. Not much, but some. Neither side got exactly what it predicted.
W: Today, most researchers describe a mostly African origin with a little interbreeding along the way. Which is a good reminder that a debate framed as either-or sometimes ends with a messier answer.

lt-ts070.x: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
sc: M: Some Roman harbor walls have been sitting in seawater for about two thousand years, and they're still standing. Modern concrete in the same conditions can start breaking down within decades. So what did the Romans know that we've, well, apparently forgotten?

M: One long-standing explanation focuses on volcanic ash. Roman builders mixed lime with ash from the area around the Bay of Naples, and ancient writers, including Vitruvius, praised this material for hardening even underwater.

M: In the twenty tens, researchers studying samples of harbor concrete found that seawater slowly seeping through it had caused rare minerals to grow in its cracks and pores. In other words, the material kept strengthening over time instead of just wearing away.
M: Then, in two thousand twenty-three, another team proposed a second factor. Roman concrete contains small white lumps of lime, which had long been dismissed as a sign of careless mixing.

M: The team argued that the lumps came from mixing with quicklime, which heats up as it reacts. When a crack forms and water gets in, the lumps can dissolve and refill the crack. A kind of self-healing.
M: Now, these explanations aren't really competitors. One is about structures in seawater, the other about cracks in general. They could both be true.

M: What strikes me is the second one. Something experts had written off as sloppy work might turn out to be deliberate technique. That's worth remembering whenever we judge old methods by modern standards.

lt-ts071.x: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
sc: W: In the nineteen nineties, a research group in Italy recording from single neurons in monkeys noticed something surprising. Certain cells in a motor area of the brain fired when a monkey grasped an object, and also when it simply watched someone else grasp one.

W: These became known as mirror neurons, and the excitement was enormous. Within a few years they were being proposed as the basis of imitation, of understanding other people's intentions, of empathy, even of language. One well-known scientist predicted they would do for psychology what DNA did for biology.

W: So what's the problem? First, most of the direct evidence comes from monkeys. In humans we mostly rely on brain scans, which show activity across whole regions, not individual cells. So we're often inferring mirror neurons rather than observing them.

W: Second, critics point out that a cell responding to an action doesn't mean it causes understanding of that action. It might reflect understanding that happens somewhere else, or simply learned links between seeing and doing.
W: And there's an awkward fact for the grand version: monkeys have these neurons, yet they imitate very little compared with human children.

W: None of this means the discovery wasn't real or important. It was. But I'd separate the cells, which are well documented, from the big theories built on top of them, which are, let's say, still waiting for their evidence.

lt-ts072.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: M: Where did the Moon come from? Before the Apollo missions, there were three main ideas. It split off from a fast-spinning Earth. It formed alongside Earth from the same material. Or it was a passing body captured by Earth's gravity.

M: The rocks the astronauts brought back caused trouble for all three. The Moon turned out to be very dry and to have only a small iron core, and none of the old ideas explained that combination well.

M: So by the mid nineteen eighties a new favorite had emerged: the giant impact hypothesis. A body roughly the size of Mars struck the young Earth, and debris thrown into orbit gathered to form the Moon. The heat would have driven off water, and much of the iron would have stayed with Earth.
M: Computer simulations of the impact, though, created a new puzzle. They suggested that most of the Moon's material should come from the impactor, not from Earth.

M: If so, the Moon's rocks should look chemically different from Earth's. But careful measurements of certain isotopes, versions of elements like oxygen and titanium, show the two are almost identical.
M: Researchers have responded with variations: a more violent impact that mixed everything thoroughly, or an impactor that happened to be made of very similar material.
M: The giant impact is still the best story we have, so don't throw it out. But it's a story that has needed some revisions to fit the evidence, and it may need more.

lt-ts073.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: M: Children learn their first language remarkably fast, and mostly without formal teaching. The question is how. One influential answer comes from Noam Chomsky, whose work from the late nineteen fifties onward changed the field.

M: Chomsky's argument is often called the poverty of the stimulus. The language children hear, he said, is too limited and too messy to teach them all the rules they end up knowing. They rarely hear examples of certain complex structures, and they're seldom corrected. So some knowledge of grammar must be built in from birth.
M: The rival view is usually called usage-based or statistical learning. It says children are extraordinary pattern detectors, and the input is much richer than Chomsky assumed.

M: A famous experiment from nineteen ninety-six supports this. Eight-month-old babies listened to a stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. Afterward, they could tell apart syllable sequences that had appeared together often from ones that hadn't. In effect, they'd started to find word boundaries on their own.
M: Now, the nativist side replies that finding words is one thing, but learning abstract grammar is a much bigger leap.
M: And that's fair. The baby study doesn't settle the grammar question.

M: Still, notice the direction of the research. Decade after decade, we keep finding that children can learn more from what they hear than anyone expected. That doesn't prove nothing is built in, but it does shrink how much needs to be.

lt-ts074.x: Listen to part of a talk in a philosophy of science class.
sc: W: Here's a question that sounds simple: when a scientific theory works, should we believe that the things it describes are real? Electrons, say, or genes before anyone could see them. Philosophers who say yes are called scientific realists.

W: Their strongest argument is sometimes called the no miracles argument. Our best theories make astonishingly precise predictions. If they weren't at least roughly true, that success would be a miracle, and nobody likes explaining things with miracles.

W: The opposing camp, the anti-realists, has a historical reply. Look at theories that were once extremely successful and are now abandoned. For much of the nineteenth century, physicists explained light as waves traveling through an invisible substance called the ether. That theory made excellent predictions. And there's no ether.
W: So, the argument goes, if past successful theories turned out false, why expect our current ones to be different? Philosophers call this the pessimistic induction.

W: Realists have tried to soften the blow. Some argue that what survives from old theories is their mathematical structure, even when the objects they described don't. Many of the equations for light waves, for example, were kept.
W: I find that move clever, though I notice it gives up quite a bit. If what we can trust is the structure and not the things, then the realist is believing less than she started out believing.

lt-ts075.x: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
sc: M: In nineteen ninety-five, wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park after being absent for about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology.

M: The story goes like this. Wolves hunted elk, and they also made elk nervous. Elk began avoiding open valleys and riverbanks where they could easily be trapped. Willow and aspen, which elk had been eating heavily, started to recover, and beavers came back to use the willows.
M: A chain like this, predator to prey to plants, is called a trophic cascade. And the fear effect, elk changing where they go, is sometimes called the landscape of fear.

M: More recent research, though, has made the story more complicated. Some field studies that tracked elk with collars found that elk didn't avoid risky places nearly as strongly as the original accounts suggested.
M: Other things were changing at the same time. Bears and cougars were taking more elk calves, people were hunting elk outside the park, and a run of dry years affected plant growth.
M: And along some streams, willows haven't recovered much at all, partly because, without beavers and their dams, the water table dropped and the soil dried out.
M: So did wolves matter? Almost certainly. But the tidy version, where one animal restores a whole landscape, probably gives the wolves more credit than any single species deserves.

lt-ts076.x: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
sc: W: In nineteen fifty-eight, the economist Bill Phillips published a study of British data covering nearly a century. He found that when unemployment was low, wages tended to rise quickly, and when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly.

W: Other economists soon turned this into a relationship between unemployment and inflation, which became known as the Phillips curve. Policymakers read it almost as a menu. Accept a bit more inflation, and you could buy lower unemployment.

W: In the late nineteen sixties, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that this menu wouldn't last. Their point was about expectations. If workers and businesses come to expect higher inflation, they build it into wages and prices, and then the extra inflation stops buying any extra jobs.

W: The nineteen seventies seemed to prove them right. Many countries had high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, something the simple curve said shouldn't happen. People called it stagflation.

W: Economists didn't throw the curve away, though. They rebuilt it with expectations included. In the newer version there's a short-run trade-off, but in the long run unemployment returns to a natural level, whatever the inflation rate.

W: And more recently the curve has puzzled people again. In several countries, unemployment fell very low in the years before twenty twenty without much rise in inflation, and economists still debate why.
W: So this history isn't really a theory being refuted. It's a theory being repaired, more than once, and maybe not for the last time.

lt-ts077.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: W: When you picture ancient Greek sculpture, you probably imagine gleaming white marble. That image shaped centuries of European art. In the seventeen hundreds, the writer Johann Winckelmann praised the whiteness of classical statues as part of their beauty, and later sculptors copied that look on purpose.

W: There's just one problem. Many of those statues were originally painted. Traces of pigment survive on a number of them, and ancient writers mention painted sculpture. Today, with ultraviolet light and other techniques, researchers can detect colors the naked eye can't see.

W: Some scholars have made full-color reconstructions, and you may have seen them in exhibitions: bright blues and reds, patterned clothing. Visitors are often shocked. Some find them garish, even a little cartoonish.

W: Now, there's a fair criticism of these reconstructions. The surviving traces usually tell us which pigment was used in a spot, but not how it was blended or shaded. So many reconstructions use flat, solid colors, partly because that's what the evidence directly supports. The originals may have been far subtler.
W: In other words, the reconstructions may be wrong in their details, but the basic point, that the statues were colored, isn't really in doubt.
W: What interests me is the reaction. When people call the painted versions tasteless, they're often judging them by a standard of white marble that was itself, in large part, a later invention.

lt-ts078.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: M: In nineteen twelve, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined together and had slowly drifted apart. He called the ancient supercontinent Pangaea.

M: His evidence was actually pretty good. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. Fossils of the same land animals and plants appear on continents now separated by oceans. And rock layers and signs of ancient glaciers line up across those oceans too.

M: Yet most geologists, especially in Britain and North America, rejected the idea for decades. Why? The main objection was the mechanism. Wegener couldn't explain what force could push whole continents through the solid ocean floor, and physicists showed that the forces he suggested were far too weak.

M: It's tempting to call the critics stubborn, but put yourself in their place. A theory with no workable mechanism, proposed by someone who wasn't trained as a geologist. Skepticism wasn't unreasonable.

M: What changed things was the ocean floor itself. In the nineteen fifties and sixties, surveys revealed long underwater mountain ridges, with magnetic stripes in the rock on either side that matched like mirror images. New sea floor was forming at the ridges and spreading outward.
M: That gave a mechanism. Continents don't plow through the ocean floor. They ride along on moving plates.
M: So Wegener was right about drift but wrong about how it worked. And the theory that won, plate tectonics, kept his conclusion while throwing out his explanation.

lt-ts079.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: W: Why did people start farming? It's not as obvious as it sounds. Studies of skeletons suggest that many early farmers were shorter and had more dental problems than the hunter-gatherers before them. Farming meant harder work and a narrower diet. So what pushed people into it?

W: An early answer, from the archaeologist Gordon Childe in the nineteen twenties and thirties, was environmental. As the climate dried after the last ice age, people, plants and animals crowded together around sources of water, and close contact led to domestication. This became known as the oasis theory.
W: Later research found that the climate record didn't fit very well, and that idea lost support. Others proposed population pressure: as numbers grew, people needed more food from the same land.

W: Then came Gobekli Tepe, a site in what is now southeastern Turkey. Its huge carved stone pillars were put up around eleven thousand years ago, by people who, as far as we can tell, were still hunting and gathering.
W: For the excavators, this suggested a reversal of the usual order. Maybe large gatherings for ceremonies came first, and the need to feed those crowds encouraged people to cultivate wild grains.
W: It's an exciting idea, but I'd be careful. One site, however remarkable, can't carry the whole explanation, and farming began independently in several parts of the world.
W: More likely, different pressures mattered in different places. The search for a single cause may be the real mistake.

lt-ts080.x: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
sc: M: How did the ancient Egyptians lift millions of stone blocks to build the Great Pyramid at Giza? Most researchers agree ramps were involved. The argument is about what kind.

M: The simplest idea is a single straight ramp up one side. The trouble is the geometry. To keep the slope gentle enough for hauling heavy blocks, the ramp would have had to be enormously long, containing almost as much material as the pyramid itself.
M: A second idea is a ramp spiraling around the outside of the pyramid. That's shorter, but it would have covered the corners and edges, which the builders needed to see to keep the shape accurate.

M: About twenty years ago, an architect proposed something bolder: a ramp inside the pyramid, spiraling up just beneath the surface. It's clever and solves both problems, but there's little direct physical evidence for it, and many Egyptologists remain unconvinced.

M: What we do have is evidence from quarries. In twenty eighteen, archaeologists described a steep ramp at an ancient alabaster quarry, with staircases on both sides and holes for wooden posts. It seems workers used posts and ropes to haul blocks up much steeper slopes than people had assumed.
M: That quarry isn't the pyramid site, or a complete answer. But it changes the geometry argument. If steep ramps were possible, a simple ramp needn't be as huge as critics claimed.
M: Notice the lesson here. Sometimes progress comes not from a new theory but from questioning an assumption hidden inside the old objections.

lt-ps001.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: W: Today let's answer a question that many people get wrong. Why is summer warm and winter cold? A lot of people think it's because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. But that's not the reason.
W: In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. That's winter in the northern half of the world. So distance can't explain the seasons.

W: The real reason is that Earth is tilted. Its axis, the line it spins around, leans over by about twenty-three and a half degrees. And it stays tilted in the same direction all year as Earth travels around the Sun.

W: So for part of the year, the northern half leans toward the Sun. Sunlight hits it more directly, and the days are longer. That's summer in the north. Six months later, the northern half leans away. The light comes in at a low angle, the days are short, and it's winter.

W: Here's a simple way to picture it. Shine a flashlight straight down at a table, and you get a small, bright circle. Tilt the flashlight, and the same light spreads over a bigger area, so each part gets less.
W: This also explains why the seasons are opposite in the two halves of the world. When it's summer in Canada, it's winter in Argentina.

lt-ps002.x: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
sc: M: Today I want to tell you about a small animal with a very big job: the sea otter. Sea otters live along the Pacific coast of North America, in cold water near the shore.
M: Along much of this coast, there are underwater forests of a giant seaweed called kelp. Kelp forests are home to many kinds of fish, crabs and other sea life.
M: Now, sea urchins, which are small, spiny animals, love to eat kelp. And sea otters love to eat sea urchins. So otters keep the number of urchins down, and that protects the kelp.

M: We know this partly because of what happened when otters disappeared. In the eighteen hundreds and early nineteen hundreds, people hunted sea otters for their thick fur, and in many places the otters were almost all gone. Without otters, urchin numbers grew, and they ate the kelp forests down to bare rock.
M: After the hunting stopped and otters returned to some areas, the kelp forests came back too.

M: Ecologists call an animal like this a keystone species. The keystone is the stone at the top of an arch that holds the other stones in place. Take it out, and the arch falls down. In the same way, removing one species can change a whole community.

lt-ps003.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: W: Today we're looking at sand dunes, the hills of sand you find in deserts and along some beaches. Maybe you think of a dune as something that just sits there. But many dunes actually move.
W: Here's how it works. Wind blows sand up the gentle side of the dune, the side facing the wind. The grains bounce and roll along the surface until they reach the top.

W: Then they fall over the edge onto the other side, which is much steeper. This steep side is called the slip face. As sand keeps piling up there, the whole dune slowly moves forward, in the same direction the wind blows.
W: How fast? It depends on the wind and the size of the dune. Small dunes can move more than ten meters in a year. Very large dunes move more slowly, because there's so much more sand to carry.

W: This can cause real problems. In some dry regions, moving dunes cover roads, fields and even buildings. One common solution is to plant grasses and bushes. Their roots hold the sand in place, and the plants slow down the wind near the ground.
W: So the next time you see a dune, remember that it may be on a very slow journey.

lt-ps004.x: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
sc: M: Today's topic is a strange experience reported by many people who have lost an arm or a leg. Even years later, they may still feel the missing limb. It itches, it feels cold, and sometimes it even hurts. This is called a phantom limb.

M: For a long time, doctors assumed the feeling came from damaged nerve endings where the limb had been. That may be part of the story. But research since the nineteen nineties points to the brain as well.

M: Here's why. On the surface of the brain there's a strip of tissue that works like a map of the body. Each body part has its own area, and, oddly, the area for the hand sits right next to the area for the face.

M: When a hand is lost, its area on the map doesn't just go quiet. Neighboring areas, like the face area, can gradually take it over. In some patients, touching the cheek actually produces a feeling in the missing hand.
M: This tells us the adult brain can reorganize itself more than scientists once believed. That ability is often called plasticity.

M: It has also led to a simple treatment called mirror therapy. A patient places the remaining hand next to a mirror, so its reflection appears where the missing hand would be. Moving the real hand seems to move the phantom one, and for some people this reduces pain.

lt-ps005.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: W: Here's a rare event in linguistics: researchers got to watch a new language being born. In the late nineteen seventies and early eighties, new schools for deaf children opened in Nicaragua. Before that, most deaf children there had grown up apart from each other, communicating with their families through simple home signs.

W: The schools actually taught lip-reading and Spanish, with little success. But on the playground and on the school buses, the children started signing to each other, combining their home signs into a shared system.
W: The first group of children developed something fairly basic. It worked, but it was rough and limited.

W: Then something interesting happened. Younger children who joined the schools learned this system from the older ones, and they didn't just copy it. They made it more regular and more complex. For example, they developed consistent ways of showing who did what to whom, and they used the space around the body to keep track of people in a story.
W: Researchers noticed that the youngest learners added the most structure. Students who arrived at an older age tended to sign less fluently, even after many years.

W: Why does this matter? It suggests that young children don't just absorb language from adults. Given rough material, they can actively build grammar into it. Of course, this is one case, so researchers are careful about how far to generalize.

lt-ps006.x: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
sc: M: Today's idea comes from the economist David Ricardo, who wrote about it in eighteen seventeen. It's called comparative advantage, and it explains why trade can benefit both sides, even when one side is better at everything.
M: Let's start with a simple example. Imagine a lawyer who is also the fastest typist in town. She types faster than her assistant. So should she do all her own typing?

M: Probably not. Every hour she spends typing is an hour she isn't working as a lawyer, which pays much more. Economists call what you give up the opportunity cost, and for her, the opportunity cost of typing is very high.

M: Her assistant types more slowly, but his opportunity cost is much lower, because he isn't giving up legal work. So it makes sense for him to type and for her to practice law. Together, they get more done.

M: Ricardo applied the same logic to countries. His example was England and Portugal, cloth and wine. Even if Portugal could produce both more efficiently, both countries could gain if each focused on the good it gave up the least to produce, and then traded.
M: Notice the key word: comparative, not absolute. What matters isn't who's best at something, but who gives up the least to do it.
M: Real trade is more complicated, of course. Some workers and industries can lose out, even when a country gains overall. But the basic idea remains one of the most important in economics.

lt-ps007.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: W: When we talk about the Impressionists, painters like Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, we usually focus on their style: quick brushstrokes, bright colors and scenes of everyday life. But today I want to talk about a piece of technology that helped make that style possible: the paint tube.

W: Before the eighteen forties, painters usually prepared their paints in the studio, grinding colored powders and mixing them with oil. Paint was often stored in small bags made from pig bladders, which were awkward to carry and easily burst.
W: In eighteen forty-one, an American painter named John Goffe Rand patented a squeezable metal tube. Paint stayed fresh inside, and you could carry dozens of colors in a box.

W: This made painting outdoors much easier. Painting outside wasn't new, but now artists could finish whole works in the open air, in front of the scene, trying to capture the changing light. This is often called plein air painting, from the French for open air.
W: Brighter new pigments were also becoming available in tubes around the same time, which helps explain the Impressionists' strong colors.

W: Renoir is reported to have said that without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism. That's probably an exaggeration, since art movements have many causes. But it's a good reminder that changes in tools can shape changes in art.

lt-ps008.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: M: You may have heard the claim that humans can maintain only about a hundred and fifty meaningful relationships. That's Dunbar's number, proposed in the early nineteen nineties by the anthropologist Robin Dunbar.

M: The reasoning behind it is clever. Among monkeys and apes, species with a larger neocortex, the outer layer of the brain, tend to live in larger social groups. Dunbar plotted that relationship and then used the size of the human neocortex to predict a natural human group size. The answer came out at around one hundred and fifty.
M: He then pointed to supporting examples, such as the typical size of some traditional villages and of certain historical military units.
M: The idea caught on, especially in business. Some companies have reportedly tried to keep their units below that size.

M: Critics, though, have raised serious questions. In two thousand twenty-one, a team reanalyzed the primate data with newer statistical methods. Depending on the method, their estimates for humans ranged from just a handful of people to more than five hundred. In other words, the data can't pin down a single number.
M: Critics also note that human social life depends heavily on culture, language and technology, not just brain size, so a prediction based on other primates may not transfer well.
M: Dunbar has defended his work, and the debate goes on. But I'd suggest treating one hundred and fifty less as a law of human nature and more as a rough, and rather contested, rule of thumb.

lt-ps009.x: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
sc: W: For centuries, sailors could work out their latitude, how far north or south they were, fairly easily from the height of the Sun or certain stars. Longitude, their east-west position, was far harder, and errors could leave a ship badly off course.

W: The principle was understood. Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. So if you know the local time on your ship and, at the same moment, the time at your home port, the difference gives your longitude. The problem was knowing the home port time at sea.
W: In seventeen fourteen, the British government offered a large prize for a practical solution, and two very different approaches competed.

W: Astronomers favored the lunar distance method. By measuring the angle between the Moon and a particular star, and checking printed tables, a navigator could work out the home port time. It needed accurate tables and long calculations, but no costly equipment.

W: The other approach was to carry the home port time with you in a clock. Most experts doubted any clock could stay accurate on a rolling ship. But a self-taught clockmaker, John Harrison, spent decades proving them wrong, and his sea watch performed remarkably well on trial voyages in the seventeen sixties.
W: What the heroic story often leaves out is that these clocks stayed expensive for decades, so many ships kept using lunar distances well into the eighteen hundreds.
W: So the experts' preference for astronomy wasn't just snobbery. For a long time, it was the method most ships could actually afford.

lt-ps010.x: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
sc: M: In the nineteen seventies, the scientist James Lovelock, working with the biologist Lynn Margulis, proposed what he called the Gaia hypothesis, named after a Greek goddess of the Earth. The claim was that living things and their surroundings form a self-regulating system that keeps conditions on Earth suitable for life.

M: Lovelock pointed to some striking facts. The amount of oxygen in the air has stayed fairly stable for hundreds of millions of years. And although the Sun has grown brighter over Earth's history, the surface has stayed within a range where liquid water can exist.

M: Biologists were quick to object. Natural selection acts on individual organisms and their genes. So how could countless separate organisms end up regulating a whole planet? It sounded as if life were planning ahead, which evolution doesn't do.

M: Lovelock answered with a computer model called Daisyworld, a planet with only dark and light daisies. Dark daisies absorb heat and light ones reflect it. As the sun warms, the balance between them shifts, and the temperature stays fairly steady, without any daisy aiming for that.
M: The model persuaded some critics that regulation without planning was possible in principle. Whether Earth actually works that way is another question.

M: Today, the strong version of Gaia has few supporters. But the broader idea, that life and the physical planet shape each other, has become central to what's now called Earth system science. So a hypothesis can be largely rejected and still leave a lasting mark.

lt-ts001.x: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.
sc: M: OK, so last time we looked at how owls hunt by sound. Today I want to talk about animals that don't just listen. They actually make the sound themselves. I'm talking about echolocation in bats.

M: Here's the basic idea. A bat produces very high-pitched calls, usually too high for us to hear. Those calls bounce off objects around it, and the bat listens to the echoes. From the time it takes an echo to return, the bat can tell how far away something is.

M: Now, here's the interesting part. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster. Researchers call this the feeding buzz. Why speed up? Well, more calls mean more updates, so the bat gets a sharper picture just when the insect is trying to escape.

M: And it's not a one-sided contest. Some moths have evolved ears that can detect bat calls. When they hear one, they suddenly drop or spiral toward the ground. A few tiger moths even produce clicks of their own, which can jam or confuse the bat's signal.
M: So you could think of this as an arms race. Every improvement on one side puts pressure on the other side to adapt.
M: Oh, and one common myth I want to clear up. Bats aren't blind. Most species can see perfectly well. Echolocation just works better in the dark, when vision isn't much help.

lt-ts002.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: W: Let's start with a question. How does solid rock end up hanging from a cave ceiling like an icicle? To answer that, we need to follow a single drop of water.

W: When rain falls, it picks up carbon dioxide from the air and, even more, from the soil. That makes the water slightly acidic. It's a weak acid, nothing dangerous, but it's strong enough to slowly dissolve limestone as it seeps down through cracks in the rock.

W: So the water now carries dissolved minerals. When it drips into an open cave, some of the carbon dioxide escapes into the cave air, and the water can't hold all of its mineral anymore. A tiny ring of calcite is left behind on the ceiling.

W: Drop after drop, that ring grows into a thin hollow tube. Cavers call these soda straws. If the tube gets blocked, water flows down the outside instead, and the formation thickens into a cone. That's a stalactite.
W: Meanwhile, water that falls to the floor builds a stalagmite upward. Given enough time, the two can meet and form a column.

W: And time is the key word here. Many of these formations grow less than a millimeter a year. That's why cave guides ask you not to touch them. Oil from your skin can stop the growth at that spot, and a broken one may take thousands of years to replace.

lt-ts003.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: M: So, if you look at the Moon tonight and again next month, you'll see the same patterns, the same dark patches. Ever wondered why we never see the other side? The answer is something called tidal locking.

M: A lot of students assume this means the Moon doesn't spin. Actually, it does spin. It just turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to go around Earth once, about twenty-seven days. So the same face always points toward us.

M: How did that happen? Earth's gravity pulls a little harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, so the Moon gets stretched slightly into a bulge. Long ago the Moon spun faster, and Earth kept tugging on that bulge. Over millions of years, that tugging slowed the spin until it matched the orbit.

M: Now, you'll sometimes hear the far side called the dark side. That's misleading. It gets just as much sunlight as the side we see. It was only dark in the sense that it was unknown, at least until a spacecraft photographed it in nineteen fifty-nine.

M: And this isn't unique to our Moon. Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, are both locked, so each one always shows the same face to the other. In fact, the process is still going on here, too. Earth's own spin is very gradually slowing down.

lt-ts004.x: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.
sc: W: Let's try a quick experiment in your heads. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words, just once, and then ask you to write down as many as you can. Which words do you think you'd remember?

W: If you're like most people, you'd remember the first few words and the last few words pretty well, and the ones in the middle would mostly disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

W: There are really two effects here. The advantage for the first items is called primacy. The idea is that when the list begins, you've got time to repeat those words to yourself, so they're more likely to get into long-term memory.
W: The advantage for the last items is called recency. Those words are still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can just, sort of, read them off.

W: Now, here's how we know these are separate processes. If you make people wait about thirty seconds before writing, and keep them busy, say, counting backward, the recency effect disappears. But the primacy effect stays. The delay wipes out short-term memory, but it doesn't touch what's already been stored.
W: And this has practical consequences. Think about a long day of job interviews. The candidates in the middle may be at a real disadvantage, through no fault of their own.

lt-ts005.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: M: Think about the last graduation ceremony you went to. People wear unusual clothing, they walk across a stage one by one, and then suddenly they're graduates. Anthropologists have a name for events like this. They're called rites of passage.

M: The term comes from a French scholar, Arnold van Gennep, who wrote about it in the early nineteen hundreds. He noticed that ceremonies marking a change in status, like birth, adulthood or marriage, tended to share the same three-part structure, no matter which society he looked at.

M: First comes separation. The person is removed from their old role, sometimes physically, sometimes just symbolically, with a change of clothes, for example. Then there's a transition phase. And finally there's incorporation, when the person rejoins the community in their new role.

M: Now, the middle phase is the one later anthropologists found most fascinating. Victor Turner called it liminal, from the Latin word for threshold. During this phase, people are betwixt and between. They're no longer what they were, but not yet what they'll become. And often, everyone going through it together is treated as equal, whatever their background.
M: So, back to graduation. The gowns are identical for everyone, right? That's the liminal phase in action. Then you cross the stage, and you come out the other side with a new title.

lt-ts006.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: W: Today we're looking at fresco, the technique behind many of the great wall paintings of Renaissance Italy, including Michelangelo's ceiling in the Sistine Chapel. The word fresco just means fresh in Italian, and that tells you a lot about how it works.

W: In true fresco, the artist paints onto wet lime plaster. The pigments are mixed only with water. There's no glue, no oil. So what holds the color on the wall? Well, as the plaster dries, it reacts with carbon dioxide in the air and forms a hard crystal layer, and the pigment gets locked inside it. The color becomes part of the wall itself.

W: But here's the catch. Plaster only stays wet for so many hours. So painters spread just enough fresh plaster for what they could finish in one day. These sections are called giornate, which means days. If you look closely at some frescoes, you can actually see the seams between one day's work and the next.
W: And mistakes? You can't just paint over them. The artist had to chip away the plaster and start that section again.

W: Some painters took a shortcut and painted on dry plaster instead. It's much more forgiving. The problem is that the paint just sits on the surface, so over the centuries a lot of it has flaked away, while true fresco has survived remarkably well.

lt-ts007.x: Listen to part of a talk in a music class.
sc: M: Here's a puzzle that bothered musicians for centuries. If you tune an instrument using perfectly pure intervals, the kind based on simple number ratios, it sounds beautiful in one key. But move to a distant key, and some chords sound terrible. Why?

M: Well, the math doesn't quite work out. Take the perfect fifth. If you stack twelve pure fifths on top of each other, you should end up on the same note, seven octaves higher. But you don't. You overshoot by a small amount. And that leftover has to go somewhere.

M: Older tuning systems hid the leftover in keys people rarely used. That worked fine, as long as composers stayed in the comfortable keys. Some intervals in the remote keys were so sour that musicians nicknamed one of them the wolf, because it howled.

M: The solution that eventually won is called equal temperament. You divide the octave into twelve exactly equal steps. That spreads the error evenly, so every interval except the octave is a tiny bit out of tune. Most listeners can't hear it, but every key is usable.
M: So it's a compromise. You give up a little purity, and in exchange you get total freedom to move between keys. By the late nineteenth century, it had become the standard way to tune pianos.

lt-ts008.x: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.
sc: W: In business, there's a popular belief that being first to market is the key to winning. It even has a name, first-mover advantage. Today I want to look at whether that belief really holds up.

W: There are some real benefits to going first. A first mover can build brand recognition before anyone else shows up. It can lock up scarce resources, like the best store locations or the most reliable suppliers. And sometimes it creates switching costs. Once customers have learned your system, moving to a competitor feels like a hassle.

W: But going first is also expensive. The pioneer has to convince people they need a product that's never existed before. It pays for all the trial and error. And here's the thing: competitors are watching. A second company, what we call a fast follower, can copy what worked, skip what didn't, and enter with a better product at a lower cost.
W: Think about internet search. The earliest search engines weren't the ones that ended up dominating. A later company studied what users wanted and simply did it better.
W: So my view is that timing matters, but being first isn't enough on its own. What matters more is whether a company can keep learning faster than the ones coming after it.

lt-ts009.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: W: Imagine a busy port a few hundred years ago. Traders and workers arrive from many places, and they don't share a language. But they need to buy, sell, and work together. So what happens? Very often, a pidgin develops.

W: A pidgin is a simplified contact language. Most of its words usually come from the language of the most powerful group, but the grammar is stripped down. There may be no endings for tense or plural, and the word order is kept simple. And here's the important point. A pidgin is nobody's first language. Everyone who uses it speaks something else at home.

W: Now, things change when children are born into that community and grow up hearing the pidgin all around them. Those children don't just copy it. They expand it. Within a generation or two, it develops consistent ways to mark time, more complex sentences, and a much richer vocabulary. At that point, linguists call it a creole.

W: A good example is Tok Pisin, in Papua New Guinea. It started as a pidgin used on plantations. Today it has native speakers, it's used in newspapers and broadcasting, and it's one of the country's official languages.
W: So creoles show us something remarkable. Give children a limited system, and they'll build a full language out of it.

lt-ts010.x: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
sc: M: Today's topic sounds like a good thing at first. More nutrients in a lake. Plants need nutrients, right? So how could extra food be a problem? Well, this process, called eutrophication, is one of the most common causes of poor water quality in the world.

M: It usually starts on land. Fertilizer from farms and lawns contains nitrogen and phosphorus. When it rains, some of that washes into streams and eventually into lakes or coastal waters. Untreated sewage can add even more.
M: Algae respond fast. They multiply into what we call a bloom, sometimes turning the water bright green. The bloom shades out the plants growing on the bottom, so those plants die.

M: But here's the twist. The real damage comes after the algae die. Bacteria break down all that dead material, and as they do, they use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Fish and other animals that can't swim away suffocate. Areas like this are called dead zones. A large one forms in the Gulf of Mexico every summer, near the mouth of the Mississippi River.

M: The good news is that it can be reversed. In the nineteen seventies, several countries limited phosphates in laundry detergent, and some badly affected lakes recovered noticeably. Today, many farmers also plant strips of grass and trees along streams to catch fertilizer before it reaches the water.

lt-ts011.x: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.
sc: W: Last week we talked about warning coloration, how some poisonous or stinging animals advertise it with bright colors, so predators learn to leave them alone. Today, let's look at the cheaters.

W: In Batesian mimicry, a harmless species evolves to look like a dangerous one. Hoverflies are a nice example. They can't sting at all, but with their yellow and black stripes, a lot of birds, and a lot of people, mistake them for wasps.

W: Now, think about this from the predator's point of view. The trick only works because the predator has learned, maybe painfully, that the pattern means trouble. So what happens if the mimics become very common? A bird keeps catching striped insects that turn out to be harmless and tasty. Pretty soon, the stripes stop meaning anything.
W: That's why this kind of mimicry tends to work best when the mimic is rarer than the species it copies.

W: I should mention one famous case that turned out to be more complicated. For decades, textbooks said the viceroy butterfly was a harmless copy of the bad-tasting monarch. But when researchers actually fed viceroys to birds, they found that viceroys taste bad too. So that's really a case of two unpleasant species looking alike, which is a different kind of mimicry altogether.

lt-ts012.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: M: Picture yourself walking across a flat field, and right in the middle there's a boulder the size of a house. Now, here's the strange part. It's made of a completely different kind of rock than anything else around it. The nearest rock like it is hundreds of kilometers away. So how did it get there?
M: Geologists call boulders like this glacial erratics. The word erratic comes from the Latin for wandering, which is a nice way to put it.

M: Back in the early eighteen hundreds, this was a real mystery. Some naturalists suggested that huge floods had swept the rocks along. Others thought icebergs had floated them across ancient seas and dropped them as they melted. Then, in the eighteen thirties and forties, scientists like Louis Agassiz argued for a much bolder idea. Massive sheets of ice had once covered large parts of the continents, and those ice sheets had carried the boulders and left them behind as they melted.

M: Today, erratics are actually useful evidence. If you can match a boulder to the bedrock it came from, you know which direction the ice was moving. And if you find a whole line of them, you can trace the path of a glacier that disappeared thousands of years ago.
M: So these odd rocks turned out to be one of the key clues that led to our understanding of the ice ages.

lt-ts013.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: W: One of the hardest problems in astronomy is measuring distance. A star might look dim because it's faint, or because it's really far away. From here, those two cases can look exactly the same. So how do we tell them apart?
W: The breakthrough came from a type of star called a Cepheid variable. Cepheids pulse. They get brighter and dimmer in a regular rhythm, over a few days or a few weeks.

W: In the early nineteen hundreds, Henrietta Leavitt, working at the Harvard College Observatory, studied hundreds of these stars in a nearby group called the Small Magellanic Cloud. And she had a clever insight. Since all those stars were in the same cloud, they were all roughly the same distance from Earth. So any difference in brightness had to be real. And she found a pattern. The longer a Cepheid takes to complete one pulse, the brighter it really is.

W: Why does that matter so much? Because now, if you find a Cepheid anywhere, you just time its pulse. That tells you how bright it truly is. Compare that with how bright it looks, and you can work out how far away it is.

W: A few years later, Edwin Hubble used exactly this method on Cepheids in the Andromeda nebula, and showed it was far outside our own galaxy. So Leavitt's careful work changed our picture of the size of the universe.

lt-ts014.x: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.
sc: M: Have you ever done something that didn't match what you believe, and then felt kind of uncomfortable about it? Psychologists have a name for that feeling. It's called cognitive dissonance, and the idea goes back to Leon Festinger in the nineteen fifties.

M: The basic claim is simple. When our actions and our beliefs conflict, we feel tension, and we're motivated to reduce it. Often the easiest way isn't to change what we did. We can't undo that. Instead, we change what we think.

M: The classic experiment went something like this. Participants spent about an hour doing an extremely boring task, turning pegs on a board. Then they were paid to tell the next participant that the task was fun. Some were paid one dollar, others twenty dollars. Later, they were asked how much they'd actually enjoyed it.

M: So, who said they liked it more? Most people guess the twenty-dollar group. But it was the one-dollar group. Why? Well, if you got twenty dollars, you had a good reason for saying something untrue. If you got only one dollar, that's not much of an excuse. So, to ease the discomfort, those people came to believe the task wasn't so bad after all.
M: You can see this in everyday life, too. After making an expensive purchase, people often go looking for good reviews of the thing they've already bought.

lt-ts015.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: W: In the late eighteen hundreds, a lot of anthropologists never actually met the people they wrote about. They worked from libraries, reading reports from travelers and traders, and then built big theories from that. Later, people jokingly called them armchair anthropologists.

W: That changed in the early twentieth century. Researchers like Bronislaw Malinowski, who spent long periods in the Trobriand Islands in the Pacific, argued that you can't really understand a way of life from a distance. You have to live it. This approach is called participant observation.

W: So what does it involve? First, you stay a long time, often a year or more. Why a year? Because many activities follow the seasons, like planting, harvests and festivals, and you want to see the whole cycle. Second, you learn the local language, so you aren't depending on a translator. And third, you take part in daily life while carefully recording what you see in field notes.

W: Now, there's an obvious problem. If a stranger with a notebook shows up, people may act differently. That's a real concern. But one advantage of staying so long is that people get used to you. After a few months, you're just part of the scenery, and everyday behavior returns to normal.
W: Participant observation is still the core method of cultural anthropology today, and it's spread to fields like sociology and even business research.

lt-ts016.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: M: If you look at a lot of European paintings from the Middle Ages, space can seem a little strange. Buildings tilt at odd angles, and the most important figure is often the biggest, no matter where they're standing. That's not because the artists lacked skill. They just had different goals. Size showed importance, not distance.

M: Then, in Florence, in the early fourteen hundreds, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small picture of a building in the city and drilled a hole through it. A viewer looked through the hole from the back, at a mirror held in front. When the mirror was lowered, the real building appeared in exactly the same place. The painting matched reality.

M: The system behind it is called linear perspective. The key idea is that parallel lines moving away from us, like the edges of a road, seem to meet at a single point on the horizon, the vanishing point. And objects get smaller at a regular rate as they get farther away.
M: A few years later, the writer Leon Battista Alberti explained the method in a book on painting, so other artists could learn the rules. Within a generation, it had spread across Italy.
M: So perspective wasn't just a new trick. It reflected a new idea of what a painting should be, a window onto a believable world.

lt-ts017.x: Listen to part of a talk in a music history class.
sc: W: Today let's talk about the instrument a lot of you probably started on, the piano. And I want to begin with its name, because the name tells the whole story.

W: Before the piano, the main keyboard instrument was the harpsichord. When you press a harpsichord key, a small device plucks the string, a bit like a guitar pick. It's a lovely sound, but there's a limitation. Whether you press the key gently or hard, the volume comes out almost the same.

W: Around seventeen hundred, in Florence, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori solved that problem. Instead of plucking, his instrument used small hammers that struck the string and then immediately bounced back, so the string could keep ringing. And now, the harder you pressed, the louder the note. He called it, roughly translated, a harpsichord with soft and loud. In Italian, that's piano e forte. Over time, the name was shortened to pianoforte, and then just piano.

W: Now, Cristofori's piano would sound pretty quiet to us. The big change came in the eighteen hundreds, when makers started using iron frames. Those frames could hold the strings much tighter, which made the instrument louder and stronger, strong enough to fill a concert hall.
W: So when you hear a pianist move from a whisper to a roar, remember, that was the whole point of the invention.

lt-ts018.x: Listen to part of a talk in a marketing class.
sc: M: Have you noticed that some stores sell certain items so cheaply that they can't possibly be making money on them? That's not a mistake. It's a strategy, and it's called a loss leader.

M: Here's how it works. A store picks a popular product, say, a turkey before a holiday, or a big pack of batteries, and prices it at or even below what the store paid for it. The product itself loses money. But it leads customers into the store, and that's where the profit comes from. Once you're there, you'll probably also buy potatoes, drinks, maybe a new pan. Those items carry normal prices, and the store comes out ahead.
M: Notice where supermarkets often put basic items like milk and eggs. Usually at the back. To get there, you walk past a lot of other products, and some of them end up in your cart.

M: Now, the strategy has a weakness. Some shoppers, sometimes called cherry pickers, come in, grab only the discounted item, and leave. If too many customers do that, the store just loses money. So stores often set a limit, like two per customer.
M: And by the way, in some countries, selling below cost is actually restricted by law, partly to protect smaller shops that can't afford to compete that way.

lt-ts019.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: W: If you've ever wondered why English spelling seems so unpredictable, especially with vowels, a big part of the answer is something called the Great Vowel Shift.

W: Between about fourteen hundred and seventeen hundred, the long vowels of English changed their pronunciation, step by step. And they didn't change randomly. They moved together, like a chain. Each vowel was pronounced higher in the mouth than before, and the vowels that were already as high as they could go turned into two-part sounds.

W: Let me give you some examples. In Chaucer's time, the word bite sounded more like beet. House sounded something like hoose. And name had a vowel closer to the one in father. So if you read Middle English aloud with the old sounds, it sounds surprisingly like other European languages.

W: Now, here's why this matters for spelling. Around the same period, printing arrived in England, in the fourteen seventies. Printers helped make spellings more fixed. But the pronunciation kept moving. So we ended up with spellings that record how words sounded before the shift was complete. That's why the letter i in bite doesn't sound like the i in, say, Spanish or Italian.
W: As for why the shift happened at all, honestly, linguists still debate it. There are several theories, but no single explanation that everyone accepts.

lt-ts020.x: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
sc: M: On a hot summer evening, if you drive from the countryside into a big city, you might notice the temperature on your car's display going up. Sometimes by several degrees. This is called the urban heat island effect.
