M: So what makes a city warmer? A few things. First, surfaces. Asphalt roads and dark roofs absorb a lot of sunlight during the day. Then, at night, they slowly release that heat back into the air. That's why the difference between city and countryside is often largest after sunset, not at noon.

M: Second, there's less vegetation. Trees and plants release water vapor through their leaves, and that evaporation cools the air around them. Replace a field with a parking lot, and you lose that natural cooling.
M: Third, tall buildings close together can trap heat between them and block the wind. And finally, cities produce heat directly, from cars, factories and air conditioners.

M: Now, here's the frustrating part. When it's hot, people turn up the air conditioning. But air conditioners push heat outside, and the power plants that run them add more. So the problem can actually feed itself.

M: The solutions are fairly simple, at least on paper: lighter-colored roofs that reflect sunlight, rooftop gardens, more trees along streets. Several cities are already painting roofs white for exactly this reason.

lt-ts021.x: Listen to part of a talk in a zoology class.
sc: W: Let me introduce one of my favorite animals. It's less than a millimeter long, it has eight stubby legs, and under a microscope it looks a bit like a tiny bear. In fact, its nickname is the water bear. Scientists call it a tardigrade.

W: Tardigrades live almost everywhere, but a great place to find them is in a clump of damp moss. And moss has a problem. It dries out, sometimes for months. So how does an animal that needs water survive that?

W: Here's the trick. As its surroundings dry, a tardigrade pulls in its legs and curls into a shape called a tun. It loses almost all the water in its body, and its metabolism slows down so much it's barely measurable. In some species, special proteins form a kind of glass inside the cells that holds everything in place. Add water again, and within hours, it can be walking around.
W: In this dried state, tardigrades have survived extreme cold, high radiation, and even several days exposed to outer space on a research satellite.

W: Now, you'll often read online that tardigrades are indestructible. That's an exaggeration. When they're active, they're actually fairly delicate. Their toughness depends almost entirely on that dried-out state. So it's not that they can't be harmed. It's that they've found a very clever way to wait out bad conditions.

lt-ts022.x: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
sc: M: Most volcanoes on Earth are found near the edges of tectonic plates, where plates pull apart or push together. But Hawaii is right in the middle of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from any edge. So why are there volcanoes there?

M: The leading explanation is called a hotspot. The idea, first proposed in the nineteen sixties, is that there's a fixed area of unusually hot material deep below the plate. It melts rock and feeds a volcano at the surface. Now, the key point is that the plate keeps moving, very slowly, toward the northwest, several centimeters a year. The hotspot stays put.

M: So what happens? A volcano forms over the hotspot, and then the plate carries it away. Cut off from its supply, it goes quiet, and a new volcano starts to form behind it. Over millions of years, you get a line of islands, like footprints.

M: And the evidence fits nicely. The Big Island, at the southeastern end, is the youngest, and it still has active volcanoes. As you move northwest, the islands get older, more eroded, and smaller. Kauai, near the other end, is about five million years old.

M: And here's a nice prediction. Off the southeast coast of the Big Island, there's an underwater volcano that's growing right now. Someday, probably tens of thousands of years from now, it'll break the surface and become the next Hawaiian island.

lt-ts023.x: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
sc: W: Here's a question I ask every year. Why is it hotter in summer than in winter? And every year, a lot of people say, because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. It sounds reasonable. But it's wrong.

W: Here's a quick way to see why. Earth's orbit is almost a circle, but not quite, and we're actually closest to the Sun in early January. That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. And another clue: when it's summer in Canada, it's winter in Argentina. If distance were the cause, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time.

W: So what's really going on? Earth's axis is tilted, by about twenty-three and a half degrees. As we travel around the Sun, that tilt stays pointed the same way in space. So for part of the year, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and for the other part, it leans away.

W: When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, two things happen. First, sunlight hits the ground more directly. Think of a flashlight. Shine it straight down, and you get a small, bright spot. Tilt it, and the same light spreads over a bigger area, so each part gets less energy. Second, the days are longer, so there's more time to heat up.
W: So it's the angle, not the distance, that gives us our seasons.

lt-ts024.x: Listen to part of a talk in an educational psychology class.
sc: M: Let's say you have ten hours to study for an exam. You could spend all ten hours the night before. Or you could spread them out, one hour a day over ten days. Same total time. Which works better?

M: Research going back more than a century gives a pretty clear answer. Spreading it out wins. This is called the spacing effect. One of the first people to document it was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist in the eighteen eighties, who tested his own memory by learning long lists of nonsense syllables.

M: Now, here's what's tricky. Cramming often feels like it's working. Right after a long session, the material seems familiar, so you feel confident. And for a test the very next morning, cramming can do okay. The problem is what happens a week or a month later. Most of it is gone.

M: Why does spacing help? One popular explanation is that when you come back to material after a break, you've forgotten a little, so you have to work to pull it back up. And that effort seems to make the memory stronger.

M: In fact, many flashcard apps are built around this idea. They show you a card again just as you're about to forget it, and the gaps get longer each time. So, my advice: don't save it all for the night before. Your future self will thank you.

lt-ts025.x: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
sc: M: Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable finds in the study of human origins. It's not a skull or a skeleton. It's a set of footprints.

M: In the late nineteen seventies, a team led by Mary Leakey was working at a site called Laetoli, in Tanzania. And they found a trail of footprints, preserved in hardened volcanic ash, about three point six million years old.

M: How could footprints possibly survive that long? Well, it took a lucky combination of events. A nearby volcano covered the area in a layer of fine ash. Then a light rain fell, turning the ash into something like wet cement. Animals walked across it, including at least two individuals who walked upright. The sun dried the ash hard, and then more ash buried it and protected it.

M: So what do the prints tell us? They show a heel striking the ground first, a raised arch, and a big toe lined up with the other toes, rather than sticking out to the side the way it does in a chimpanzee's foot. In other words, these individuals walked a lot like we do.

M: And here's why that matters. At that time, our ancestors still had small brains, not much bigger than a chimpanzee's. And the footprints are older than any stone tools we've found. So the footprints suggest that walking on two legs came first, long before big brains or toolmaking.

lt-ts026.x: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
sc: W: When we talk about Impressionism, we usually talk about the artists, Monet, Renoir, and their new way of seeing light. But today I want to talk about a much humbler object that helped make it possible: the paint tube.

W: Until the mid-eighteen hundreds, most painters, or their assistants, made paint by hand. They ground the colored powder and mixed it with oil in the studio. Storing it was a real problem. Paint was often kept in little bags made from animal bladders, which you'd poke with a tack to squeeze some out. They leaked, they burst, and the paint dried out quickly. So painting outdoors for a whole day just wasn't practical.

W: Then in eighteen forty-one, an American portrait painter living in London, John Rand, patented a small, squeezable metal tube that could be sealed with a cap. Suddenly, paint was portable and stayed fresh.

W: Now combine that with a few other changes, like folding easels and new railway lines out of the city, and painters could work directly in the countryside, catching changing light as it happened. Monet, for example, painted the same haystacks again and again at different times of day.

W: Renoir is often quoted as saying that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Maybe that's a slight exaggeration, but it makes a fair point. Sometimes a change in art depends on a change in technology.

lt-ts027.x: Listen to part of a talk in a music theory class.
sc: M: If you look at a page of music from the Baroque period, roughly sixteen hundred to seventeen fifty, you'll often notice something odd at the bottom. There's a bass line, and above or below some of the notes, there are little numbers. What are those numbers doing there?

M: They're part of a system called basso continuo, or just continuo. The word continuo means continuous, because this part plays all the way through the piece, underneath the melody. It was the foundation of almost all Baroque music.

M: The continuo was usually played by at least two people. One played the bass line on a low instrument, like a cello or a bassoon. The other played chords on a keyboard, like a harpsichord or an organ, or sometimes on a lute. But here's the interesting part. The composer didn't write out those chords. The keyboard player only got the bass line and those numbers, which showed which chords to play. The player had to make up the actual notes on the spot.
M: If that sounds familiar, it should. A jazz pianist reading chord symbols is doing something very similar. So Baroque keyboard players had to be skilled improvisers.

M: By the later seventeen hundreds, composers started writing out more of the parts in full, and the continuo slowly faded away. But for about a hundred and fifty years, you could hardly imagine music without it.

lt-ts028.x: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.
sc: W: When you walk into a fast-food restaurant or a hotel that's part of a big brand, you might assume the big company owns it. Very often, it doesn't. It's a franchise. Today let's look at how that model works, and why it's so common.

W: In a franchise, there are two sides. The franchisor is the company that owns the brand and the system. The franchisee is usually a local businessperson who buys the right to open a location using that brand. The franchisee pays an upfront fee, and then ongoing payments called royalties, usually a percentage of sales.

W: So what does each side get? The franchisor can grow very quickly without spending its own money on every new location, because the franchisee puts up most of the investment. And a local owner who's risking their own savings tends to work harder than a hired manager might.

W: The franchisee, on the other hand, gets a proven system. Customers already know the name, there's training, and there are deals with suppliers. Starting a business from scratch is risky, and this lowers the risk.

W: But of course, there's a price beyond the fees. Franchisees have to follow strict rules about the menu, the decor, even the uniforms. They give up a lot of independence. And for the franchisor, one badly run location can hurt the reputation of the whole brand.

lt-ts029.x: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
sc: W: If you've ever listened to bilingual friends talking, you may have noticed them moving between two languages, sometimes in the middle of a single sentence. Linguists call this code-switching.

W: For a long time, people saw it as a sign of weakness. The assumption was that speakers switched because they didn't know either language well enough, so they grabbed whatever word came first. Some teachers even tried to discourage it.

W: But when researchers started recording real conversations, they found something very different. In a well-known study of Spanish and English speakers in New York around nineteen eighty, the speakers who switched most smoothly, even within sentences, tended to be the ones who were most fluent in both languages. And the switches weren't random. They tended to happen at points where the grammar of both languages fit together, so neither language's rules were broken.

W: So why do people switch? Often, it's social. A switch can show a shared identity, as if to say, we're part of the same community. It can add emphasis, or mark a quotation, when you repeat what someone said in the language they said it in. And sometimes, a word in one language just captures an idea better.
W: So rather than a sign of confusion, code-switching is now generally seen as a skill, a flexible use of two complete systems.

lt-ts030.x: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
sc: M: Most trees would die if you flooded their roots with seawater twice a day. But mangroves thrive in exactly those conditions, along tropical and subtropical coastlines around the world.

M: So how do they manage it? There are two big challenges: salt and oxygen. For salt, different species have different tricks. Some filter most of the salt out at the roots. Others take it in and then push it out through their leaves. You can sometimes see tiny salt crystals on the leaf surface.

M: Oxygen is the other problem. Coastal mud is waterlogged, so there's very little oxygen in it. Some mangroves solve this with roots that grow upward, sticking out of the mud like pencils. At low tide, these roots take in air.

M: Now, why should we care about mangroves? Well, that dense tangle of roots slows down waves and holds the soil in place, so mangroves protect the coastline from erosion and storm waves. The roots also make a sheltered nursery where young fish can grow up, away from larger predators. And mangrove soils store huge amounts of carbon, often more per hectare than many forests on land.

M: Unfortunately, large areas have been cleared over the past few decades, for shrimp farms and coastal building. The good news is that many countries are now replanting them, and when it's done in the right places, they can recover fairly well.

lc-ts077.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a registrar's office employee.

lc-ts079.x: Listen to a conversation between two students planning a field trip.

lc-ts080.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and her academic advisor.

lc-ts082.x: Listen to a conversation between two coworkers at a campus cafe.

lc-ts083.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at a career fair.

lc-ts084.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a landlord about a security deposit.

lc-ts085.x: Listen to a conversation between a graduate student and a professor.

lc-ts086.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a computer lab assistant.

lc-ts099.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about a campus lecture.

lc-ts100.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a coordinator for a campus tour group.

lc-ts101.x: Listen to a conversation between a graduate student and her advisor.

lc-ts102.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a landlord.

W: Well, I'll have to discuss it with the club. Can you give me until tomorrow to decide?
M: Of course. Just let me know by noon.

lc-ts106.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the registrar's office.
sc: W: Hi, I'm hoping to withdraw from my economics course. I know the deadline passed on Friday.
M: It did. Once it passes, a withdrawal needs the dean's approval.
W: I figured as much. Is there any wiggle room if there's a medical reason?
M: There can be. Do you have documentation?
W: I was in the hospital for a week in October. My doctor wrote a letter, but I didn't submit it earlier because I was catching up on everything.
M: I see. Well, I can't promise the dean will agree, but a letter helps a great deal.
W: How long does the decision take?
M: Usually about ten days. In the meantime, I'd keep attending class, just in case.
W: That makes sense. I'd hate to fall further behind.
M: Fill out this form and attach the letter. I'll walk it over this afternoon.

lc-ts107.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a technology help desk worker.
sc: M: My thesis file won't open. It says it's corrupted, and I have a draft due tomorrow.
W: Oh no. When did you last save it?
M: Around noon. I've been working on it for hours since, but the program froze, and I had to restart.
W: Let's not panic yet. Most programs create a hidden backup. Let me look for a recovery copy.
M: I tried searching but found nothing.
W: You wouldn't have. It's stored in a different folder. Ah, here it is. This one was saved at three fifteen.
M: That's great. That's only about forty minutes of work I'd have to redo.
W: Exactly. I'd also suggest turning on cloud storage, so this doesn't happen again.
M: I always thought that was more trouble than it's worth.
W: After today, you may change your mind.

lc-ts108.x: Listen to a conversation between two students planning a field trip.
sc: W: I just heard back from the park office. They can't take our group on the twelfth.
M: Seriously? We booked the bus for that date.
W: I know. They said a school group already reserved the guide that day. But they offered the nineteenth.
M: The nineteenth is the week of midterms. A lot of people will say no.
W: That's what I thought. What if we skip the guide and just hike the trail on our own?
M: The guide was the main selling point, though. She explains the rock formations.
W: True. Well, we could record a short audio guide ourselves and play it at the viewpoints.
M: Hmm, that's ambitious, but it could work. It'd need more preparation than I'd like.
W: Let's ask Professor Diaz. She may know another guide.
M: Good thinking. I'll cancel the bus only after we hear from her.

lc-ts109.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in a study group.
sc: M: Before we start, I should tell you I won't be able to make the next two sessions. My part-time job added shifts on Tuesdays, since they're short-staffed.
W: That's a shame. We were counting on you to explain the statistics section.
M: I know. I feel bad. Maybe I could record a summary and send it to everyone?
W: That would help, but explaining in person is better. We can ask questions.
M: Fair enough. How about this? I'll meet one of you on Friday for an hour, and you can pass it on.
W: Hmm. Friday is when most of us go home for the weekend.
M: Then what do you suggest?
W: Let me ask the others. Maybe we can switch the group to Wednesday.
M: I'd be grateful. Honestly, I don't want to drag the group down.

lc-ts110.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a supervisor at a part-time job in the campus bookstore.
sc: W: Kwame, can I borrow you for a moment? We're about to launch the new loyalty card program, and I'd like you to sign customers up. Each person who joins gets ten percent off their next purchase.
M: That sounds like an easy sell.
W: You'd think so, but many students feel pressured when staff ask them to sign up.
M: Right. I've seen people roll their eyes when they're asked.
W: So here's my idea. Don't push it. Just mention it once, while ringing up the order, and let them decide.
M: A soft sell, in other words.
W: Precisely. Another thing, the form requires an email address, so please check the spelling before you submit it.
M: Got it. Should I start today?
W: Tomorrow. I'll hold a ten-minute briefing at opening.

lc-ts111.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor in the professor's office.
sc: W: Professor Adeyemi, I was hoping you'd consider taking me on as a research assistant this spring.
M: I'm flattered, Olga. You did excellent work in my seminar.
W: Thank you. I'd mostly be entering data and helping with interviews.
M: The thing is, my grant doesn't cover student positions this year, and I'm already stretched thin.
W: I'd be willing to volunteer for credit instead of pay.
M: That's generous. Have you spoken with Dr. Kim? She's launching a project on migration, and I happen to know she's looking for help.
W: I haven't, but my interests lean toward your area.
M: I understand. Still, a start with her could open doors, and I'd be glad to write you a recommendation.
W: I see. I suppose it wouldn't hurt to ask her.
M: Exactly. Tell her I sent you.

lc-ts112.x: Listen to a conversation between a tenant and a landlord.
sc: W: Mr. Brooks, I wanted to talk to you about the lease. My roommate is moving out in May.
M: I see. Do you intend to stay through August?
W: I'd like to. But I can't afford the rent on my own.
M: Have you found someone to replace your roommate?
W: Not yet. I've posted a notice at the student center. What if I can't find someone in time?
M: Then I could let you move to a smaller unit on the first floor. It's cheaper, but there's a waiting list.
W: A waiting list? Hmm. I'd rather not leave things up in the air.
M: Then I'd put your name down today, just as a backup.
W: That sounds like a sensible precaution.

lc-ts113.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about a campus event.
sc: M: Are you still planning to come to the poetry reading on Thursday?
W: I was, but something came up. My lab partner can only meet that evening.
M: That's too bad. I thought you were looking forward to hearing Professor Alvarez.
W: I was. Is it recorded?
M: Probably not. They usually just stream it live.
W: Then maybe I'll try to catch the first twenty minutes. I could meet my partner later.
M: Won't that be rushed? The reading starts at six, and you said the lab closes at eight.
W: It will be tight. Honestly, I'm torn.
M: You know, you could ask your partner to switch to Friday. Labs are usually open all day.
W: Hmm. It's worth a try. I'll text her tonight.

lc-ts114.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and an advisor about graduation requirements.
sc: W: I just got my degree audit, and it says I'm missing a humanities credit. I thought I'd finished all of them.
M: Let me pull it up. Ah, I see. The art history course you took last year counted as a social science, not a humanity.
W: That doesn't make sense. It's taught in the humanities building.
M: I agree it's confusing, but the classification follows the catalog, not the building.
W: So I need another course. I'm graduating in May.
M: You've got time. There are several options this spring, and some meet online.
W: Online is better, since I'm working three days a week.
M: Then I'd look at the philosophy of science course. It fits the requirement, and the workload is moderate.
W: Okay. That sounds like a plan. Can you enroll me today?
M: Gladly. Let me just make sure there's space.

lc-ts115.x: Listen to a conversation between a graduate student and a lab technician.
sc: W: Ivan, did you get a chance to look at my request to use the freezer space?
M: I did. The thing is, we're nearly full. Everyone's been storing samples there this month.
W: I only need one shelf for a few weeks.
M: I get that, but there's a process. The lab director decides who gets space.
W: Can't you make an exception? You've done it before.
M: That was for a short-term project. Yours sounds more like a permanent arrangement.
W: Fair point. Is there a different freezer I could use?
M: The one in the basement has room, though it's not temperature-monitored. For delicate samples, I wouldn't risk it.
W: Mine are quite delicate. I suppose I'll have to ask the director then.
M: I'll mention it to her today, so your name's on her radar.

lc-ts116.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in a linguistics study group.
sc: M: So are we agreed on who presents the phonetics part on Monday?
W: I thought I'd do it, but honestly, I'm swamped this week. I've got two papers due.
M: I can take it. I did the phonetics reading last night anyway.
W: That would be a huge help. I'll make it up to you by handling the slides.
M: Deal. But the professor wants a short demonstration, and I'm not sure what to show.
W: What about recording a few classmates saying the same word and comparing how it sounds?
M: Interesting. That would show regional differences, which ties in with the lecture.
W: Right. And it takes only five minutes.
M: Then I'll need volunteers. Would you be willing to be one?
W: Sure, as long as I don't have to say anything embarrassing.

lc-ts117.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and the manager of a campus cafe.
sc: W: Mr. Patel, I'm sorry to bring this up, but I need to talk about my hours.
M: Sure, what's going on?
W: My coursework has gotten heavier, and the Friday closing shifts leave me exhausted for my Saturday class.
M: I see. We're short on weekends, so I can't simply remove them.
W: I understand. Would it be possible to swap with someone who prefers evenings?
M: Maybe. I'd have to see who would be willing. Have you asked around?
W: Not yet. I wanted to speak to you first, out of respect.
M: I appreciate that. Tell you what, post a note in the staff room, and if someone bites, I'll approve it.
W: Thank you. And if no one does?
M: Then we'll revisit it. I don't want you burning out.

lc-ts118.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a student events organizer.
sc: W: Welcome to the planning meeting for the spring festival. What do you have in mind for your booth?
M: We want to run a small competition where visitors drive tiny robots through an obstacle course.
W: That sounds fun. The only concern is space. Most booths get a table and a small area.
M: We'd need about four meters in length.
W: That's larger than usual. We might be able to put you near the end of the lawn, but there's a drainage ditch.
M: Is that a serious problem? Could we build over it?
W: Not really, I'm afraid. The grounds team wouldn't allow it.
M: Okay. Then we'll try to design a shorter course. Is three meters possible?
W: I'll check. Come back to me by Wednesday.

lc-ts119.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a technology help desk worker.
sc: W: I'm having trouble with the online exam software. It keeps telling me my camera isn't detected.
M: Is the camera working in other programs?
W: Yes, it works fine in video calls.
M: Then the exam program may not have permission. Check your privacy settings and allow the exam program to use the camera.
W: I did that already. It still doesn't recognize it.
M: In that case, try a different browser. This software behaves better on certain ones.
W: I'm already using the one the instructions recommended.
M: Hmm. Well, I'd rather not have you guessing. When is your exam?
W: Tomorrow at nine.
M: Then let me open a ticket and mark it urgent. Someone from the technical team should call you tonight.

lc-ts120.x: Listen to a conversation between two students planning a field trip to a local farm.
sc: W: I just spoke to the farm owner. She says we can visit on the sixth, but only from nine to noon.
M: That's quite short. I was hoping we'd see the harvest and the soil testing.
W: She said the harvest takes place in the afternoon, so we'd miss it.
M: Then maybe a different date is better. What about the following week?
W: The professor can't make it that day. And the bus is booked for the sixth already.
M: Hmm, so our hands are tied.
W: Pretty much. But we could ask the owner to demonstrate the soil testing in the morning instead.
M: That might work. Could she show a few harvested vegetables too?
W: I'll ask. She sounded flexible.
M: Great. I'll write up the schedule so everyone knows what to expect.

lc-ts121.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and her advisor about a study abroad program.
sc: W: I wanted to ask about the exchange program in Lisbon. The application is due Friday.
M: Yes, I remember you mentioned it. Have you gathered your documents?
W: Mostly. I still need a letter from a professor, and I'm worried it won't arrive in time.
M: Which professor did you ask?
W: Dr. Fonseca. She said she'd get to it when she could.
M: Well, that doesn't sound like a firm promise. I'd send her a polite reminder first, and mention the Friday deadline plainly.
W: And then what?
M: If you don't hear back by Wednesday, come see me. Then I'll write a note of support myself, and we'll see if the committee accepts it.
W: That's a load off my mind. Thank you.

lc-ts122.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a lab supervisor.
sc: W: Hamza, I noticed the chemical storage cabinet was left unlocked last night.
M: Oh, I'm so sorry. I was the last one out, and I was in a hurry.
W: I understand. But with the shared lab, we can't afford any slip-ups, even small ones.
M: It won't happen again. I'll double-check the cabinet before I leave.
W: I'd appreciate that. We also have a checklist taped to the door for exactly this reason.
M: I saw it, but I assumed it was for the evening technicians.
W: It applies to everyone, I'm afraid. Please read it carefully.
M: Will I have to sign something?
W: Not this time. Consider it a gentle reminder. But if it happens again, I'd have to report it to the director.
M: Understood. Thanks for being reasonable about it.

lc-ts123.x: Listen to a conversation between two students planning a campus event.
sc: M: Have you finalized the guest list for the career panel?
W: Almost. The alumni from the marketing firm confirmed, but the engineer hasn't answered.
M: We can't wait much longer. The posters need to go up Monday.
W: I know. I'll send a last email tonight. If she hasn't replied by tomorrow, I'll call her office.
M: What if she says no? We'd have only three speakers.
W: Then we could ask Dr. Osei to join. He's known to be generous with his time.
M: Great, but a professor isn't quite the same as someone working in the industry.
W: True. Still, he worked in an engineering firm for ten years before teaching.
M: Oh, I didn't know that. That would work nicely.
W: Let's keep it as plan B. I'm hopeful she'll agree.

lc-ts124.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the housing office.
sc: W: Hello, I'd like to ask about changing my residence hall for next year.
M: Sure. Are you applying for a specific building?
W: I'd love Maple Hall. My friends are living there.
M: Maple Hall is popular. Rooms are assigned by lottery, and your number is drawn at random.
W: Is there any way to improve my odds?
M: Not exactly. But if you and a friend apply together as a pair, you share the better of your two numbers.
W: That's useful. And if we don't get Maple?
M: Then you'd be placed in the next available hall, which could be across campus.
W: That would be a hassle, since my classes are near the library.
M: It's a gamble, but many students find a good fit anyway. The deadline is next Thursday.

lc-ts125.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at an on-campus print shop.
sc: W: Hi, I need my poster printed by tomorrow morning. It's for a conference.
M: What size is it?
W: Thirty-six by forty-eight inches.
M: That's one of our larger formats. Normally we need two business days.
W: Two days? My presentation is tomorrow at nine.
M: I see. Let me check the schedule. Hmm, our big printer is running a job right now, but I could squeeze yours in tonight.
W: That would save me. Is there an extra charge for rush work?
M: Fifteen dollars, I'm afraid.
W: That's fine. Honestly, I should have started earlier.
M: It happens a lot before conferences. Send the file now, and I'll check it for problems before printing.

lc-ts126.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor about a late assignment.
sc: W: Professor Hall, I'm afraid I haven't finished the research paper. Could I get an extension?
M: Hmm. The paper was assigned five weeks ago.
W: I know. I had a lot going on, and I underestimated how long the analysis would take.
M: I appreciate your honesty. But I did make the deadline clear, and others have turned theirs in.
W: Of course. I wouldn't ask if I had any other choice.
M: Let me think. I can't give you a week, but I could accept it by Monday morning, with a small deduction.
W: That would be very generous. How much of a deduction?
M: Ten percent. Think of it as a fair compromise.
W: I'll take it. I'll work through the weekend.
M: Good. And next time, come to me sooner. Problems are easier to solve early.

lc-ts127.x: Listen to a conversation between two researchers in a biology lab.
sc: M: Have you seen the readings from the tank this morning? The oxygen levels dipped overnight.
W: I did. I think the pump slowed down. I've asked maintenance to check it.
M: If the fish are stressed, our whole growth study might be affected.
W: That's what worries me. But I wouldn't jump to conclusions. Let's look at the fish first.
M: They seem sluggish, though not badly so.
W: Then we should keep the data but add a note about the dip.
M: Or we could rerun this week's measurements once the pump is fixed.
W: That would be cleaner, but our grant report is due Friday.
M: Right. We can't rerun them and still finish on time.
W: So we'll flag it in the report and explain. Honest reporting is better than hiding a flaw.

lc-ts128.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a landlord about a broken appliance.
sc: W: Mr. Lopez, the washing machine in the basement has been out of order for a week.
M: I know, and I'm sorry. The repair person was supposed to come on Monday.
W: Did she come?
M: She called to say she was running behind. I'm waiting to hear when she can come.
W: I see. It's just that laundry is becoming a problem. The laundromat is across town.
M: I understand. Look, I can't make her come faster, but I could offer you a credit on your rent for the inconvenience.
W: Honestly, I'd rather have a working machine than a credit.
M: Fair enough. Let me call another company and see if they can come tomorrow.
W: I'd appreciate that. Thank you for being flexible.
M: Of course. I'll message you once it's arranged.

lc-ts129.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a help desk worker about email.
sc: M: I'm not getting any emails from my professors. I checked my spam folder and found nothing.
W: Let me look at your account. Hmm, your inbox is at its storage limit.
M: Really? I thought it had plenty of room.
W: Attachments pile up quickly. New messages get blocked once it's full.
M: That explains why Professor Wu said she sent me the syllabus twice.
W: Most likely. I can clear some space, but you should delete the old ones yourself, so I don't remove anything important.
M: Which ones should I look at first?
W: Sort by size. Those with large attachments take up the most space.
M: Great idea. Will the blocked messages come back?
W: Unfortunately not. Anything sent while it was full is gone, so ask your professors to resend what you missed.

lc-ts130.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in a study group preparing for a psychology test.
sc: W: I printed the review sheet, but some of the terms aren't covered in our notes.
M: Like which ones?
W: Cognitive dissonance, for one. I don't recall the professor explaining it.
M: She did, in the second week, using the example of a smoker who knows smoking is harmful.
W: Oh right. The discomfort someone feels when their beliefs and actions don't match.
M: Exactly. And people usually resolve it by changing one or the other.
W: I'd have trouble explaining that on a test, though.
M: Try coming up with your own example. It sticks better than a definition.
W: Okay. Someone who values health but skips exercise?
M: Perfect. That's a solid example, and now you won't forget it.

lc-ts131.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the registrar's office.
sc: W: Hi, I think there's an error on my record. It says I haven't completed the swimming requirement.
M: Let me look. Hmm, it shows an incomplete mark from two years ago.
W: I did pass that course. I remember receiving a certificate.
M: Do you still have it?
W: Not with me, but my instructor might. I could ask her.
M: That would help. The instructor can email us a corrected grade form.
W: How long does the change usually take?
M: Once we receive the form, about three business days. But I wouldn't wait until the last minute.
W: My graduation check is next Friday.
M: Then I'd contact her today. It's not unheard of for these things to drag on.

lc-ts132.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about a change in a field trip plan.
sc: M: I heard the trip to the observatory might be canceled. Is that true?
W: Not canceled, exactly. The clouds are forecast for Saturday, so the professor is thinking of moving it.
M: Moving it where? Another observatory?
W: No, to the planetarium downtown. We'd see simulated skies instead.
M: Honestly, that sounds like a consolation prize.
W: I thought so too. But she says the planetarium offers a guided talk about the telescope images.
M: That's something, I guess. When would we go?
W: Friday afternoon, during our regular class time. We wouldn't need to travel on the weekend, which might be convenient for those who work Saturdays. She's polling the class tonight.
M: Then I'll vote for the planetarium. A real sky would be better, but a certain talk beats a cloudy night.

lc-ts133.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a manager at a campus gym where the student works.
sc: W: Luis, thanks for stopping by. I'd like to talk about the new member check-in system.
M: Is there a problem? I've been scanning the cards as trained.
W: No, you're doing well. Actually, I wanted your opinion. A few members complained it's slower than the old system.
M: To be honest, it is. The scanner sometimes needs two tries.
W: That's helpful to know. Do you think the problem is the scanner or the cards?
M: Probably the cards. The older ones are worn, so the code doesn't read well.
W: I suspected that. We could replace the cards, but it'd cost a fair bit.
M: What about replacing only the worst ones? Members could bring them in.
W: Interesting. That's a smaller commitment. Could you make a list of what you've seen?
M: Sure, I'll keep track during my shifts this week.

lc-ts134.x: Listen to a conversation between a graduate student and her advisor about a conference.
sc: W: I got the email. My abstract was accepted for the conference in Toronto.
M: Congratulations! That's great news. When is it?
W: In March. But the registration fee is steep, and I don't think the department covers travel.
M: Actually, it might. There's a fund for students presenting their own work. Have you applied?
W: I didn't know about it. Is it competitive?
M: Not very. But the application asks for a letter from your advisor, which I'd be happy to write.
W: That's wonderful. I was ready to pay out of my own pocket.
M: Don't do that yet. Apply first. The deadline is in two weeks.
W: I'll start tonight. Should I mention my other publication?
M: Absolutely. Anything that shows momentum helps.

lc-ts135.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in a research lab.
sc: W: I'm thinking of asking Dr. Chen if I can switch to the morning lab section.
M: Why? I thought you liked the afternoon one.
W: I did, but I just got a job offer on campus that starts at one.
M: Congratulations! Will it conflict with anything else?
W: Possibly. The morning section runs until twelve thirty, which leaves me barely enough time to eat.
M: That's tight. But you'd manage.
W: I think so. The real question is whether there's room in the morning group.
M: I heard it's almost full. You may want to ask soon.
W: I'll email her tonight. Do you think she'll say yes?
M: Honestly, she's pretty reasonable. Just explain the job situation. She likes students who work.

lc-ts136.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor after class.
sc: W: Professor Mensah, do you have a minute? I wanted to ask about the group project.
M: Of course. What's on your mind?
W: My group hasn't been pulling together. Two members haven't replied to messages in a week.
M: That's frustrating. Have you tried meeting in person?
W: I suggested it, but they said they were too busy.
M: I see. Well, I don't usually step in. Learning to manage a team is part of the exercise.
W: I understand. I just don't want my grade to suffer.
M: Keep a record of your own contributions. If the work is uneven, I'll take that into account.
W: So you won't change the groups?
M: Not at this stage. But if you document everything, you'll be protected.

lc-ts137.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about a campus concert.
sc: M: Did you manage to get tickets for Saturday's concert?
W: I was going to, but they sold out in an hour. I was a few minutes too late.
M: Too bad. I got two, actually. My friend can't come, so I have a spare.
W: Really? How much?
M: Face value, fifteen dollars. I'd feel bad charging more.
W: That's kind. Are you sure you wouldn't rather invite someone else?
M: Honestly, I'd rather go with someone who loves the band, and you've talked about them all semester.
W: I have. Okay, I'll take it. Can I pay you tomorrow?
M: Sure, no rush. Just meet me at the entrance by seven thirty.
W: Perfect. I owe you one.

lc-ts138.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a landlord about subletting.
sc: W: Mr. Chowdhury, I'm hoping to sublet my room this summer while I'm away at an internship.
M: That's something I'd need to review. Who would be staying there?
W: A friend of mine from my department. Her name is Sofia.
M: Has she lived in the building before?
W: No, but she's very responsible. She's a graduate student.
M: I'm sure she is. The thing is, the lease says all occupants must be approved, and the process takes about two weeks.
W: I'm leaving in ten days.
M: Then it's cutting it close. I could rush it if she sends the paperwork tomorrow.
W: I can have her do that tonight.
M: Good. Remember, you're still responsible for the rent, regardless of who lives there.

lc-ts139.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus technology help desk.
sc: W: Hi, I'm trying to install the statistics software, but the installer says my computer doesn't meet the requirements.
M: What kind of computer do you have?
W: An older laptop. It's about six years old.
M: That could be the issue. The latest version needs more memory than most older machines have.
W: That's frustrating. Is there any way around it?
M: A couple of options. There's an older version that might run, though it lacks some features your course may require, or you could use the lab computers.
W: Hmm. I prefer working at home, though.
M: Understood. In that case, there's also a web version you can use in your browser. It's slower, but it works with any computer.
W: That might be best. How do I log in?
M: Use your student ID. I'll write the address down for you.

lc-ts140.x: Listen to a conversation between two students working in a psychology research lab.
sc: W: How did the pilot session go yesterday?
M: Mixed, I'd say. The participants understood the task, but the timer kept freezing.
W: That's a problem. Dr. Roy wants to start the real sessions on Monday.
M: I know. I contacted the software company, and they're looking into it.
W: Do you have a backup plan?
M: I could use a stopwatch. It's old school, but it would work.
W: Wouldn't that introduce human error? A fraction of a second matters in this study.
M: You're right. I hadn't considered that.
W: What if we ask Dr. Roy to postpone until the software is fixed?
M: She won't like it, but a delay is better than unreliable data.

lc-ps001.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a landlord.
sc: W: Hello, Mr. Smith. The light in my kitchen isn't working.
M: Oh, I'm sorry. Did you try a new light bulb?
W: Yes, I did. I put in a new one this morning, but it still doesn't turn on.
M: Then maybe the switch is broken. I can send an electrician.
W: That would be great. When can he come?
M: Tomorrow afternoon, around three. Will you be home?
W: I have class until four. Can he come after that?
M: Sure. I'll ask him to come at four thirty.
W: Thank you very much. I'll be home by then.

lc-ps002.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in the library.
sc: M: Hi, Maria. Are you studying for the biology test?
W: Yes, it's on Friday. I'm reading chapter five now.
M: Chapter five is hard. I don't understand the part about cells.
W: I can help you. I made some notes yesterday.
M: Really? That would be great. Can I see them?
W: Sure. They're in my bag. Here you are.
M: Wow, your notes are very clear. Thank you!

lc-ts029.x: Listen to a conversation between two students on a train.

M: Hi, Priya. I'm going to visit my sister in the city. She just moved there for work.
W: Oh, nice. I'm going to a concert tonight. It's my favorite band.
M: Really? Which one?
W: The Blue Rivers. They're playing at the big theater near the station.
M: I've heard of them. Aren't they from your country?
W: Yes, they are! They rarely tour here, so I bought tickets months ago.
M: That's great. Maybe my sister and I could go next time.
W: Definitely. I'll let you know when they come back.

lc-ts030.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a gym trainer.
sc: W: Hi, I'm Dana. Are you new here?
M: Yes. I want to build muscle, but I don't know where to start.
W: Do you have any injuries?
M: Just a sore shoulder from last year. It's mostly fine now.
W: Okay. Then let's avoid heavy lifting at first. We'll use lighter weights and do more repetitions.
M: How often should I come?
W: Three times a week is plenty for a beginner. Rest days are important too.
M: Great. Can you show me the machines now?
W: Sure. Follow me, and we'll start with a short warm-up.

lc-ts031.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore clerk.
sc: W: Hi. Do you buy back used textbooks?
M: We do, but only if the book will be used next semester. What's the title?
W: Introduction to Economics, the newest edition.
M: Let me check the computer. Yes, we need that one. We can give you thirty dollars for it.
W: Thirty? I paid eighty-five for it.
M: I know, it's not much. You could also sell it online and get more, but then you'd have to wait for a buyer.
W: I'd rather get money today. Does the book look okay?
M: It looks fine, just a few notes in pencil. I'll take it.

lc-ts032.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor during office hours.
sc: W: Professor Singh, I wanted to ask about the research position you mentioned in class.
M: Yes, I need a student to help me enter data in the spring. It's about ten hours a week.
W: That sounds perfect. Do I need any special skills?
M: You should be comfortable with spreadsheets. Have you used them?
W: In my statistics class last term. I got an A.
M: Excellent. Then I'd like to interview you on Monday. Can you come at two?
W: I have a class then. Could we meet at four instead?
M: Four works. I'll see you then, and please bring your resume.

lc-ts033.x: Listen to a conversation between two roommates.
sc: W: Mateo, did you take my yogurt from the fridge?
M: Oh no. I thought it was mine. I'm so sorry.
W: It's okay, but it happened twice this week. Maybe we should label our food.
M: Good idea. I could buy some stickers tomorrow.
W: Or we could use separate shelves. You take the top one, and I'll take the bottom.
M: That's even easier. Let me move my things now.
W: Thanks. And I'll buy you a new yogurt tomorrow, since I used your milk last week.
M: Ha, okay. Then we're even.

lc-ts034.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a club member.
sc: W: Welcome to the chess club. Are you interested in joining?
M: Yes. I learned chess when I was young, but I haven't played in years.
W: That's fine. We have players of all levels. We meet on Thursdays from five to seven.
M: Do I need to bring my own board?
W: No, we have plenty. But if you want to improve, I recommend our beginner lessons on Mondays.
M: I'd like that. Are they free?
W: Yes, they're free for members. The annual fee is just five dollars.
M: That's a bargain. Where do I sign up?
W: Right here. Just write your name and email.

lc-ts035.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a train ticket agent.
sc: W: Hi, I bought a ticket online, but I need to change the date.
M: Let me look it up. Name, please?
W: Chen Wei. I'm traveling to Boston on Friday, but I'd like to go Saturday instead.
M: I see it. Changing costs fifteen dollars, plus the difference in fare. Saturday trains are a little more expensive.
W: How much more?
M: Five dollars. So twenty in total.
W: That's okay. I have a family event on Friday that I forgot about.
M: No problem. Here's your new ticket. The train leaves at nine from platform two.

lc-ts036.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a cafeteria cashier.
sc: W: Hi. Is that everything today?
M: Yes, just the sandwich and a juice. Oh, wait. Is there a discount for students?
W: Only if you pay with your campus card.
M: I have it somewhere. Hold on. Here it is.
W: Perfect. Let me scan it. That's four dollars and twenty cents.
M: Wow, that's cheaper than I expected. Last week I paid six dollars for the same meal.
W: The discount just started on Monday. It's every day until the end of the term.
M: Great news. I'll be here more often then.

lc-ts037.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a library worker.
sc: W: Hello. I'd like to know how to find articles for my history paper.
M: Sure. Do you know which database you want?
W: No. My professor only said to use academic sources, not websites.
M: Then start with the library's main search page. You can type your topic and choose only peer-reviewed articles.
W: Peer-reviewed? What does that mean?
M: It means other experts checked the article before it was published, so it's more reliable.
W: Oh, I see. Can I do this from my dorm?
M: Yes, just log in with your student number. And there's a workshop on Thursday if you want more help.

lc-ts038.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a roommate about chores.
sc: W: Kwame, can I ask you something? Are you planning to stay in this apartment next year?
M: I think so. Why?
W: My cousin is looking for a place, and she might want my room if I leave.
M: Are you leaving? I thought you liked it here.
W: I do, but I got an internship in another city next fall.
M: Congratulations! That's great news. When will you know for sure?
W: I'll find out next week. I'd like to tell the landlord as early as possible.
M: Okay. If you move, I wouldn't mind meeting your cousin first.

lc-ts039.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a health center doctor.
sc: W: So, Aaron, you said you've been having headaches. How often?
M: Almost every afternoon for two weeks.
W: Are you drinking enough water?
M: Probably not. I drink coffee, mostly.
W: That could be part of it. How about sleep?
M: I stay up late studying. Maybe five hours a night.
W: That's definitely too little. I'd like you to sleep at least seven hours and drink more water. Come back in two weeks if the headaches continue.
M: I'll try. Exams are next week, though.
W: I understand. Even short breaks will help.

lc-ts040.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bus station worker.
sc: W: Can I help you find something?
M: Yes, I left my backpack on the number twelve bus this morning. It's black with a red zipper.
W: Do you remember what time you got off?
M: Around eight thirty, at the university stop.
W: Let me check the lost and found. We got several bags from that route today.
M: My laptop is inside. I'm really worried.
W: I see a black bag with a red zipper here. Can you tell me what else is in it?
M: A blue notebook, a water bottle, and my keys.
W: That matches. Here you go. Please check everything.

lc-ts041.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.
sc: W: Hi. I'm doing a project on urban gardening, and I'm struggling to find recent research.
M: What have you tried so far?
W: I searched the catalog, but most of the books are from the nineties.
M: Books can get outdated quickly in that field. Have you tried the journal databases?
W: I looked at one, but there were hundreds of results. I didn't know which ones to trust.
M: Let's narrow it down. We can limit the dates to the last five years and add the word community.
W: Oh, that's a smart way to filter. Will that exclude useful older studies?
M: Possibly, but you can cite a few classic ones separately. I'd start with the recent ones, though.
W: That makes sense. Could you show me how to save the search?
M: Sure, it only takes a moment.

lc-ts042.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
sc: W: Daniel, I got your email about the lab report. What's the issue?
M: I ran the experiment twice, and the results don't match my hypothesis. I'm afraid I did something wrong.
W: Not necessarily. Tell me what you expected.
M: I predicted that the plants with more light would grow taller. But the ones in the shade grew faster.
W: That's interesting. Did you control the water and the soil?
M: I tried to, but the shaded pots were near the window, so they might have been warmer.
W: That could be a confounding variable. Mention it in your discussion section.
M: So I shouldn't change my results?
W: Absolutely not. Report what you found and explain possible reasons. Honest data is more valuable than perfect data.

lc-ts043.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a housing office worker.
sc: W: Housing office. How can I help you?
M: Hello. I received a notice that my dorm will be closed for repairs over winter break.
W: Yes, the heating system is being replaced in Oak Hall. All residents need to move out by December twentieth.
M: But I'm an international student. I can't fly home for just three weeks.
W: We understand. There's a limited number of spaces in Pine Hall for students in your situation.
M: How do I apply?
W: You fill out a short form online, and you need a letter from your department explaining why you'll stay.
M: A letter? That might take some time.
W: The deadline is next Friday, so there's time. After that, we assign rooms on a first-come basis.

lc-ts044.x: Listen to a conversation between two students in a cafeteria.
sc: W: Hamza, you look exhausted. Did you stay up late again?
M: I did. I was working on my business plan for the entrepreneurship class.
W: Isn't that due next month?
M: It is, but I want to start early. Last term I left everything to the last minute, and my grade suffered.
W: I did the same thing in chemistry. I thought I worked better under pressure.
M: Do you?
W: Not really. I made silly mistakes. This term I break big assignments into small steps.
M: That sounds smart. Could you show me your method?
W: Sure. I use a calendar app and set mini deadlines every few days. I'll send you a template tonight.

lc-ts045.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a gym employee.
sc: W: Hi, how can I help you?
M: I'd like to cancel my membership. I'm moving to another city at the end of the month.
W: I'm sorry to hear that. Our policy says you need to give thirty days' notice.
M: Thirty days? But I'm leaving in three weeks.
W: Then you'd be charged for the extra week. It's about twelve dollars.
M: That seems unfair. I've been a member for two years, and I've never missed a payment.
W: I understand. Let me ask my manager. Sometimes we can make an exception for longtime members.
M: I'd appreciate that.
W: Give me a minute. I'll be right back.

lc-ts046.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
sc: W: Professor Alvarez, thanks for meeting with me. I'm having trouble choosing between two topics for my sociology paper.
M: Tell me about them.
W: One is about how social media affects friendships. The other is about why people move from small towns to big cities.
M: Both are interesting. Which one do you have more access to data on?
W: Probably the social media one. There are lots of surveys online.
M: But is that what you're passionate about?
W: Honestly, I grew up in a small town, so the migration topic feels more personal.
M: Then I'd lean toward that one. Personal interest keeps you motivated, and I can suggest some census sources.
W: That would be a big help. Thank you.

lc-ts047.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore manager.
sc: W: Hi. Can I help you with something?
M: Yes. I ordered a textbook online last week for pickup here, but I haven't received an email.
W: Let me look. What's your name?
M: Ryan Park.
W: I see the order, but the status says 'delayed.' The publisher is out of stock.
M: Oh no. My class starts tomorrow, and I'll need the book for the first assignment.
W: I'm sorry. We could rent you a copy from the shelf, though. It's the same edition, but it's used and has some highlighting.
M: How much is that?
W: Thirty dollars for the term. And if your new copy arrives, you can return the rental for a full refund.
M: That works. I'd rather have a marked-up book than none.

lc-ts048.x: Listen to a conversation between two roommates.
sc: W: Lucas, we need to talk about the electricity bill. It's almost double what it was last month.
M: Really? That's strange. We haven't done anything different.
W: Well, you've been leaving your computer on all night, and the heater runs constantly.
M: I use the computer for downloads, so I leave it on. And the apartment is freezing.
W: I understand, but maybe we can wear sweaters and turn the heater down a few degrees. I'd also use a timer for your computer.
M: A timer? I didn't know that was possible.
W: You can buy one for about ten dollars. It turns the power off at a certain hour.
M: Fine. I'll pick one up this weekend. It's worth it if we save money.
W: Thanks. Let's look at next month's bill and see if it helps.

lc-ts049.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and an internship supervisor.
sc: W: Mateo, how is your first month going?
M: Good, but I have a question. In my last project, I noticed that the customer data was entered in two different formats.
W: And that bothers you?
M: It makes the reports hard to read. I wonder if we could create a standard template.
W: That's a thoughtful observation. Have you started making one?
M: I drafted something, but I wasn't sure I was allowed to change how the team works.
W: Interns aren't usually expected to, but good ideas are always welcome. Show me the draft tomorrow, and if it looks useful, we'll present it at Friday's meeting.
M: Really? I'd be honored.
W: Just keep it short. The team has limited time.

lc-ts050.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a train station employee.
sc: W: Excuse me, my train to Hartford was supposed to leave at noon. The board says it's canceled.
M: I'm sorry. A signal problem closed that line this morning. We're offering free seats on the one fifteen train instead.
W: One fifteen? That's an hour late. I have a job interview at three.
M: The ride takes about an hour and a half, so you'd arrive around two forty-five.
W: That's cutting it close. Is there any faster option?
M: You could take the bus. It leaves in ten minutes and takes the highway, so it's about the same time. But traffic can be unpredictable.
W: Then the train is safer. Can I get a seat near the door? I want to get out quickly.
M: I'll note it on your ticket. Here you are.

lc-ts051.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a health center nurse.
sc: W: Hi, Tomas. What can I do for you today?
M: I'd like to get a flu shot before the semester gets busy.
W: Smart idea. Have you ever had a bad reaction to a vaccine?
M: No, never. But I'm a little afraid of needles.
W: Many people are. It only takes a second, and I can talk with you to distract you.
M: Okay. Does it make you feel sick afterward?
W: Some people have a sore arm or feel tired for a day. It's usually mild, and much better than the real flu.
M: That's what I figured. I have a big presentation next week, so I can't afford to get sick.
W: Then you made a good choice. Roll up your sleeve, please.

lc-ts052.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
sc: W: Professor Okafor, I'd like to talk about the group presentation. One of my teammates hasn't done any work.
M: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you spoken to him?
W: Twice. He says he's busy with another class, but we present on Thursday.
M: Okay. First, are the other members managing without him?
W: Yes, but it means more work for the rest of us.
M: I see. Here's what I suggest. Talk to him once more, and give him a specific task and a deadline. If he doesn't respond, email me, and I'll step in.
W: And what about his grade? It doesn't seem fair if he gets the same as us.
M: Don't worry. Each student fills out a peer evaluation, and I take that into account.
W: That's a relief. Thank you.

lc-ts053.x: Listen to a conversation between two students at a club fair.
sc: W: Chen, are you thinking about joining a club?
M: Maybe. I'm torn between the debate club and the robotics club.
W: Those are very different. What do you like about each?
M: Debate would improve my public speaking. But robotics matches my major, and it'd look good on my resume.
W: Why not do both?
M: Time. Debate meets Tuesday and Thursday, and robotics meets Wednesday and Saturday. I also work weekends.
W: Then Saturdays are out for robotics.
M: Exactly. I could do their Wednesday workshops, but the big building sessions are Saturdays.
W: In that case, I'd go with debate. You can always join robotics next year when your schedule changes.

lc-ts054.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a cafeteria manager.
sc: W: Hi, you must be Daniel. Thanks for coming in about the job.
M: Thank you for seeing me. I'm interested in the evening shift.
W: Do you have any experience in food service?
M: Not directly. I've worked at a library desk, and I helped at my family's shop.
W: Customer service is customer service. The main challenge here is the dinner rush. It gets loud, and you need to work quickly.
M: I think I can handle that. I'm used to being busy during exams, too.
W: Ha, that's a different kind of busy. But I like your attitude. We'd start with training next Monday.
M: That would be great. Do I need to bring anything?
W: Just your ID and a pair of closed shoes. We provide the uniform.

lc-ts055.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a campus bus driver.
sc: W: Good morning. Where are you headed?
M: To the stadium. I have a game, and my team needs me there by nine.
W: This bus doesn't go there. It goes to the north dorms and then circles back to the main gate.
M: Oh no. The schedule said the green line stops at the stadium.
W: It did, but only before this term. They changed the route in September.
M: I didn't know. Is there another way?
W: Get off at the main gate and take the red line. It stops right outside the stadium. It runs every fifteen minutes.
M: That might work. What time is it now?
W: Eight twenty. If you catch the next red bus, you'll make it with a little time to spare.

lc-ts056.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.
sc: W: Hi, I borrowed a book last month, and I think I returned it, but the system says it's overdue.
M: Let me look. What's the title?
W: A History of Modern Architecture.
M: Yes, it shows that it's still checked out under your name. The fine is already six dollars.
W: I remember putting it in the return box outside. Maybe it got stuck.
M: That does happen. I'll have someone check the shelves and the box. In the meantime, I can pause the fine for a week.
W: Thank you. That's a relief.
M: If we find the book, we'll cancel the fee completely. If not, you'd need to pay for a replacement.
W: I understand. I'll come back on Friday.

lc-ts057.x: Listen to a conversation between two roommates.
sc: W: Kwame, my parents are visiting next weekend, and they'd like to stay here for two nights.
M: In our apartment? Where would they sleep?
W: I could give them my bed, and I'd use the couch. Is that okay with you?
M: Well, it's fine with me, but I have a presentation on Monday, and I need to practice. It might be noisy.
W: I'll make sure we're quiet. They usually go out in the afternoon anyway. They like to explore.
M: Then it sounds fine. Just let me know when they arrive.
W: I will. And I'd like to cook dinner on Saturday for all of us.
M: Now you're talking. I'll buy dessert.
W: Deal. Thanks for being so understanding.

lc-ts058.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
sc: W: Hello, Jun. You wanted to see me about the midterm?
M: Yes. I'd like to understand why I lost points on the essay question.
W: Let's look at it. You described the causes of the economic crisis clearly. But the question asked you to evaluate the government's response.
M: I thought describing the causes was enough.
W: It was only half. You needed to judge whether the policies worked and give evidence.
M: I see. I misread the word evaluate.
W: That's common. Look for action words in the question: compare, explain, evaluate. They tell you what to do.
M: Is it too late to improve my grade?
W: Not for the final. If you get the same question there, you'll know what to do.

lc-ts059.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a gym front desk worker.
sc: W: Hi, can I scan your card?
M: Sure. Actually, I wanted to ask about the pool. It was closed yesterday.
W: Yes, we had a filter problem. It's open again today, but the water is still being tested, so only lap swimming is allowed.
M: What does that mean?
W: No games or classes. Just swimming back and forth in lanes.
M: That's fine. I just need to do my laps. Do I need to reserve a lane?
W: Not today, but arrive early. Lanes fill up quickly when people hear it's reopened.
M: Good tip. Is the locker room open too?
W: Yes, but the showers on the left are out of order. Use the ones on the right.

lc-ts060.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a club leader.
sc: W: Hi, I'm the new treasurer for the film club. I think I'm supposed to meet you.
M: Right, Aisha. Welcome. The previous treasurer left a folder with receipts and a list of our budget.
W: Great. How much money do we have for this semester?
M: About eight hundred dollars. Most of it goes to renting the projector and buying the licenses for the movies.
W: Licenses? I didn't realize we had to pay for those.
M: Yes, to show a film publicly, we need permission. It costs around fifty dollars for each title.
W: Then we can only show about ten movies?
M: Roughly, if we don't spend on anything else. Last year, we also bought snacks, and we ran out of money in April.
W: I'll make a plan so we don't run out again.

lc-ts061.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a health center counselor.
sc: W: Come in, Marco. What's on your mind?
M: I've been feeling overwhelmed lately. I have three exams next week, a paper due, and I'm working at the cafe.
W: That's a lot. How are you sleeping?
M: Not well. I wake up thinking about everything I have to do.
W: That's very common during exam periods. Let's make a plan. Which task is due first?
M: The paper on Tuesday.
W: Then spend tonight and tomorrow on that. Could you ask your manager to change your shifts this week?
M: I could try. I've never asked before.
W: Most managers understand during exams. And do something relaxing each day, even for twenty minutes.

lc-ts062.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore clerk.
sc: W: Hi. I'm looking for a gift for my brother. He's starting college next month.
M: Congratulations to him. What's he studying?
W: Engineering. He likes building things, but he isn't much of a reader.
M: Then maybe a book isn't ideal. We have a section of desk accessories, like lamps and organizers.
W: A lamp could be useful. Which ones are popular?
M: This one is. It has an adjustable arm and a USB port, so he can charge his phone while he studies.
W: That looks practical. How much is it?
M: Twenty-eight dollars. We also have a student discount, which would make it twenty-five.
W: Perfect. I'll take it. Could you wrap it?
M: Of course. It's free.

lc-ts063.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about a class assignment.
sc: W: Daniel, did you understand today's lecture on supply and demand?
M: Mostly. The part about price changes was clear, but I got lost on elasticity.
W: Me too. The professor said it measures how much demand changes when price changes.
M: Right, but I couldn't follow the formula. Do you think we should go to office hours?
W: Maybe. Or we could watch a video first. My friend recommended a channel that explains economics with simple examples.
M: That's a good start. If we still don't get it, we can ask the professor.
W: Agreed. I'll send you the link tonight. There's a short video on elasticity of coffee prices.
M: Coffee? I might actually remember that one.
W: Exactly. Real examples help me too.

lc-ts064.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and an internship coordinator.
sc: W: Mr. Evans, I wanted to talk about my internship at the hospital. I'd like to end it early.
M: Early? You're only three weeks in. What happened?
W: Nothing bad. I realized that I'm more interested in research than patient care, and the internship is mostly the second.
M: I see. Have you discussed this with your supervisor?
W: Not yet. I wanted to check the university's rules first. Will I still get credit?
M: Only if you complete at least eighty hours. You've done about sixty.
W: So I'd need twenty more hours.
M: Right. Perhaps you could ask your supervisor to assign you research tasks for those hours. That might be the best of both worlds.
W: That's a creative solution. I'll ask tomorrow.

lc-ts065.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a train conductor.
sc: W: Tickets, please.
M: Here you go. I have a student discount, and my card is right here.
W: Thank you. Hmm, this ticket is for the morning train. This is the afternoon one.
M: Really? I must have bought the wrong time. The website was confusing.
W: I'm afraid I can't accept it. You'll need to pay the difference, which is eight dollars.
M: That's a lot, but I understand. Can I pay by card?
W: Yes, I have a reader here. Alternatively, you can get your money back for the original ticket at the station office.
M: Good to know. I'll do both. I'd hate to waste the first ticket.
W: Smart. Keep your receipt with you.

lc-ts066.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.
sc: W: Professor Reyes, I wanted to ask about the recommendation letter you mentioned.
M: Of course. Are you applying to graduate school?
W: Yes, to a marine biology program. The deadline is in three weeks.
M: That's enough time, but I'll need some information from you. Could you send me your resume and a short statement of your goals?
W: I've already written the statement. Should I include my research from last summer?
M: Definitely. That's the kind of detail that makes a letter specific.
W: Great. Also, the application asks whether you want to see the letter. Is it okay if I choose not to?
M: Most professors prefer that, actually. It keeps the letter honest and confidential.
W: Then I'll check that box. Thanks so much.

lc-ts067.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a housing office worker.
sc: W: Housing office. How can I help?
M: Hi. I'm calling about the noise in my building. There's a party almost every night in the apartment above mine.
W: I'm sorry. Have you spoken to your neighbors?
M: I did, twice. They apologized, but nothing changed.
W: Okay. In that case, I'll need you to fill out a complaint form. It can be anonymous.
M: Anonymous? I'd rather give my name so you can contact me.
W: That's fine. After you submit it, we send the residents a warning. A second complaint leads to a meeting with the hall director.
M: I hope it doesn't get that far. Can I get the form online?
W: Yes, on the residents' page, under Quick Forms.

lc-ts068.x: Listen to a conversation between two students about their weekend plans.
sc: W: Mateo, are you doing anything this weekend? A few of us are going to the lake.
M: I'd love to, but I have to finish a lab report. It's due Monday.
W: Can't you do it on Sunday night?
M: I tried that last time, and it was a disaster. I was so stressed that I made mistakes.
W: Then do most of it on Friday, and join us on Saturday.
M: That's actually a good idea. If I finish the data analysis tonight, I'd only need to write the conclusion.
W: Exactly. Then you can relax at the lake.
M: Okay, count me in. What time are you leaving?
W: Ten in the morning. We'll pick you up at your dorm.

lc-ts069.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a cafeteria worker.
sc: W: Hi. What can I get you?
M: I'd like the chicken wrap, please. But I have an allergy to nuts. Does it contain any?
W: Let me check the ingredients. The sauce has a bit of almond paste, I'm afraid.
M: Oh, thanks for checking. What else would you recommend?
W: The grilled fish plate is nut-free, and so is the vegetable stir-fry. The salad dressings might contain nuts, though.
M: I'll take the fish, then, with plain rice.
W: Good choice. Do you want a drink?
M: Just water. And do you have a list of allergens somewhere?

lc-ts070.x: Listen to a conversation between a student and a gym employee.

It is mostly used by new students each term.

questions.s: What must students have before applying?

A two-page report on their grades.
A letter from the research office.
A willing faculty mentor.

questions.s: What is the purpose of the workshop on the sixth?

o: To match students with professors.
To announce which students were chosen.
To help students write proposals.
To review work done during the summer.

questions.s: What will students do in this week's lab?
questions.e: Students will 'explain your solution to a classmate' in a code review. The speaker says the purpose is 'not to find mistakes' and the session 'will not be graded'.

Write a new program at a computer.
Correct errors in their classmates' work.
Take a graded test on programming.

questions.s: Why does the teaching assistant ask students to submit their assignment today?
questions.e: She says to submit it 'so that you have something to discuss'. Attendance is recorded separately, and the review is not graded.

So they will have work to talk about.
Because attendance depends on it.
So she can grade it before Thursday.

questions.s: What do people need to do while waiting?
questions.e: The speaker asks people to 'have your confirmation email ready, either on your phone or printed'. The shirts are collected later at a different table, and the badge, not the ticket, gives access to sessions.

Prepare their confirmation email.
Write their name on a meal ticket.
Learn which sessions they can enter.

questions.s: Where can attendees pick up a conference T-shirt?
questions.e: The speaker says to collect it 'from the table by the stairs, not at the registration desk'. Both registration desks are therefore wrong, and no meal ticket counter is mentioned.

At the left registration desk.
At the right registration desk.
At a table near the stairs.

questions.s: Why are first and second floor residents asked to take the stairs?
questions.e: She says to use the stairs 'so people living on higher floors or with mobility needs can use the elevator more easily'. Nothing is said about repairs to the stairs or the work schedule.
o: To leave room in the elevator for others.
Because their floors have no elevator access.
To help workers finish earlier.
Because the stairs have just been repaired.

questions.s: What can residents who cannot use the stairs do?
questions.e: The announcement says they can 'contact the front desk to arrange a room on the ground floor temporarily'. The north elevator is closed for a month, and the south elevator is open at all times.

Wait for the north elevator to open.
Ask for a ground-floor room.
Use the elevator only in the morning.

questions.s: Why does the speaker tell people not to drive near the course?
questions.e: She says roads 'will be closed from seven thirty'. The run starts at eight as planned, and the club is where numbers are collected, not a free parking lot.

Because the roads will be shut.

Because the finish line has moved.

It is faster than collecting it on Saturday.

Touch the plants with green tags.
Remove their jackets.

To find out the date and time of the final exam.
To borrow a book about energy from her shelf.
To get advice about a paper topic.
