You should have played better in the second half.
The team won its last two games.
questions.sy: M: Our team lost, but at least we gave it our best shot.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The proverb gently corrects an assumption. Admitting the mistake fits. The others take it literally.
o: I bought the cover separately from the book.
Yes, the book was judged fairly by the committee.
Fair enough. I shouldn't have assumed.
The cover looks quite expensive, though.
questions.sy: W: You can't judge a book by its cover, you know.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Call it a night' means stop for the evening. A farewell fits. The others misuse call.
o: You should call a cab before it gets late.
I called it a day at about noon today.
Night classes start at eight tomorrow.
Okay. Get some rest and see you tomorrow.
questions.sy: M: I'm going to call it a night and head home.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Touch base' means briefly connect. Agreeing and setting a place fits. The others misuse touch or base.
o: Sounds good. I'll meet you outside the hall.
I compared my notes with Dana yesterday.
The lecture notes are posted online.
We compared our notes before the lecture ended.
questions.sy: W: Let's touch base after the lecture and compare notes.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Under the weather' means a bit ill. A good wish fits. The others take weather literally.
o: The weather has been warm since Sunday.
I hope she feels better soon.
She should go out in the sunshine more.
I saw her at the library on Sunday.
questions.sy: M: She's been under the weather since Sunday.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Take with a grain of salt' means be skeptical. Agreeing and suggesting a check fits. The others take it literally.
o: I added a pinch of salt to the soup.
The report was very long.
Yes, check another source first.
Yes, it's the most reliable source out there.
questions.sy: W: I'll have to take that with a grain of salt.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Out of the blue' means unexpectedly. Sharing the surprise fits. The others take it literally.
o: The deadline was posted on the first page.
It came from the blue folder on my desk.
Yes, I knew about it weeks ago.
I know. Nobody saw it coming either.
questions.sy: M: That deadline came out of the blue.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The speaker hints at a cost problem. Mentioning a possible discount addresses it. The others ignore the money issue.
o: There might be a discount for students.
The club hikes up the northern ridge in spring.
I joined the photography club last semester.
Hiking boots are available in most stores.
questions.sy: W: I was going to join the hiking club, but the fees are steep.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The man declines indirectly with a reason. Accepting and moving on fits. The others pressure him or ignore the refusal.
o: Six is a good time to start the lab.
No problem. I'll ask someone else.
Lab work always goes faster with help.
Then let's both skip the lab today.
questions.sy: M: I'd love to help, but I've got a lab until six.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The speaker complains about quality. Agreeing with a detail fits. The others are literal or generic.
o: The pizza at the place downtown is great.
The cafeteria is downhill from the main gate.
I noticed that too. It's mostly crust now.
I think the cafeteria's coffee is worse.
questions.sy: W: The cafeteria's pizza has gone downhill lately.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He assumes she would already be there. Explaining her plan responds to that. The others give place facts or misuse figure.
o: The fair is held in the large gym hall.
I figured it would be crowded by now.
The booths are free for students.
I'm heading over after this class.
questions.sy: M: I figured you'd be at the career fair by now.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She wants to avoid the topic. Respecting it fits. The others continue or contradict her wish.
o: Understood. We can drop the subject.
The policy states that grades are final.
I'd rather have a higher grade, too.
Let's discuss it again after the break.
questions.sy: W: Honestly, I'd rather not discuss the grading policy again.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: A conditional wish is a polite request. Agreeing and acting fits. The others misuse look over or give advice.
o: I looked over the draft a minute ago.
Happy to. Send it to me tonight.
I'd write a new one if I were you.
Cover letters should be about one page.
questions.sy: M: It would be great if you could look over my cover letter.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She is waiting for an answer. Suggesting a follow-up fits. The others state facts or contradict.
o: The admissions office is next to the café.
I heard that it will be closed tomorrow.
Maybe give them a call tomorrow.
You haven't been to the office since June.
questions.sy: W: I haven't heard back from the admissions office yet.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: With 'mind', a yes would mean refusal, so 'not at all' accepts. The others misuse mind or sit.
o: Yes, I sit in the front row each week.
The seminar this week is about ecology.
I mind the noise from the corridor a lot.
Not at all. There's space in the back.
questions.sy: M: Do you mind if I sit in on your seminar this week?

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: News of a rent rise invites an echoing remark. The others add general facts.
o: That's the second time this year.
January is the coldest month of winter.
A landlord must give notice in writing.
The rent was lower in the autumn months.
questions.sy: W: Our landlord is raising the rent again in January.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He declines driving for a reason. Offering to navigate solves it. The others lecture or ignore the reason.
o: The roads are being repaired this week.
Don't worry. I'll navigate from here.
Then you can drive us there tomorrow morning.
Familiar roads are easier to drive on at night.
questions.sy: M: I'd offer to drive, but I'm not familiar with the roads.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She doubts the date. Confirming it with evidence fits. The others state opinions or give another timeline.
o: Chemistry is the hardest subject of all.
I'm sure we have until next week.
I double-checked. It's on the syllabus.
I handed mine in the day before yesterday.
questions.sy: W: The chemistry assignment can't possibly be due tomorrow.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He complains about the machine, so a practical tip fits. The others ignore the problem.
o: The machine is on the second floor corridor.
I only use the one in the library.
Dollar bills are harder to get these days.
There's a refund button on the side.
questions.sy: M: Looks like the vending machine ate my dollar again.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She is lukewarm. Sharing a similar opinion fits. The others contradict or change the topic.
o: Not my thing either. I nearly fell asleep.
It finished at ten past eleven.
Endings are often the best part, I suppose.
I guess you prefer older movies.
questions.sy: W: The movie was fine, I guess, if you like slow endings.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'I suppose' offers an option. Pushing back gently with a reason is indirect. The others repeat or ignore the suggestion.
o: Bills are paid at the front counter.
Actually, I only had a salad.
It's a lot more than I expected.
I suppose I could be on time tonight.
questions.sy: M: I suppose we could split the bill evenly.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The line gives good news. Relief fits. The others misread the message.
o: She also said the exam would be harder.
She said not to arrive late for the test.
That's a relief. I was dreading that.
That's what I told her about my own paper.
questions.sy: W: The professor said not to worry about the late penalty this once.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He has little time, so shortening the meeting fits. The others misread booked or ignore the limit.
o: I booked a room for the whole afternoon.
Afternoons are the best time to study here.
Then let's meet for a long lunch.
Then let's keep it to ten minutes.
questions.sy: M: I can only meet briefly, as my afternoon is booked solid.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She politely asks about the bag. Confirming it and thanking her fits. The others ignore the question.
o: Oh, thanks for asking. It's mine.
Thanks, I'll move it to the closet.
The door by the bag is locked.
Bags like that are cheap at the market.
questions.sy: W: I hate to bother you, but is this your bag by the door?

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He suggests leaving soon. Agreeing and getting ready fits. The others misuse pick up or shift the topic.
o: We headed out after the news yesterday.
Good call. Let me grab my coat.
Traffic in this city is worse than in Lahore.
Let's wait until the traffic picks up.
questions.sy: M: We should probably head out before the traffic picks up.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She faces a dilemma. Asking about an advisor offers help. The others are generic, literal or past.
o: Just drop it. Nobody will notice.
Requirements are listed in the catalog online.
Have you talked to your academic advisor?
I dropped the course last year as well.
questions.sy: W: I'm thinking of dropping the course, but it's a requirement.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: A polite complaint is answered by an apology. The others defend or misuse the phrase.
o: I'm not being rude, I'm just excited.
You're the one who's being loud.
Quiet voices carry in the library, though.
Sorry. I didn't realize I was loud.
questions.sy: M: Not to be rude, but could you lower your voice a bit?

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: A complaint about weather leads to a helpful suggestion. The others state facts or misread words.
o: Let's go to the library. It's air-conditioned.
Humid days happen mostly in the monsoon season.
I can hardly believe it's already July.
Today is the fourth of this month, right?
questions.sy: W: It's so humid I can hardly breathe today.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'I wonder if' voices a question without addressing anyone. Suggesting a call helps. The others misuse wonder or stock.
o: I wonder how many copies they ordered.
Why not call and find out?
The store keeps its books on the top shelves.
I left my books at home.
questions.sy: M: I wonder if the bookstore has this in stock.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Lost the thread' means became confused. Agreeing with evidence fits. The others take it literally.
o: The talk was scheduled for halfway through the morning.
Halfway is better than not finishing at all.
I noticed. The slides didn't match.
I thought the presenter was extremely well prepared.
questions.sy: W: I think the presenter lost the thread halfway through.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Didn't exactly rave' implies mild criticism. Asking for details fits. One reply contradicts him.
o: Outlines should always include a conclusion.
Yes, she said it was perfect.
I'm glad she liked it so much.
Did she say what needs improvement?
questions.sy: M: The tutor didn't exactly rave about my outline.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The question is a complaint, not a literal question. Conceding fits. The others answer literally.
o: Okay, okay. I'll do them tonight.
Dishes are best washed in hot water.
It wouldn't kill you to cook sometimes either.
Yes, it would be a lot of work.
questions.sy: W: Would it kill you to wash a dish once in a while?

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He is confused. Offering to work through it fits. The others take it literally.
o: I'll flip a coin to decide.
Let's go through it one step at a time.
Charts are best drawn with color pencils.
I make charts for my research in the lab.
questions.sy: M: I can't make heads or tails of this chart.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She wants to finish. Offering a summary fits. The others misuse wrap or run out.
o: Let's keep going. We still have ten minutes.
Please wrap the gifts before the party.
Right. I'll summarize the key points.
We ran out of time last week as well.
questions.sy: W: We're running out of time, so let's wrap it up.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He shares good news with self-doubt. Reassurance fits. The others ignore his worry.
o: I got a different job last summer.
The job was advertised on the board.
Yes, I'm ready to start tomorrow.
You'll do fine. You earned it.
questions.sy: M: I got the job, but I'm not sure I'm ready for it.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The comment is critical. Asking for specifics is a productive response. The others take thin literally or change the topic.
o: Which parts did she mean exactly?
I thought my argument was solid.
I argued with the reviewer about the deadline.
Thin arguments can be fixed with more evidence.
questions.sy: W: The reviewer said my argument was a bit thin in places.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'In two minds' means undecided. Asking about benefits helps. The others take it literally.
o: Two minds are better than one in a test.
What would you gain by moving out?
The campus has two main buildings and a garden.
I moved off campus last year.
questions.sy: M: I'm in two minds about moving off campus.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She gives a mild criticism. Agreeing with a reason fits. The others are off-topic.
o: I thought the opening chapter was weaker.
Frankly, I expected you at the end.
Same here. It felt rushed to me.
The final chapter was longer than the first.
questions.sy: W: Frankly, I expected more from the final chapter.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He apologizes for limits. Reassurance and thanks fit. One reply is rude, and the others miss the point.
o: The notice board is on the ground floor.
You can do better than that, can't you?
I gave you plenty of notice yesterday.
It's plenty. Thanks for trying.
questions.sy: M: That's the best I can do on such short notice.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: She has been postponing a task. Encouraging her fits. The others misuse meaning or card.
o: It only takes a minute at the desk.
Library cards are free for new students.
The library closes at eight tonight.
I renewed mine in the spring of last year.
questions.sy: W: I keep meaning to renew my library card.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The host apologizes politely. Reassuring with humor fits. The others misread the situation.
o: You should have cleaned before I arrived.
Don't worry. You should see my room.
Company policy says to arrive early.
I wasn't expecting to come either, actually.
questions.sy: M: You'll have to excuse the mess. I wasn't expecting company.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The remark invites an explanation. Giving a reason fits. One reply contradicts the word optional, and the others sidestep.
o: The lecture hall seats around three hundred.
The professor takes attendance every week.
Can you blame them? It's at eight a.m.
Everybody has to sign in at the door.
questions.sy: W: Seems like everybody's skipping the optional lecture.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Could murder a sandwich' means he is very hungry. Agreeing and suggesting food fits. One reply takes murder literally.
o: Sandwiches are best made with fresh bread.
Right now the café is closed for repairs.
I made one an hour ago, thanks.
Me too. Let's hit the café.
questions.sy: M: I could murder a sandwich right now.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: The question disagrees politely. Conceding a little and defending fits. The others miss the argument.
o: Maybe, but we're getting nowhere fast.
Yes, we finished the project last week.
The project began at the end of June.
It's never too early to start a new one.
questions.sy: W: Isn't it a bit early to be giving up on the project?

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: 'Not that I'm complaining' introduces a gentle complaint. Offering to adjust it fits. The others miss it.
o: Complaints go to the front desk, I think.
I'll turn it down a notch.
The heating bill is paid at the end of the month.
It's not much warmer than yesterday.
questions.sy: M: Not that I'm complaining, but the heating is a little much.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: A hopeful remark invites hopeful agreement. The others play on words or ignore her.
o: The end of the story was a bit dark.
I work better in the evening.
I hope so. Fingers crossed.
Work in the evening is easier for me too.
questions.sy: W: I'm sure it'll all work out in the end.

questions.s: Choose the best response.
questions.e: He suggests rest after effort, so enthusiastic agreement fits. The others are literal or irrelevant.
o: The day started with a thick fog outside.
Our deadline was set by the teacher.
I'd say we should start the next project early.
Absolutely. Let's not touch email tomorrow.
questions.sy: M: I'd say we've earned a day off after that deadline.

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks 'Why is summer warm and winter cold?' and explains that 'the real reason is that Earth is tilted'. Distance is mentioned only to show that it is not the reason.
o: How far Earth is from the Sun in each month of the year
What causes the seasons on Earth
How to use a flashlight in a science experiment
Why winters are colder in Canada than in Argentina

questions.s: According to the professor, when is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.e: She says 'Earth is closest to the Sun in early January', which is winter in the north. Many people think it is closest in summer, but she says that is wrong.
o: In the middle of summer in the north
In late June, at the start of summer
It is always the same distance from the Sun
In early January

questions.s: Why does the professor talk about a flashlight?
questions.e: Straight light makes 'a small, bright circle', but tilted light 'spreads over a bigger area, so each part gets less'. This helps explain why direct sunlight in summer gives more heat. She never explains how to measure the tilt.
o: To show why direct light warms a place more
To explain how scientists measure the tilt of Earth's axis in degrees
To describe an experiment that students will do at home
To show that the Sun is very bright

questions.s: What does the professor say about the seasons in the two halves of the world?
questions.e: She says 'the seasons are opposite in the two halves of the world': 'When it's summer in Canada, it's winter in Argentina.' The first option says the reverse.
o: They happen at the same time everywhere on Earth
They are longer in the north than in the south
They are opposite to each other
They depend on the distance from the Sun

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how otters 'keep the number of urchins down, and that protects the kelp'. Hunting is mentioned only to show what happened when otters disappeared.
o: Why people hunted sea otters for their fur in the eighteen hundreds
How kelp grows in cold water
How one animal helps protect an ocean habitat
The different kinds of fish that live near the shore

questions.s: According to the professor, what do sea otters eat?
questions.e: He says 'sea otters love to eat sea urchins'. It is the urchins, not the otters, that 'love to eat kelp', so the second option mixes up the two animals.
o: Sea urchins
Giant kelp and other kinds of seaweed
Small fish and crabs that live in the kelp
Mostly plants that grow on rocks

questions.s: What happened when sea otters disappeared from many areas?
questions.e: Without otters, 'urchin numbers grew, and they ate the kelp forests down to bare rock'. The first option says the opposite: urchin numbers went up, not down.
o: The number of sea urchins went down very quickly
Kelp forests grew larger than before
More fish moved into the area
Urchins destroyed the kelp forests

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the stone at the top of an arch?
questions.e: He uses the arch to explain the term 'keystone species': take the keystone out 'and the arch falls down', just as removing one species can change a community. The arch is a comparison, not a real place on the coast.
o: To describe the shape of the rocks along the Pacific coast
To explain the meaning of a term
To show how sea otters build their homes
To give an example of a very old building

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says 'many dunes actually move', explains how, and then describes 'one common solution' to the problems they cause. Plants are mentioned only as one way to hold the sand.
o: Why deserts have very little rain and strong winds
How ocean waves form beaches
Different kinds of desert plants
How sand dunes move and how they can be stopped

questions.s: According to the professor, what is the slip face of a dune?
questions.e: Sand falls 'onto the other side, which is much steeper. This steep side is called the slip face.' The gentle side is the one facing the wind, so the first option describes the wrong side.
o: The gentle side of the dune that faces into the wind
The very top of the dune
Its steep side, away from the wind
The ground under the dune

questions.s: Why do very large dunes move more slowly than small ones?
questions.e: Very large dunes move more slowly 'because there's so much more sand to carry'. The professor does not say the wind is weaker near large dunes.
o: The wind is weaker where large dunes are usually found
They have much more sand to move
Plants always grow on them
Their slip faces are gentle

questions.s: What is one way people stop dunes from moving?
questions.e: She says 'one common solution is to plant grasses and bushes', whose roots 'hold the sand in place'. Roads and buildings are things that moving dunes cover, not a way to stop them.
o: By planting grasses and bushes
By building roads and buildings next to the dunes to block the wind
By removing the slip face
By pouring water on the sand

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes phantom limbs and explains that research 'points to the brain', showing it 'can reorganize itself'. Nerve endings are mentioned as the older explanation, but repairing them is never discussed.
o: What phantom limbs reveal about the brain
How doctors repair damaged nerve endings after an injury to an arm or leg
Why some patients are afraid of mirrors
How the skin senses heat and cold

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that touching a patient's cheek can produce a feeling in the missing hand?
questions.e: The example follows the point that the face area 'can gradually take over' the hand area, because the two sit 'right next to' each other on the brain's map. The connection is in the brain, not in the nerves of the face and arm.
o: To show that nerves in the face are connected directly to the nerves in the arm
To show that nearby brain areas can take over
To describe a side effect of mirror therapy
To explain why phantom limbs itch

questions.s: According to the professor, what did doctors first think caused phantom limbs?
questions.e: Doctors 'assumed the feeling came from damaged nerve endings where the limb had been'. The brain map explanation came later, from research 'since the nineteen nineties', so the first option is the newer view.
o: Changes in the map of the body on the surface of the brain
Patients imagining the feeling
Damaged nerves where the limb had been
Too much use of the remaining limb

questions.s: How does mirror therapy work?
questions.e: The reflection of the remaining hand 'appears where the missing hand would be', so 'moving the real hand seems to move the phantom one'. The cheek appears in a different example, about the brain map.
o: Patients watch their face in a mirror while someone touches their cheek
A mirror is used to shine light onto the injury
Patients learn to stop moving the hand that remains
A reflection makes the missing hand seem to move

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor says researchers 'got to watch a new language being born' and describes how deaf children built and developed a shared sign system. The schools' lessons in lip-reading are a background detail, and they had 'little success'.
o: Why schools in Nicaragua taught deaf children to read lips and speak Spanish
How families created home signs for their children
How a new language developed among a group of children
Why older students learn languages faster than younger ones

questions.s: Where did the children first begin signing to each other?
questions.e: She says 'on the playground and on the school buses, the children started signing to each other'. The lessons taught 'lip-reading and Spanish', not sign language, so the first option is wrong.
o: In lessons where teachers taught them sign language
Outside the classroom, for example on buses
At home with their families
In a university research center

questions.s: According to the professor, what did the younger children do with the signing system?
questions.e: The younger children 'didn't just copy it. They made it more regular and more complex.' The second option is the tempting one because it uses the word 'copy', but she says the opposite.
o: They made it more regular and complex
They copied it exactly as the older children used it
They replaced it with spoken Spanish
They taught it to their parents at home

questions.s: What does the professor suggest about young children?
questions.e: She concludes that 'given rough material, they can actively build grammar into it'. The youngest learners 'added the most structure', which contradicts the second option.
o: They need adults to teach them grammar rules before they can sign well
They learn languages more slowly than older students do
They stop using home signs once they start school
They can add structure to the language they learn

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor introduces comparative advantage, which 'explains why trade can benefit both sides', and uses a lawyer and two countries as examples. England and Portugal are Ricardo's example, not the topic.
o: How England and Portugal became the largest producers of cloth and wine in Europe
Why lawyers earn more money than their assistants
How office workers can learn to type faster
An idea that explains why trade can benefit both sides

questions.s: Why does the professor talk about a lawyer who types fast?
questions.e: He says 'let's start with a simple example' and uses the lawyer to explain opportunity cost before applying 'the same logic to countries'. The second option reverses his point: even though she types faster, she should not do all her own typing.
o: To illustrate an economic idea with a familiar case
To show that people should do every task they are good at by themselves
To compare the salaries of different jobs
To explain why typing is a useful skill

questions.s: What does the professor mean by opportunity cost?
questions.e: He says 'economists call what you give up the opportunity cost'. For the lawyer, an hour of typing means giving up an hour of better-paid legal work. Paying the assistant is not mentioned as the cost.
o: The money a person pays to hire an assistant to do a task
What a person gives up by choosing one activity
The price of goods traded between countries
The time needed to learn a new skill

questions.s: According to the professor, what does the word comparative stress?
questions.e: He says 'what matters isn't who's best at something, but who gives up the least to do it'. The second option is the idea of absolute advantage, which he contrasts with comparative advantage.
o: Which country produces the most goods in total
Who is the very best at a task
Who gives up the least, not who is best
How prices in two countries are compared

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: She says she will talk about 'a piece of technology that helped make that style possible: the paint tube'. Grinding powders is only how paint was made before tubes.
o: How painters in the eighteen hundreds ground colored powders to make their own paints
How a new invention influenced a style of painting
The life and career of Claude Monet
Why French words are used to describe painting

questions.s: According to the professor, what was one problem with storing paint before the eighteen forties?
questions.e: Paint was kept in bags 'which were awkward to carry and easily burst'. The first option is wrong because metal tubes came later and kept paint 'fresh inside'.
o: Paint stored in metal tubes dried out too quickly to be used
Painters could not find colored powders
The containers were awkward to carry and could burst
Paint could only be bought in America

questions.s: What does the professor say about painting outdoors?
questions.e: She says 'this made painting outdoors much easier' and adds 'painting outside wasn't new'. So the Impressionists did not invent it, which rules out the first option.
o: It was invented by Monet and Renoir after they bought their first paint tubes
It became too difficult for most artists
It became less popular after tubes appeared
It was not new, but tubes made it much easier

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of Renoir's reported statement?
questions.e: She calls it 'probably an exaggeration, since art movements have many causes'. She still thinks tubes mattered, but not that they alone created Impressionism. She does not question whether Renoir said it.
o: It overstates the importance of a single cause
It is completely accurate and explains every part of the movement
It was probably never said at all
It is really about pigments, not tubes

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains Dunbar's number, how it was derived, and then the 'serious questions' critics have raised. Business is mentioned only as an example of the idea's popularity.
o: A proposed limit on human relationships and doubts about it
How companies have organized their workers into units of the ideal size
Why monkeys and apes have larger brains than humans
How people can make and keep more friends

questions.s: How did Dunbar arrive at the number one hundred and fifty?
questions.e: Dunbar 'plotted' the link between neocortex size and group size in monkeys and apes, then 'used the size of the human neocortex to predict' a group size. Villages and military units came afterward, as 'supporting examples', not as the source of the number.
o: By counting the members of traditional villages in many countries around the world
By surveying workers at large companies
By studying the size of historical military units
By extending a pattern found in other primates

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the study from two thousand twenty-one?
questions.e: The reanalysis gave estimates from 'just a handful of people to more than five hundred', so 'the data can't pin down a single number'. Five hundred is only the top of the range, not a new answer.
o: To prove that the true number of relationships people keep is about five hundred
To support Dunbar's original estimate
To show that the data allow very different estimates
To explain how the neocortex grows

questions.s: What is the professor's view of Dunbar's number?
questions.e: He suggests treating it 'less as a law of human nature and more as a rough, and rather contested, rule of thumb'. Dunbar 'has defended his work', so the third option is wrong.
o: It is a law of human nature supported by strong evidence from many fields
It should be treated as a rough guide at most
It has been disproven, and Dunbar has given it up
It applies only to businesses

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains why longitude was hard to find and then describes 'two very different approaches': the lunar distance method and Harrison's clock. Latitude is mentioned only as the easier problem, for contrast.
o: How sailors measured latitude from the height of the Sun and the stars
The early life of John Harrison as a self-taught clockmaker
Two competing solutions to a navigation problem
Why the British government built more ships in the seventeen hundreds

questions.s: According to the professor, why did knowing the home port time make it possible to find longitude?
questions.e: Because 'Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour', the difference between local time and home port time 'gives your longitude', the east-west position. The second option describes latitude, which sailors could already find.
o: The home port time showed the exact height of the Sun above the horizon at noon
It showed sailors how far north the ship was
It told sailors when to look at the stars
The time difference shows how far east or west a ship is

questions.s: What was a disadvantage of the lunar distance method?
questions.e: The method 'needed accurate tables and long calculations, but no costly equipment'. The second option describes Harrison's approach instead, which was the expensive one.
o: It required long calculations and printed tables
It needed an expensive clock that could stay accurate on a rolling ship
It could be used only close to the home port
It could not be used when the Moon was visible

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the experts' preference for astronomy?
questions.e: She says it 'wasn't just snobbery', because for a long time lunar distances were 'the method most ships could actually afford'. Ships kept using the method 'well into the eighteen hundreds', so the preference did not end with the trial voyages.
o: It came from jealousy of Harrison's great talent as a clockmaker
It had practical reasons and was not simply prejudice
It ended as soon as Harrison's watch was tested
It was the reason the clocks became cheap

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor presents the Gaia hypothesis, the biologists' objection, Lovelock's reply and the idea's influence today. The Sun's brightness is just one of the facts Lovelock used.
o: How the brightness of the Sun has changed over the history of the solar system
A bold idea about Earth and how scientists responded
How daisies survive in hot climates
The career of the biologist Lynn Margulis

questions.s: What was the biologists' main objection to the Gaia hypothesis?
questions.e: Natural selection 'acts on individual organisms', and the hypothesis 'sounded as if life were planning ahead, which evolution doesn't do'. The second option reverses one of Lovelock's facts: oxygen 'has stayed fairly stable'.
o: Evolution does not make organisms plan for the planet
The amount of oxygen in the air has changed greatly over millions of years
The Sun has grown dimmer over Earth's history
Daisies cannot grow on other planets

questions.s: Why does the professor describe Daisyworld?
questions.e: Daisyworld shows temperature staying steady 'without any daisy aiming for that', which answered the objection about planning. The professor adds that whether 'Earth actually works that way is another question', so the model proves nothing about Earth itself.
o: To prove that Earth's temperature is controlled entirely by the colors of its plants
To describe a real planet discovered by astronomers
To explain why dark flowers are more common than light ones
To show how regulation could happen without any goal

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the Gaia hypothesis today?
questions.e: He says 'the strong version of Gaia has few supporters', but its broader idea 'has become central' to Earth system science. A hypothesis can be 'largely rejected and still leave a lasting mark', which rules out the first two options.
o: Most Earth system scientists accept it in its strong form
It has had no influence on later science
It influenced science even though its strong form is doubted
It was finally proven by the Daisyworld model

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor introduces 'echolocation in bats' and then explains how some moths fight back, calling it 'an arms race'. Owls are only mentioned as last week's topic, so the option about owls and bats competing is not the subject of the talk.
o: How owls and bats compete for the same flying insects at night
How bats use sound to locate prey and how moths respond
Why most species of bats have very poor eyesight
How scientists record high-pitched animal calls

questions.s: According to the professor, why does a bat call more rapidly as it approaches an insect?
questions.e: The professor says 'more calls mean more updates, so the bat gets a sharper picture.' More frequent information paraphrases 'more updates'. Moths drop toward the ground because they hear the calls, but the bat is not trying to scare them; nothing is said about weaker hearing.
o: To scare the insect into dropping toward the ground
To warn other bats to stay away from its prey
Because its hearing becomes weaker when it is very close to an insect
To get more frequent information about the target

questions.s: Why does the professor mention tiger moths?
questions.e: Tiger moths 'produce clicks of their own, which can jam or confuse the bat's signal.' Jamming the signal means interfering with echolocation. The professor never says that bats avoid moths because of their taste.
o: To show that some prey can interfere with echolocation
To give an example of an insect that bats avoid because it tastes bad
To explain how moths find their way in the dark
To compare the hearing of moths with that of humans

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the idea that bats are blind?
questions.e: He calls it 'one common myth I want to clear up' and says 'Most species can see perfectly well.' A common myth is a mistaken belief many people hold. The option about why echolocation developed is tempting, but he says echolocation simply works better in the dark, not that it replaced missing sight.
o: It is true of most species that hunt insects at night
It explains why bats developed echolocation in the first place
It is a mistaken belief that many people hold
It was first suggested by researchers who studied moths

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says 'we need to follow a single drop of water' and then explains how soda straws, stalactites, stalagmites and columns form. She asks visitors not to touch formations, but she never says caves are dangerous; the weak acid is 'nothing dangerous'.
o: Why limestone caves can be dangerous places for visitors to explore
How cavers measure the age of cave formations
How dripping water creates formations in caves
The differences between limestone and other rocks

questions.s: According to the professor, what causes the water to leave calcite on the cave ceiling?
questions.e: She says 'some of the carbon dioxide escapes into the cave air, and the water can't hold all of its mineral anymore.' Oil from skin is mentioned, but it stops growth rather than causing it, and freezing is never mentioned.
o: Some carbon dioxide escapes from the water
The water freezes when the cave becomes colder in the winter months
The water mixes with oil from visitors' skin
Bacteria in the cave break down the dissolved minerals

questions.s: How does the professor organize the information in the talk?
questions.e: She follows one drop of water from rain, through the soil and limestone, into the cave, then to soda straws, stalactites, stalagmites and columns. That is a process told in order. She mentions a problem at the end, touching formations, but it is not how the whole talk is organized.
o: She compares caves in several different parts of the world
She lists cave formations from the most to the least common
She describes a problem and then offers several solutions
She follows the stages of a process in order

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that many formations grow less than a millimeter a year?
questions.e: Right after the growth rate she says 'That's why cave guides ask you not to touch them,' because damage may take thousands of years to repair. The slow rate actually suggests great age, so the option about the last few centuries reverses her point.
o: To show that soda straws are older than stalactites
To explain why visitors are asked not to touch them
To suggest that most caves formed only within the last few centuries
To compare cave growth with the amount of rainfall

questions.s: What is the professor mainly explaining?
questions.e: He asks 'why we never see the other side?' and answers 'tidal locking,' then explains how it happened. The far side does not get less sunlight; he says it 'gets just as much sunlight as the side we see,' so that option reverses his point.
o: Why the same side of the Moon always faces Earth
How the dark patches on the Moon formed long ago through volcanic activity
Why the far side of the Moon receives less sunlight
How spacecraft were used to map the Moon's surface

questions.s: According to the professor, what do many students wrongly believe about tidal locking?
questions.e: He says 'A lot of students assume this means the Moon doesn't spin. Actually, it does spin.' Not spinning means it has stopped rotating. The photograph from nineteen fifty-nine is about the far side, not about discovering tidal locking.
o: That it happens only to very large moons
That it was discovered from photographs taken in the twentieth century
That the Moon has stopped rotating
That Earth's gravity is weaker than the Moon's

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Pluto and Charon?
questions.e: He introduces them with 'this isn't unique to our Moon,' so they are another example of tidal locking. Each still has a far side, since each 'always shows the same face to the other,' and Pluto's status as a planet is never discussed.
o: To explain why Pluto is no longer called a planet
To show that tidal locking happens elsewhere too
To compare the size of Charon with the size of our Moon in the sky
To give an example of a moon that has no far side

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of the phrase 'the dark side of the Moon'?
questions.e: He says 'That's misleading. It gets just as much sunlight as the side we see.' A misleading phrase gives a false idea. He only accepts 'dark' in the sense of 'unknown', so he does not think the phrase is accurate.
o: He thinks it describes the far side accurately
He believes astronomers should use it more often in their scientific work
He thinks it was invented by a spacecraft team
He thinks it gives a false idea about sunlight

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes 'the serial position effect': first and last words are remembered better than middle ones. The option about forgetting words heard once repeats the setup of the experiment, but the talk is about which words are remembered, depending on their position.
o: Ways to improve memory before an important exam
The differences between short-term memory in children and in adults
Why people forget words that they hear only once
How an item's place in a list affects recall

questions.s: According to the professor, why are the first items in a list remembered well?
questions.e: She says 'you've got time to repeat those words to yourself, so they're more likely to get into long-term memory.' Rehearse means repeat to yourself. Being in short-term memory explains the last items, recency, not the first ones.
o: They are still in short-term memory at the end
People have more time to rehearse them
They are usually shorter and more familiar than the words in the middle
People pay less attention once the list ends

questions.s: Why does the professor describe making people count backward before they write?
questions.e: She introduces it with 'here's how we know these are separate processes': the delay removes recency but primacy stays. The method does not improve recall; it removes part of it, so the first option is wrong.
o: To show a way to improve recall of the middle items
To illustrate a mistake made by early memory researchers in their labs
To give evidence that two separate processes are involved
To explain why people dislike memory experiments

questions.s: What can be inferred about job candidates who are interviewed in the middle of the day?
questions.e: Applying the serial position effect, the professor says the middle candidates 'may be at a real disadvantage, through no fault of their own,' because middle items are remembered less. 'Through no fault of their own' rules out the idea that they prepare less.
o: Interviewers may remember them less clearly
They usually prepare less carefully than the first and last candidates
They tend to be more nervous than the others
They are the most likely to be offered the job

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor explains van Gennep's idea that ceremonies marking a change in status 'share the same three-part structure.' Graduation is used as one example, not compared across countries, and van Gennep is named only as the source of the term.
o: To compare graduation ceremonies in different countries around the world
To explain a common structure found in many ceremonies
To argue that modern ceremonies have lost their meaning
To describe the life and career of Arnold van Gennep

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens in the first phase of a rite of passage?
questions.e: In separation, 'The person is removed from their old role.' Rejoining the community is the last phase, incorporation, and equal treatment belongs to the middle, liminal phase.
o: The person leaves behind an old role
The person rejoins the community with a new title at the end
Everyone in the group is treated as an equal
The community votes on the person's new status

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that graduation gowns are identical?
questions.e: He says 'The gowns are identical for everyone' and adds 'That's the liminal phase in action,' linking back to people being 'treated as equal, whatever their background.' The word liminal comes from the Latin for threshold, not from the gowns.
o: To criticize universities for making ceremonies too formal
To explain where the word liminal comes from
To suggest that graduates dislike wearing special clothing at ceremonies
To illustrate the equality of the liminal phase

questions.s: What does the professor suggest about the transition phase?
questions.e: He says the middle phase 'is the one later anthropologists found most fascinating' and then cites Victor Turner. Nothing is said about how long it lasts or about van Gennep thinking it unimportant.
o: Van Gennep himself considered it the least important of the three phases
It is found only in ceremonies for young adults
It has drawn special interest from later scholars
It usually lasts longer than the other two phases

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how pigment bonds with wet plaster and what that requires: working in daily sections and chipping away mistakes. Michelangelo's ceiling is only a famous example in the first line, so it is not the main topic.
o: Michelangelo's life and his long work on the Sistine Chapel ceiling
Why Renaissance painters preferred oil to water
How the fresco technique works and what it demands
How modern experts restore damaged wall paintings

questions.s: According to the professor, what holds the pigment in place in true fresco?
questions.e: She says the plaster 'forms a hard crystal layer, and the pigment gets locked inside it.' She stresses 'There's no glue, no oil,' so the options about glue and oil contradict the talk.
o: A thin layer of glue mixed into the water
Oil that the painter adds after the plaster has completely dried
The heat of the sun on the finished wall
A hard layer that forms as the plaster dries

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the seams that can be seen in some frescoes?
questions.e: The seams are 'between one day's work and the next,' so they show that painters worked in giornate, one day's plaster at a time. She does not call them a flaw, and flaking is linked to painting on dry plaster, not to the seams.
o: To point out a common flaw in poorly made frescoes
To show evidence of painting in daily sections
To explain why many frescoes have flaked away over the centuries
To argue that artists often worked much too quickly

questions.s: What can be inferred about painting on dry plaster?
questions.e: She calls it 'a shortcut' that is 'much more forgiving,' which means easier, but 'a lot of it has flaked away,' which means it lasts less well. Becoming 'part of the wall itself' describes true fresco, so that option mixes up the two methods.
o: It was easier but less durable
It was used only by painters who had no training in the true fresco method
It was the method that Michelangelo preferred
It allowed colors to become part of the wall

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor explains that pure fifths do not add up evenly, 'the math doesn't quite work out,' and that equal temperament spreads the error. Remote keys are part of the problem he describes, but avoiding them is not the main topic.
o: How pianos are built so that they stay in tune for many years
Why composers avoided writing music in remote keys
The history of the perfect fifth in folk music
A tuning system that solved a mathematical problem

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens when twelve pure fifths are stacked?
questions.e: He says 'You overshoot by a small amount,' which means going slightly past the expected note. The first option is what 'should' happen, but he says 'But you don't,' so it reverses his point.
o: You land exactly seven octaves above the starting note
You go slightly past the note you expect
You produce an interval that musicians call the wolf because it sounds bad
You create the twelve steps of equal temperament

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the nickname 'the wolf'?
questions.e: Some remote intervals were 'so sour' that one was called the wolf 'because it howled.' The nickname shows how out of tune they were. It is the opposite of a pure interval, so the third option reverses the meaning.
o: To show how bad some intervals sounded in older tunings
To explain where many musical terms come from
To give an example of an interval that is perfectly pure
To describe a well-known piece written long ago in a distant key

questions.s: What is the professor's view of equal temperament?
questions.e: He calls it 'a compromise': 'You give up a little purity' for 'total freedom to move between keys.' He also says 'Most listeners can't hear' the error, so it does not sound noticeably worse.
o: It is mathematically perfect and has no weaknesses
It makes music sound noticeably worse than older tunings did
It is a sensible trade-off between purity and flexibility
It became popular mainly because pianos are cheaper to build

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: She says 'I want to look at whether that belief really holds up' and concludes that 'being first isn't enough on its own.' Store locations and search engines are only small examples within that discussion.
o: To question a popular belief about entering a market
To explain how companies choose the best store locations for a new business
To describe the history of internet search engines
To encourage students to start their own companies

questions.s: According to the professor, how can switching costs help a first mover?
questions.e: She explains that once customers have learned your system, 'moving to a competitor feels like a hassle.' So customers are less likely to change to a rival. Reliable suppliers are a separate benefit, locking up scarce resources.
o: They allow the company to charge lower prices
They make it cheaper for the company to find reliable suppliers in a new market
They discourage customers from moving to a rival
They reduce the cost of developing a new product

questions.s: Why does the professor mention internet search?
questions.e: The earliest search engines did not dominate; 'A later company studied what users wanted and simply did it better,' just like the fast follower she described. 'Always lose' is too extreme, since she says only that being first 'isn't enough on its own.'
o: To show that first movers always lose in technology markets
To explain how search engines build brand recognition with users over time
To describe a market with unusually high switching costs
To give an example of a fast follower succeeding

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion about being first to market?
questions.e: She says 'timing matters, but being first isn't enough on its own. What matters more is whether a company can keep learning.' The option saying it always costs more than it is worth is too extreme, because she lists 'real benefits' of going first.
o: It guarantees long-term success if the product is good
It can help, but continued learning matters more
It always costs more than it is worth for companies in every industry
It matters only for companies that sell technology

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how a pidgin forms and how, when children expand it, 'linguists call it a creole.' Papua New Guinea is only the setting of one example, Tok Pisin, so it is not the main topic.
o: Why traders in ports often learned several foreign languages fluently
How children learn grammar from their parents at home
How a simple contact language can become a full one
The history of languages spoken in Papua New Guinea

questions.s: According to the professor, what is true of a pidgin?
questions.e: She stresses 'A pidgin is nobody's first language.' The most powerful group supplies most of the words, not the grammar, which is 'stripped down', so the third option mixes two details.
o: It usually becomes the first language of every child in the community
No one speaks it as a first language
It takes most of its grammar from the most powerful group
It has more complex grammar than a creole

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Tok Pisin?
questions.e: Tok Pisin 'started as a pidgin used on plantations' and 'Today it has native speakers,' which is how she defines a creole. The plantations are its past, not its use today, and it is used in newspapers, not avoided by them.
o: To show that pidgins are used mainly on plantations today
To compare the grammar of two languages spoken in one country
To explain why newspapers avoid using creole languages
To give a real case of a pidgin becoming a creole

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the role of children in creating creoles?
questions.e: She calls it 'something remarkable' that children 'build a full language out of' a limited system. Remarkable shows she is impressed. She says children 'don't just copy it. They expand it,' so she does not doubt their influence.
o: She is impressed by what they achieve
She doubts that children can really change a language
She thinks children make a pidgin harder for the adults around them to use
She believes their role has been greatly exaggerated

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor explains eutrophication: nitrogen and phosphorus wash into water, cause algal blooms, and lead to dead zones. Fertilizer is one source of nutrients, but the talk is not about how farmers choose amounts.
o: How farmers decide how much fertilizer to put on their crops each season
Why algae are an important food source for fish
The history of laundry detergents
How extra nutrients can damage bodies of water

questions.s: According to the professor, what directly causes fish to die in a dead zone?
questions.e: Bacteria breaking down dead algae 'use up the oxygen dissolved in the water,' so fish 'suffocate.' Blocked sunlight is mentioned, but it kills the bottom plants, not the fish, so that option mixes two details.
o: The oxygen in the water is used up
Algae release poisons that spread quickly through the water
Fertilizer makes the water too warm
Sunlight can no longer reach the bottom

questions.s: Why does the professor begin by asking how extra food could be a problem?
questions.e: He starts with 'Today's topic sounds like a good thing at first,' then asks the question to set up the surprise that nutrients cause harm. He never suggests removing all nutrients, which would be too extreme.
o: To show that students already understand the process well
To point out that the process seems harmless at first
To argue that nutrients should be completely removed from all lakes and rivers
To explain why plants need nitrogen and phosphorus

questions.s: What can be inferred from the professor's comments about the nineteen seventies?
questions.e: After phosphates in detergent were limited, 'some badly affected lakes recovered noticeably,' so reducing nutrients helped. Detergent was not the only cause; he names fertilizer and sewage too.
o: Laundry detergent was the only cause of eutrophication at that time
Most affected lakes never recovered
Cutting the nutrients that enter water can improve it
Dead zones first appeared during that decade

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor defines Batesian mimicry: 'a harmless species evolves to look like a dangerous one.' Wasps and butterflies appear only as examples, so neither is the main topic.
o: How birds learn to find the tastiest insects in their environment
How harmless animals benefit from looking dangerous
Why wasps have yellow and black stripes
How butterflies defend themselves against birds

questions.s: According to the professor, when does Batesian mimicry work best?
questions.e: She says it 'tends to work best when the mimic is rarer than the species it copies.' Rarer means less common. Predators must already have learned that the pattern 'means trouble,' so the option about never meeting the dangerous species reverses her point.
o: When the mimic shares its habitat with many different kinds of predators
When predators have never met the dangerous species
When the mimic is less common than the species it copies
When the mimic is able to sting or bite

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the viceroy butterfly?
questions.e: She calls it 'one famous case that turned out to be more complicated': textbooks called it Batesian mimicry, but experiments showed viceroys taste bad too. So it is not a clear example of Batesian mimicry; it is a different kind.
o: To show that a well-known example was later revised
To give the clearest example of Batesian mimicry
To explain how monarch butterflies came to taste bad to birds over time
To compare the colors of butterflies with those of wasps

questions.s: What can be inferred about a bird that often catches harmless striped insects?
questions.e: The professor says that for such a bird, 'Pretty soon, the stripes stop meaning anything.' So it may no longer treat the stripes as a warning. Avoiding all bright insects is the opposite of what she describes.
o: It will start to avoid all brightly colored insects completely
It will become more afraid of wasps than before
It will stop eating insects of any kind
It may start to ignore the warning pattern

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk explains glacial erratics, boulders carried 'hundreds of kilometers' by ice sheets, and why they matter as evidence. Agassiz is named once as a supporter of the ice sheet idea; his career is not discussed.
o: Large rocks moved far from their origin by ice
The career of Louis Agassiz in Europe and North America
Why boulders are often found in the middle of farm fields
How icebergs form and melt in ancient seas

questions.s: According to the professor, what makes a boulder an erratic?
questions.e: The strange part is that the boulder is 'a completely different kind of rock than anything else around it.' Its size is only part of the opening picture, and the iceberg idea is an older explanation that was later replaced.
o: It is at least as large as a house
It has been worn smooth by running water over a very long time
It was dropped by a melting iceberg
It differs from the rock around it

questions.s: Why does the professor mention floods and icebergs?
questions.e: He says that 'in the early eighteen hundreds, this was a real mystery' and lists floods and icebergs as what some naturalists suggested, before Agassiz's 'much bolder idea.' They are past explanations, not accepted ones today.
o: To show that both are still accepted explanations
To describe how glaciers usually begin to form in the cold regions of the world
To present earlier explanations for a puzzle
To explain where the word erratic comes from

questions.s: According to the professor, what can a line of erratics reveal?
questions.e: He says 'if you find a whole line of them, you can trace the path of a glacier.' The route a glacier followed paraphrases its path. Ancient seas belong to the old iceberg explanation.
o: Where an ancient sea once covered the land
The route that an old glacier followed
That the boulders were carried by a flood that happened quite recently
That the bedrock is younger than the boulders

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The talk opens with the problem of 'measuring distance' and explains how Cepheids, which 'pulse,' solved it. Why stars look dim is only the starting puzzle, and Hubble appears near the end as someone who used the method.
o: Why some stars look dimmer than others
The life of Edwin Hubble and his work on galaxies
How the Small Magellanic Cloud was first discovered
How a certain kind of pulsing star allows astronomers to measure distances

questions.s: Why was it important that the stars Leavitt studied were all in the same cloud?
questions.e: Because they were 'all roughly the same distance from Earth,' she says, 'any difference in brightness had to be real.' Distance could not explain the differences, so she could compare true brightness. Nothing is said about telescopes or timing speed.
o: It made the stars easier to see with small telescopes
It showed that Cepheids exist only in small groups far from our galaxy
It meant that their differences in brightness were real
It allowed her to time their pulses more quickly

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Edwin Hubble?
questions.e: Hubble 'used exactly this method' to show Andromeda was outside our galaxy, so he applied Leavitt's discovery. The professor ends by praising 'Leavitt's careful work,' so the option about giving Hubble more credit reverses her view.
o: To show an important use of Leavitt's discovery
To explain who first noticed that Cepheids pulse
To argue that Hubble deserves more credit than Leavitt for the discovery
To describe how the Andromeda nebula got its name

questions.s: Two Cepheids look equally bright from Earth, but one has a much longer pulse. What can be inferred?
questions.e: A longer pulse means a star is 'brighter' in reality. If two stars look the same but one is really brighter, that one must be farther away. The option saying it is closer reverses the relationship.
o: The one with the longer pulse is closer to Earth
The one with the longer pulse is farther away
Both stars must be inside the Small Magellanic Cloud
The one with the shorter pulse is truly brighter

questions.s: What is the main idea of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says that when actions and beliefs conflict, 'we change what we think.' The first option reverses the experiment's result: the people paid less, not more, said they enjoyed the task.
o: People enjoy boring tasks more when they are paid well
People often adjust their beliefs to fit their actions
Most people feel uncomfortable telling strangers something untrue about an experiment
Expensive purchases usually lead to feelings of regret

questions.s: According to the professor, which participants said they enjoyed the task more?
questions.e: He says most people guess the twenty-dollar group, 'But it was the one-dollar group.' One dollar is the smaller payment. The twenty-dollar option is the tempting guess he warns against.
o: Those who received the smaller payment
Those who received twenty dollars for their help in the experiment
Those who did the task for the longest time
Those who refused to describe the task as fun

questions.s: Why does the professor ask who said they liked the task more?
questions.e: He asks the question and then says 'Most people guess the twenty-dollar group. But it was the one-dollar group.' The question sets up a surprise. Since most people guess wrong, the last option reverses his point.
o: To check whether students remember last week's reading
To find out which students have taken part in a psychology experiment before
To highlight that the result was surprising
To show that most people are good at predicting behavior

questions.s: Why does the professor mention people looking for good reviews after a purchase?
questions.e: He introduces it with 'You can see this in everyday life, too.' Searching for good reviews after buying something eases the tension of an expensive choice. He makes no claim about whether reviews are reliable.
o: To warn students about spending too much money
To show that online reviews are usually not a reliable source of information
To explain how companies pay people to write reviews
To give an everyday example of reducing dissonance

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains participant observation: 'You have to live it.' Travelers' reports describe the older approach that was replaced, and the Trobriand Islands are only where Malinowski worked.
o: The history of the Trobriand Islands in the Pacific Ocean
Why anthropologists rely on travelers' reports
A research method that involves living among people
How to write clear and useful field notes

questions.s: According to the professor, why do researchers often stay for a year or more?
questions.e: She asks 'Why a year?' and answers that 'many activities follow the seasons' and researchers want 'to see the whole cycle.' Avoiding a translator is the reason for learning the language, a separate point.
o: To earn the trust of local leaders before asking questions
To finish writing their field notes before returning to their universities
To avoid needing to use a translator
To observe activities that change with the seasons

questions.s: Why does the professor mention armchair anthropologists?
questions.e: She describes scholars who 'never actually met the people they wrote about' and then says 'That changed in the early twentieth century.' The nickname was a joke, so she is not praising them.
o: To praise scholars who built large theories from careful reading
To describe an older approach that later changed
To explain why libraries are still important for anthropology
To give an example of researchers who learned local languages

questions.s: What does the professor think about the risk that people act differently around a researcher?
questions.e: She calls it 'a real concern' but says people 'get used to you' and 'everyday behavior returns to normal' after a few months. Saying it is not a serious concern ignores her words 'That's a real concern.'
o: It is real but becomes smaller over time
It makes participant observation useless as a method of research
It is not a serious concern for most researchers
It can be solved by hiring a translator

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains linear perspective, how it was demonstrated, explained and spread. Brunelleschi appears for his demonstration only, not his life or buildings, and the professor says medieval painters did not lack skill.
o: The development of a method for showing depth in painting
The life and buildings of the architect Brunelleschi in Florence
Why medieval artists had less skill than later painters
How mirrors were used to make paintings brighter

questions.s: According to the professor, what did size usually show in medieval paintings?
questions.e: He says 'Size showed importance, not distance.' The option about distance repeats what size shows in perspective painting, so it reverses his point about medieval art.
o: How far away a figure was
How important a figure was
How old a figure was meant to be
How skilled the artist was at drawing people and buildings

questions.s: Why does the professor describe Brunelleschi's mirror demonstration?
questions.e: When the mirror was lowered, 'the real building appeared in exactly the same place. The painting matched reality.' The demonstration was about painting, not about how the building was designed.
o: To show how architects designed buildings in Florence
To explain why medieval buildings seem to tilt at strange angles in paintings
To argue that mirrors were more useful than paintings
To show that a painting could match a real view

questions.s: What does the professor imply about medieval artists?
questions.e: He says 'That's not because the artists lacked skill. They just had different goals.' The first option is the common assumption he rejects, and Brunelleschi came after the Middle Ages.
o: They did not know how to draw buildings accurately
They learned their methods from Brunelleschi's early work
Their choices reflected different aims
They were the first to use a vanishing point in their pictures

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says 'the name tells the whole story,' then explains the invention, the name piano e forte and the later iron frames. The guitar pick is only a comparison for how a harpsichord plucks its strings.
o: To compare the sound of the guitar with the sound of the harpsichord
To explain how the piano developed and got its name
To describe the life of Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence
To show students how to play both softly and loudly

questions.s: According to the professor, what was the main limitation of the harpsichord?
questions.e: She says 'Whether you press the key gently or hard, the volume comes out almost the same.' So touch could not control loudness. Concert halls are mentioned only for the later piano with an iron frame.
o: Its strings broke easily when they were plucked hard
It was too heavy to move into a concert hall
Its sound was much too loud for small rooms
Players could not change the volume by touch

questions.s: Why does the professor mention iron frames?
questions.e: Iron frames 'could hold the strings much tighter, which made the instrument louder and stronger.' They came in the eighteen hundreds, long after Cristofori, so they were not part of his design.
o: To explain why early pianos were so expensive to build
To show how harpsichords were improved before the piano appeared
To explain how pianos became louder and stronger
To describe the material Cristofori used for his hammers

questions.s: What can be inferred about the name 'piano'?
questions.e: The name comes from 'a harpsichord with soft and loud,' shortened to pianoforte and then piano, and soft and loud was exactly what the harpsichord could not do. Early pianos were quiet, but that is not why the name was chosen.
o: It is a shortened form of a phrase naming the new instrument's main advantage
It was chosen because the first pianos sounded very quiet
It comes from the name of the city where it was invented
It was given to the instrument by makers in the eighteen hundreds

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains the loss leader: a product that 'loses money' but 'leads customers into the store.' The placement of milk and eggs is one supporting example, and the laws he mentions protect small shops, not shoppers.
o: Where supermarkets place basic items
How small shops compete with large supermarkets
A pricing strategy that accepts losses on some products
Laws that protect shoppers from unfair prices

questions.s: According to the professor, how does a store make money from a loss leader?
questions.e: Once customers are inside, they buy other things that 'carry normal prices, and the store comes out ahead.' The two-item limit only reduces losses from cherry pickers; it does not create the profit.
o: Customers buy other items at regular prices
The supplier pays the store to advertise the product in its weekly flyers
The store raises the price after the holiday
Customers are limited to two items each

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that milk and eggs are often at the back of the store?
questions.e: He says 'To get there, you walk past a lot of other products, and some of them end up in your cart.' The point is store layout that draws shoppers past other goods. He never says milk and eggs are sold below cost.
o: To explain how stores keep these products fresh and cold for longer
To show how stores lead shoppers past other products
To give an example of a product that is sold below cost
To show that basic items are rarely profitable

questions.s: Why might a store limit a discounted item to two per customer?
questions.e: Cherry pickers 'grab only the discounted item, and leave,' and if too many do that 'the store just loses money. So stores often set a limit.' The laws he mentions apply 'in some countries,' not every country, and they are not linked to the limit.
o: To encourage shoppers to come back the next day
To follow laws about selling products below cost in every country
To make the product seem more valuable than it is
To cut losses from shoppers who buy only that item

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor explains the Great Vowel Shift, when 'the long vowels of English changed their pronunciation.' Chaucer's 'house' is only one example, and printing is discussed as the reason spelling stayed fixed, not as a way English spread.
o: How printing helped English spread to other European countries
The way Chaucer pronounced the word house
Why Spanish and Italian vowels are easier to learn
A historical change in how English vowels were pronounced

questions.s: According to the professor, how did the long vowels change?
questions.e: She says 'they didn't change randomly. They moved together, like a chain.' The shift took about three hundred years, from fourteen hundred to seventeen hundred, so the first option is wrong in two ways.
o: They changed randomly over a period of about fifty years
They moved together in a connected pattern
They became shorter and were finally dropped from many words
They took on the sounds of Spanish and Italian

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the arrival of printing in England?
questions.e: Printers 'helped make spellings more fixed. But the pronunciation kept moving,' so spellings record the old sounds. Printers fixed spelling; they did not cause the sound change, so the second option reverses the relationship.
o: To explain why spelling does not match pronunciation
To show that printers caused the vowels to change their sounds
To describe how Chaucer's works became popular
To give the exact date when the vowel shift ended

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward explanations for the cause of the shift?
questions.e: She says 'honestly, linguists still debate it' and there is 'no single explanation that everyone accepts.' That means the question is unresolved, so the claim that one theory is proven contradicts her.
o: She believes one theory has been clearly proven
She thinks the cause is unimportant for students of English spelling
She admits that the question is still open
She thinks printers were mainly responsible for it

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor names the urban heat island effect and gives its causes and solutions. Air conditioners and trees are each one part of the explanation, not the main topic.
o: Why cities tend to be warmer than nearby rural areas
How air conditioners work and why they use so much electrical power
The benefits of driving in the countryside at night
How trees release water vapor through their leaves

questions.s: According to the professor, why is the difference between city and countryside often largest at night?
questions.e: Asphalt and dark roofs absorb sunlight by day and 'at night, they slowly release that heat back into the air. That's why' the gap is largest after sunset. Water vapor from plants is a separate cause, and he does not link it to night.
o: Cars and factories produce the most heat after dark
Wind blows much more strongly through the countryside at night than through cities
Roads and roofs release heat they stored during the day
Plants stop releasing water vapor once the sun goes down

questions.s: Why does the professor call one part of the problem frustrating?
questions.e: People turn up the air conditioning, but air conditioners 'push heat outside,' so 'the problem can actually feed itself.' He calls the solutions 'fairly simple,' and several cities already paint roofs white, so cost is not his complaint.
o: White roofs are too expensive for most cities to install
Scientists cannot agree on what causes the effect
People refuse to plant trees along city streets
A common response to heat makes it worse

questions.s: What does the professor imply about painting roofs white?
questions.e: He lists 'lighter-colored roofs that reflect sunlight' as a solution and says cities paint roofs white 'for exactly this reason.' Since several cities are already doing it, the first option is wrong.
o: It is a costly idea that has not yet been tried in any real city
It can lower temperatures by reflecting sunlight
It works only in cities with very few tall buildings
It is less effective than planting trees

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks how an animal that needs water survives when moss dries, then explains the tun state and its limits. The trip to space is one example of their toughness, and 'water bear' is only a nickname based on looks.
o: How tardigrades survive by drying out
Where scientists usually go to collect moss for laboratory study
How tardigrades were sent into outer space
Why tardigrades are related to bears

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens when a tardigrade forms a tun?
questions.e: In the tun, 'It loses almost all the water in its body, and its metabolism slows down so much it's barely measurable.' The proteins form 'a kind of glass'; they do not make water, and no shell is mentioned.
o: It grows a hard shell to protect itself from radiation
It moves to a wetter part of the moss
It makes new water from the proteins in its body
It loses nearly all its water and its body processes almost stop

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the research satellite?
questions.e: The satellite is in a list of things tardigrades survived 'in this dried state,' along with extreme cold and radiation. Surviving several days is not the same as living and reproducing there, so the third option goes too far.
