o: To explain how scientists first discovered tardigrades in moss
To illustrate how tough dried tardigrades are
To show that tardigrades can live and reproduce in space
To describe a project that she worked on herself

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of the claim that tardigrades are indestructible?
questions.e: She calls it 'an exaggeration' and says active tardigrades are 'fairly delicate.' An exaggeration overstates something. The first option ignores her point that their toughness depends on the dried-out state.
o: She thinks it is accurate for both active and dried tardigrades
She thinks it is true only of tardigrades living in moss
She thinks it overstates their toughness
She thinks it was first made by scientists

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: He asks why there are volcanoes in Hawaii, 'thousands of kilometers from any edge,' and answers with the hotspot idea. Volcanoes at plate edges are mentioned only as the usual case, not compared in detail.
o: To describe the dangers of living near an active volcano on an island
To compare Hawaii with volcanoes at plate edges
To explain how Kauai was formed by erosion
To explain how volcanoes can form far from plate edges

questions.s: According to the professor, why does a Hawaiian volcano eventually become inactive?
questions.e: He says 'the plate carries it away. Cut off from its supply, it goes quiet.' The hotspot 'stays put' and does not cool. Erosion happens to older islands, but it is not what makes the volcano go quiet.
o: The hotspot beneath it slowly cools down
It is worn down by waves and rain over millions of years
The moving plate carries it away from its heat source
A newer volcano takes all of its magma

questions.s: How does the professor support the hotspot explanation?
questions.e: He says 'the evidence fits nicely': the Big Island in the southeast is youngest, and islands to the northwest are older, as the hotspot idea predicts. He does not name any scientist or describe an experiment.
o: By pointing out that the islands' ages fit a pattern
By describing an experiment that recreated a hotspot in a laboratory setting
By comparing Hawaii with several other island chains
By quoting the scientist who first proposed the idea

questions.s: What can be inferred about the underwater volcano southeast of the Big Island?
questions.e: New volcanoes form over the fixed hotspot, and this one is 'growing right now' at the young southeastern end, so it must be over the hotspot. He says it will surface 'tens of thousands of years from now,' not in a few years.
o: It is older than the island of Kauai
It is located above the hotspot today
It will rise above the sea within the next few years
It formed at the edge of the Pacific Plate

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: She says many people think distance causes seasons, 'But it's wrong,' and ends with 'it's the angle, not the distance.' Canada, Argentina and the flashlight are only evidence and an analogy.
o: To describe how early astronomers first measured the shape of Earth's orbit
To correct a common belief about the cause of seasons
To compare the climates of Canada and Argentina
To explain how a flashlight spreads its light

questions.s: According to the professor, when is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.e: Earth is 'closest to the Sun in early January. That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere.' The summer option is the common belief that she calls wrong.
o: During winter in the Northern Hemisphere
In the middle of summer in the Northern Hemisphere
Whenever the Southern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun
At the same time of year in every hemisphere

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a flashlight?
questions.e: Straight down, a flashlight makes 'a small, bright spot,' but tilted, 'each part gets less energy.' This shows why direct sunlight heats more. Longer days are the second, separate effect she lists afterward.
o: To show how scientists measure the brightness of sunlight on the ground
To explain why days are longer in summer
To show why direct light heats the ground more
To describe how Earth's axis is tilted

questions.s: What does the professor suggest by pointing out that Canada and Argentina have opposite seasons?
questions.e: She says 'If distance were the cause, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time.' Opposite seasons therefore rule out distance. She also says the orbit is 'almost a circle, but not quite,' so it is not a perfect circle.
o: Seasons are stronger in the north than in the south
Argentina is closer to the Sun than Canada is
Earth's orbit is a perfect circle
Distance from the Sun cannot be what causes the change of seasons

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor compares cramming with spreading study out and says 'Spreading it out wins. This is called the spacing effect.' Ebbinghaus is mentioned as an early researcher, not as the main topic.
o: How Ebbinghaus learned long lists of nonsense syllables in the eighteen eighties
Why exams should be given in the morning
Why studying in shorter sessions over time works better
How flashcard apps are designed and sold

questions.s: According to the professor, why can cramming be misleading?
questions.e: He says 'Cramming often feels like it's working' because 'the material seems familiar,' but most of it is gone a week later. The total time is the same in his example, 'Same total time,' so the first option is wrong.
o: It takes much more total time than spaced study does
It makes material feel familiar for a short time
It works only for students who use flashcard apps
It causes students to sleep badly before the test

questions.s: Why does the professor mention flashcard apps?
questions.e: He says 'many flashcard apps are built around this idea,' showing cards again with longer and longer gaps. He names no particular app and says nothing about using one himself.
o: To recommend a particular app that he has used himself for many years
To explain how Ebbinghaus tested his own memory
To show that cramming works well for short tests
To give a practical use of the spacing effect

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward cramming the night before an exam?
questions.e: He admits that 'for a test the very next morning, cramming can do okay,' but 'Most of it is gone' later, and he advises 'don't save it all for the night before.' Saying it never helps is too extreme.
o: He thinks it may help the next day but is a poor way to remember material
He believes it is the best approach for difficult subjects
He thinks it never helps on any kind of test
He has no clear opinion about it

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor describes the Laetoli footprints, how they survived and 'what do the prints tell us' about how our ancestors walked. Mary Leakey is named only as the team leader, and her other discoveries are never mentioned.
o: The career of Mary Leakey and her many other discoveries in East Africa
How volcanoes formed in Tanzania millions of years ago
What ancient footprints reveal about early human ancestors
Why chimpanzees walk differently from humans

questions.s: According to the professor, what helped the footprints survive?
questions.e: Rain turned the ash 'into something like wet cement,' and then 'The sun dried the ash hard' before more ash covered it. The surface was volcanic ash, not lake mud, so the first option is not mentioned.
o: They were made in mud beside a lake that later dried up completely
Rain made the ash soft, and it later hardened
They were covered by ice for thousands of years
Heavy animals pressed them into soft rock

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a chimpanzee's foot?
questions.e: The big toe in the prints is 'lined up with the other toes, rather than sticking out to the side the way it does in a chimpanzee's foot.' The comparison shows a difference. Tree climbing is never discussed.
o: To contrast it with the toe position in the prints
To explain why chimpanzees left no footprints at the site
To show that early ancestors spent most of their time climbing trees
To describe the animals that walked across the ash

questions.s: What does the professor conclude from the age of the footprints?
questions.e: He says 'walking on two legs came first, long before big brains or toolmaking.' The first option reverses that order, and he says the brains were 'not much bigger than a chimpanzee's,' not like ours.
o: Stone tools were invented before upright walking began
Early ancestors had brains about the size of ours
The prints were made by modern humans who moved to Africa much later
Upright walking developed before large brains

questions.s: What is the main idea of the talk?
questions.e: She focuses on 'a much humbler object that helped make it possible: the paint tube,' and ends with 'a change in art depends on a change in technology.' Monet and Renoir are both mentioned, but no disagreement between them is described.
o: Monet and Renoir disagreed about how to paint natural light outdoors
Animal bladders kept paint colors brighter
Railways allowed artists to sell paintings in the city
A simple invention helped a new art style develop

questions.s: According to the professor, what was a problem with storing paint in animal bladders?
questions.e: She says 'They leaked, they burst, and the paint dried out quickly.' Nothing is said about color, cost or heating, so the other options are not mentioned.
o: The paint often leaked or dried out
The bladders made the colors look darker and less natural
Bladders were expensive and hard to find in cities
The paint had to be heated before it could be used

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Monet's paintings of haystacks?
questions.e: Right after saying painters could catch 'changing light as it happened,' she says Monet painted the same haystacks 'at different times of day.' The paintings were made outdoors, so the studio option reverses her point.
o: To show that Monet preferred painting farms to painting cities
To give an example of a painting made in a studio
To illustrate artists capturing light as it changed
To explain why Impressionist paintings sold for high prices in their own day

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of the statement attributed to Renoir?
questions.e: She says 'Maybe that's a slight exaggeration, but it makes a fair point.' A slight exaggeration goes a bit too far, and a fair point is an important truth. She does not call it completely accurate.
o: She thinks it is completely accurate
She thinks it goes a bit too far but contains an important truth
She doubts that Renoir really said it
She thinks it ignores the role of the artists' talent

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains basso continuo, 'the foundation of almost all Baroque music.' Jazz pianists appear only in a comparison, and writing out every part is how the continuo faded at the end.
o: A system that supported the music of an earlier period
How the cello replaced the lute in Baroque orchestras
Why jazz pianists study Baroque music in such great detail
How composers learned to write out every part

questions.s: According to the professor, what did the numbers in the bass line show?
questions.e: The keyboard player got 'the bass line and those numbers, which showed which chords to play.' The word continuo means the part plays all the way through, but the numbers do not show the length of the piece.
o: How loudly each note should be played
How many players should join the continuo part at that point
Which chords the keyboard player should use
How long the piece should continue

questions.s: Why does the professor mention jazz pianists?
questions.e: He says 'If that sounds familiar, it should' and that a jazz pianist reading chord symbols does 'something very similar.' It is a comparison, not a claim that jazz came directly from Baroque music.
o: To suggest that jazz developed directly from Baroque music
To compare continuo playing with a familiar modern practice
To explain why jazz bands often use the harpsichord
To show that improvisation is less common in older music than in newer styles

questions.s: What can be inferred about Baroque keyboard players?
questions.e: The composer 'didn't write out those chords,' so the player 'had to make up the actual notes on the spot.' This is the opposite of reading every note from the score, which makes the second option wrong.
o: They usually played the bass line on a cello as well
They read every note of their part from the written score
They disliked playing continuo parts in long pieces
They had to create music while they performed

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: She says 'let's look at how that model works, and why it's so common,' and then describes both sides of a franchise. Similar menus are only one of the rules franchisees follow, not the purpose of the talk.
o: To explain why fast-food restaurants have such similar menus in every city
To advise students on how to start a new business
To explain how a common business arrangement works
To compare hotels and restaurants as investments

questions.s: According to the professor, what are royalties?
questions.e: Royalties are 'ongoing payments,' 'usually a percentage of sales.' The first option describes the 'upfront fee,' a different payment, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.
o: A single fee paid before a location opens
Money the franchisor pays to local suppliers each year
Payments franchisees receive for good service
Ongoing payments based on a share of sales

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that a local owner risks their own savings?
questions.e: She says such an owner 'tends to work harder than a hired manager might.' Working harder shows strong motivation. She is describing a benefit for the franchisor, not warning students about investing.
o: To warn students about the dangers of investing money in restaurants
To explain why franchisees may be highly motivated
To show that franchisors lose money on new locations
To explain why royalties are a percentage of sales

questions.s: What can be inferred about why franchisors set strict rules for franchisees?
questions.e: She ends by noting that 'one badly run location can hurt the reputation of the whole brand,' which explains why rules keep every location the same. Franchisees 'give up a lot of independence,' so the last option reverses her point.
o: To protect the brand's reputation everywhere
To make sure franchisees pay their fees on time each month
To help franchisees save money on uniforms
To give franchisees more independence

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor contrasts the old view, 'a sign of weakness,' with the current one, 'now generally seen as a skill.' The teachers who discouraged switching belong to the old view, which she rejects.
o: Why teachers should stop bilingual students from mixing languages in class
How views of switching between languages have changed
The history of the Spanish language in New York
How young children learn two languages at once

questions.s: According to the professor, what did researchers find about speakers who switched within sentences?
questions.e: The smoothest switchers 'tended to be the ones who were most fluent in both languages.' The switches happened where 'neither language's rules were broken,' so the option about breaking grammar rules reverses the finding.
o: They were often highly fluent in both languages
They usually knew only a few words of English
They broke grammar rules more often than other speakers in conversation
They switched only when quoting other people

questions.s: Why does the professor mention repeating what someone said in the language they used?
questions.e: It comes in her list of reasons after 'So why do people switch? Often, it's social,' along with showing identity and adding emphasis. She treats switching as a skill, not as forgetting words or making mistakes.
o: To show that bilingual speakers often forget words in one language
To explain how researchers recorded real conversations
To describe a common mistake made by language learners
To give one example of a social reason for switching between languages

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward code-switching?
questions.e: She ends by saying it is 'generally seen as a skill, a flexible use of two complete systems.' A skill is an ability. The idea of weak command is the old assumption she describes and rejects.
o: She thinks schools should discourage it
She believes it shows a weak command of language
She views it as an ability rather than a problem
She thinks it is too rare to be worth studying in detail

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor first explains how mangroves handle 'salt and oxygen,' then asks 'why should we care about mangroves?' Shrimp farms are mentioned only as one reason mangroves have been cleared.
o: How shrimp farms have changed tropical coastlines over the past few decades
Why most trees cannot survive in salty water
How young fish escape from larger predators
How mangroves survive and why they matter

questions.s: According to the professor, why do some mangroves have roots that grow upward?
questions.e: The mud has 'very little oxygen,' so these roots 'take in air' at low tide. Holding the soil and sheltering fish are benefits of the root tangle in general, not the reason these roots grow upward.
o: To push salt out of the tree more quickly
To hold the soil in place during storms
To take in air that the mud lacks
To give young fish shelter in shallow water

questions.s: Why does the professor mention salt crystals on the leaves?
questions.e: Some species 'take it in and then push it out through their leaves,' and the crystals can be seen on the surface. They show salt being removed, so the idea that mangroves need salt to grow is not supported.
o: To give visible evidence of one method mangroves use to get rid of salt
To explain why mangrove leaves are harmful to animals
To show that mangroves need salt in order to grow
To describe how seawater dries at low tide

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward efforts to replant mangroves?
questions.e: He calls replanting 'The good news' but adds that mangroves recover 'when it's done in the right places,' which is a hopeful but careful view. Replacing all lost forests soon is far more than he claims.
o: He thinks they rarely work in any location
He is cautiously hopeful about them
He thinks they matter less than shrimp farming does
He believes they will soon replace all the lost forests

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor defines catalysts as substances that 'speed up a chemical reaction without being used up' and spends the talk explaining how. Hydrogen peroxide is only an example, and enzyme selectivity is the topic for 'next time', so neither is the main idea.
o: Why some reactions release more energy than others do
How catalysts make reactions faster without being consumed
The chemical makeup of hydrogen peroxide and its uses in medicine
How enzymes choose which reactions in the body they will control

questions.s: According to the professor, how does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
questions.e: The professor says a catalyst offers 'a different path, one with a lower hill', which the correct option paraphrases as a route needing less energy to begin. The option about the hill disappearing repeats her words but reverses them: she says a catalyst 'doesn't make the hill disappear'. She also says it works 'at the same temperature' and does not change the energy released.
o: It raises the temperature of the reacting molecules
It increases the total energy the reaction gives off
It removes the need for activation energy completely, so the hill disappears
It provides a route that requires less energy to begin

questions.s: Why does the professor mention putting hydrogen peroxide on a cut?
questions.e: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down 'very slowly on its own', but on a cut 'it fizzes right away' because the enzyme catalase acts as a catalyst. The example illustrates a catalyst at work. She gives no safety warning, and the reaction happens at body temperature, not a high one.
o: To show a catalyst speeding up a normally slow reaction
To warn students that hydrogen peroxide can be dangerous to use
To explain why oxygen is produced whenever water is formed
To give an example of a reaction that needs a high temperature

questions.s: What can be inferred about the catalase in the example?
questions.e: The professor says a catalyst 'comes out of the reaction unchanged', so 'a small amount can be used again and again'. Since catalase is a catalyst, it can keep breaking down more peroxide. The idea that it is 'used up' contradicts the definition given at the start of the talk.
o: It is used up completely after a few seconds of fizzing
It changes the final products of the breakdown of peroxide
It could go on to break down more hydrogen peroxide
It works only when the peroxide is stored in a cabinet

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says every opening of a pore is 'a kind of trade: carbon in, water out', and the rest of the talk shows how plants manage that trade. Slow growth in desert plants is mentioned only at the end as a cost, so it is too narrow to be the main topic.
o: How plants store water inside their leaves during dry seasons
Why desert plants grow more slowly than other plants
How leaf pores balance taking in carbon and losing water
The way guard cells make food through photosynthesis

questions.s: According to the professor, what causes a stoma to open?
questions.e: The professor explains that with plenty of water 'the guard cells fill up, swell and bend apart, and the pore opens'. Losing pressure and going limp is what makes the pore close, so that option reverses the process.
o: Guard cells that fill with water and bend apart
Guard cells that lose pressure and go limp in the heat
A drop in the amount of carbon dioxide inside the leaf
Cooler, more humid air reaching the underside of the leaf

questions.s: Why does the professor mention cacti?
questions.e: Cacti 'keep their stomata shut during the day and open them at night', a different schedule from most plants. The tempting option about photosynthesis at night is wrong: they only take in carbon dioxide at night and 'use it for photosynthesis once the sun comes up'.
o: To show that some plants have no stomata at all
To explain why plants close their pores in the afternoon heat
To point out a plant that carries out photosynthesis only at night
To give an example of a different timing for opening pores

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the desert plants' strategy?
questions.e: He calls it 'a clever arrangement', which shows admiration, and then adds 'though it does come at a cost', namely slow growth. He never says it is not worth studying, and he states clearly that these plants 'lose far less water'.
o: He thinks it is too costly to be worth studying
He admires it but notes that it has a drawback
He believes it will soon spread to most other plants
He is unsure whether it really reduces water loss at all

questions.s: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes how the Bretton Woods plan 'fixed the value' of currencies and then how it ended when currencies began 'floating'. The nineteen thirties and the World Bank are details within that story, not its main subject.
o: The rise and fall of a system of fixed exchange rates
The reasons the price of gold kept rising after the nineteen forties
How the World Bank lends money to countries in difficulty
Why countries lowered their currency values in the nineteen thirties

questions.s: According to the professor, what was a weakness of the system?
questions.e: The professor says 'more and more dollars circulated abroad, far more than the gold the United States held'. The first option reverses the facts, since the system gave 'predictable exchange rates', and the IMF existed precisely to lend to countries in trouble.
o: Exchange rates changed too often for businesses to plan
Countries could not borrow money when they needed to
Dollars held abroad came to exceed the US gold supply
Too few dollars were in use, so international trade slowed down

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the nineteen thirties?
questions.e: The delegates 'remembered the nineteen thirties, when countries kept lowering the value of their currencies' and trade shrank, so the decade explains what the new system was meant to avoid. No gold price from the thirties is given, and the IMF was created at the 1944 conference.
o: To compare the gold price then with the price in nineteen forty-four
To explain a problem the planners hoped to prevent
To show when the International Monetary Fund was created
To argue that floating exchange rates had worked better

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the institutions created at the conference?
questions.e: She ends by saying 'the Bretton Woods system didn't last, but its institutions did. Both are still operating today.' So the IMF and the World Bank continued after the fixed rates ended. The collapse is linked to the shortage of gold, not to the institutions.
o: They were closed when the dollar stopped being tied to gold
They caused the system to collapse in nineteen seventy-one
They were designed mainly to protect the price of gold
They outlived the exchange rate system they were made for

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk explains Granovetter's finding that people often learn about jobs through acquaintances, who are 'a bridge to people and news you'd never reach otherwise'. The first option reverses the point, and the interviews are only how the finding was made.
o: Why close friends are more helpful than acquaintances
How sociologists design interview studies with people seeking jobs
The difference between family ties and friendships
Why distant contacts can be a valuable source of information

questions.s: According to the professor, why do close friends often provide less new information?
questions.e: Close friends 'tend to know each other, go to the same places and hear the same news', so what they know is 'mostly information you already have'. Seeing each other rarely describes weak ties, not close friends, so that option mixes up the two groups.
o: They are usually less willing to share what they know
They tend to share the same social circle and news
They see each other too rarely to exchange much news
They care more about emotional support than about jobs

questions.s: How does the professor organize the talk?
questions.e: He begins with 'First, some terms', defining strong and weak ties, then reports what Granovetter 'found', and then asks 'Why would that be?' before explaining. He tells no personal story and describes interviews, not the steps of an experiment.
o: He compares two theories and then rejects both of them
He tells a personal story and then draws a lesson from it
He defines terms, presents a finding and then explains it
He lists the steps of an experiment in the order they happened

questions.s: What does the professor mean when he says the strength of a weak tie 'isn't emotional'?
questions.e: He follows the remark with 'It's about access to new information', which comes from acquaintances who move 'in a different circle'. He does not claim acquaintances care more; he says close friends are helpful 'in many ways'.
o: Its value comes from reaching people outside your group
Acquaintances usually care more than close friends do
Weak ties become strong ties after people share their feelings
Close friends rarely help each other during difficult times

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains that flying buttresses moved 'much of the support outside the building', so walls 'could be thinner and opened up with glass'. Stained glass is mentioned, but its cost is not discussed, and the talk is about structure, not decoration.
o: Why stained glass was so expensive in the Middle Ages
How an outside support allowed walls with large windows
The differences between French and Romanesque church decoration
How stone vaults were lifted into place during construction

questions.s: According to the professor, what problem does the weight of a stone vault create?
questions.e: She says the vault's weight 'also pushes outward, against the tops of the walls', so the walls may lean out. The option about pressing straight down repeats her words, but she says the weight 'doesn't just press straight down', and she never mentions cracked floors.
o: It pushes the tops of the walls outward
It makes the windows too heavy to stay in place
It sinks the piers deeper into soft ground each year
It presses straight down and cracks the floor below

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Romanesque churches?
questions.e: Romanesque builders handled the outward push 'the simple way: very thick walls with small windows', which the professor contrasts with the Gothic solution of buttresses. France and the twelfth century refer to Gothic builders, so that option mixes up two details.
o: To show where Gothic builders learned to make stained glass
To argue that thick walls were stronger than flying buttresses
To explain that they were first built in France in the twelfth century
To contrast an earlier solution to the same structural problem

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of flying buttresses?
questions.e: She reports that 'some people find buttresses ugly', then gives her own view: 'I'd say they're honest. They show you exactly how the building stands up.' The scaffolding comparison is other people's opinion, not hers.
o: She agrees that they look like unfinished scaffolding
She thinks they hide the real structure of the building
She values them because they reveal how the building works
She believes they were added later to repair weak cathedrals

questions.s: What is the main idea of the talk?
questions.e: The professor concludes that 'meaning in cinema comes not only from what's inside a shot, but from how shots are placed next to each other'. Modern experiments had 'mixed results', and he still calls the effect 'real', so saying Kuleshov was proven wrong goes too far.
o: Actors in silent films needed very expressive faces
Modern experiments have shown that Kuleshov was wrong
The order of shots can change what viewers think they see
Russian filmmakers were the first to use close-up shots of actors

questions.s: According to the story, what did audiences say about the actor?
questions.e: Viewers 'said he looked hungry when he faced the soup and tender when he looked at the child'. In fact his face was neutral, but that is the professor's point, not what the audiences said; the first option describes the shot, not their reaction.
o: That he showed no emotion in any of the scenes
That he had been replaced by a different actor in each scene
That the soup and the child distracted from his acting
That his face expressed different feelings in each sequence

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the traditional story of the experiment?
questions.e: He says 'the effect seems real, but it's probably weaker than the legend suggests', which shows partial acceptance. He also says modern results are 'mixed' and the original film 'hasn't survived', so it cannot prove anything.
o: He accepts the effect but thinks it has been exaggerated
He suspects the whole story was invented by critics much later
He considers it fully confirmed by many careful modern studies
He believes the original film proves the story true

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a reaction shot?
questions.e: Right after 'Editors use this all the time', he explains that a reaction shot can make a line 'seem funny or threatening, depending on what comes right before it'. That is the Kuleshov principle in today's editing. He never says Kuleshov invented the reaction shot.
o: To describe a mistake that early editors often made
To show how editors still use Kuleshov's principle
To explain why dialogue matters more than images in film
To point out a kind of shot that Kuleshov invented himself

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk describes the jigsaw technique, in which 'no one can understand the whole lesson without listening to every member'. A famous person's life is only a sample lesson, and the competition mentioned was between students in a classroom, not between schools.
o: A teaching method that makes students depend on one another
Why shy students learn less in group activities at school
How teachers in Texas planned lessons about famous people
The history of competition between schools in the nineteen seventies

questions.s: According to the professor, what did Aronson see as part of the problem in the classrooms?
questions.e: Aronson thought the classroom itself was a problem because 'students competed for the teacher's attention'. Careful preparation is mentioned at the end as a demand of the jigsaw method, not as the original problem.
o: Teachers did not prepare their materials carefully enough
Groups of five or six students were too large to work well
Students knew too little about famous people's lives
Students had to compete with one another for attention

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a shy student?
questions.e: She says even a shy student 'suddenly holds information the group needs', which shows that the method makes every member necessary. She says nothing about leaders, and it is the other students, not teachers, who may ignore someone.
o: To show that some students should not be placed in groups
To suggest that shy students make the best expert group leaders
To illustrate how every student becomes important to the group
To explain why teachers often ignored certain students

questions.s: What does the professor imply when she says the method 'does take careful planning'?
questions.e: After listing the benefits, she adds 'though' and explains that the teacher must 'divide the material into fair pieces and prepare all of it in advance'. That is a cost for the teacher. Studies found learning 'at least as good', so the first option contradicts the talk.
o: It has not been shown to improve learning in any study
Its benefits come with extra work for the teacher
Students must plan their own lessons before class starts
It works only in schools that have recently been integrated

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor introduces dendrochronology, 'or tree-ring dating', and explains how matching ring patterns builds a calendar. Douglass and the reused beams are supporting details. Climate explains why rings differ, but the talk is not about climate change.
o: How the climate of the American Southwest changed over centuries
Why builders in the past often reused old wooden beams
The career of an astronomer who was interested in climate
How patterns in tree rings are used to date wood

questions.s: According to the professor, what often makes one tree ring wider than another?
questions.e: He says 'a year with plenty of rain produces a wide ring, and a dry year produces a narrow one'. The correct option paraphrases 'plenty of rain' as more rainfall. The tree's age and the time of cutting are not given as causes of ring width.
o: The tree being older when the ring was formed
An astronomer's records of sunshine that year
More rainfall during the year the ring grew
The beam being cut down later in the season

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that people sometimes reused old beams?
questions.e: He says tree rings show 'when a tree was cut down, not necessarily when a building went up', and reused beams are the reason. So a beam could give an earlier date than the building. He does not reject the method; he says archaeologists 'date many beams' to be careful.
o: To explain why wooden houses lasted so long in dry regions
To point out a reason a date might be misleading
To show how Douglass first discovered the method
To argue that the method should never be used on buildings

questions.s: What can be inferred about how a tree-ring record is extended further back in time?
questions.e: The professor explains that if a beam's last rings 'match the pattern in the tree's earliest rings', the two can be lined up, and this is repeated 'with older and older pieces of wood'. One living tree alone is only the starting point, so counting its rings cannot reach further back.
o: It needs older wood whose rings overlap a known sequence
It depends on counting the rings of one very old living tree as carefully as possible
It relies on records kept by early astronomers in the region
It compares the rings with dates written on old buildings

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor introduces thermohaline circulation and says 'the key idea is density'. Wind-driven surface currents are mentioned only to contrast them with this slower system, and the saltless sea ice is one step in the process.
o: How winds push currents along the surface of the ocean
Why sea ice in the Arctic contains so little salt
A slow ocean circulation driven by differences in density
How long it takes heat to travel from the equator to Greenland

questions.s: According to the professor, why does the water near Greenland become saltier?
questions.e: She explains that 'when sea ice forms, the ice is mostly fresh. The salt is left behind in the water around it.' Water from the south is mentioned, but it becomes colder, not saltier, on arrival.
o: Rivers carry salt into the sea from the land nearby
Salt is left behind in the water when sea ice forms
Warm water from the south brings extra salt with it
Deep water rising from the sea floor is full of salt

questions.s: What is the professor's view of the term 'conveyor belt'?
questions.e: She calls it 'a useful picture, as long as you remember that the real system is much messier'. That is partial approval with a warning. She does not reject the term, and she clearly does not think it is completely accurate.
o: She thinks it is misleading and should not be used
She believes it describes the system with complete accuracy
She prefers it to the scientific name of the circulation
She finds it helpful but too simple to be fully accurate

questions.s: What can be inferred about the water that sinks near Greenland?
questions.e: The deep water 'creeps southward' and only 'over a very long time' rises again, with a full trip taking 'something like a thousand years'. So it stays deep for a very long time. It sinks because of density, not wind, which drives surface currents.
o: It may not return to the surface for centuries
It rises again within a few weeks in the same place
It becomes warmer and saltier as it moves south
It is pushed down to the sea floor mainly by strong winds

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: Most of the talk explains how chromatophores, controlled 'directly by nerves from the brain', let the cuttlefish change color 'in well under a second'. Chameleons appear only as a comparison, and mating is never discussed.
o: Why cuttlefish are more closely related to squid than to octopuses
How cuttlefish skin is able to change color so quickly
How chameleons and cuttlefish use color to attract mates
Why most sea animals are unable to see in color

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens when the muscles around a chromatophore contract?
questions.e: He says contracting muscles 'pull the sac open' and 'the color spreads out'. The tiny dot is what happens when the muscles relax, so that option reverses the process. Bumps and reflecting cells are separate features of the skin.
o: The sac shrinks back into a tiny dot that is hard to see
The skin raises small bumps that copy rocks
The pigment spreads over a wider area
The cells underneath begin to reflect blue light

questions.s: Why does the professor mention chameleons?
questions.e: Right after saying 'the change is extremely fast', he adds that a chameleon 'changes color far more slowly'. The comparison highlights the cuttlefish's speed. He does not say chameleons use the same mechanism or that they are colorblind.
o: To emphasize how fast the cuttlefish's color change is
To show another animal that uses chromatophores in the same way
To explain where cuttlefish got their ability to change texture
To point out an animal that is also colorblind

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the puzzle he describes at the end?
questions.e: He says the question 'is still an open question' and calls it 'one of my favorite mysteries in biology'. So he is interested and admits nobody knows yet. He does not criticize the tests; he accepts that they 'suggest' colorblindness.
o: He thinks the tests on cuttlefish vision were badly designed
He believes the answer has already been found by researchers
He finds it unimportant compared with the muscle system
He is fascinated by it and admits it is not yet solved

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor calls the sea breeze 'a nice small-scale example of how pressure differences create wind' and explains that land and water 'heat up differently'. The beach is only a familiar setting, and Florida is a single example at the end.
o: To describe what people can do to stay cool at the beach
To compare the climate of Florida with that of other coastal areas
To show why thunderstorms are more dangerous near the sea
To explain how uneven heating produces coastal winds

questions.s: According to the professor, why does water warm more slowly than land?
questions.e: She says it 'takes a lot of energy to raise its temperature, and the heat gets mixed down into deeper layers'. The last option reverses the facts: the air over the sea is cooler and the pressure there is higher. Reflection of sunlight is never mentioned.
o: Its heat is spread into deeper layers below the surface
Cool winds blowing from the land carry its heat away
It reflects most of the sunlight back into the sky
The air above the water is warmer and has lower pressure, so heat escapes

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens at night?
questions.e: At night 'the land cools off faster than the water, so the air flows from the land out to sea', which is a land breeze. The option saying the water cools faster reverses this, and the land breeze is described as 'usually weaker', not stronger.
o: The sea breeze becomes stronger than it was during the day
Air flows from the land toward the sea
The water cools faster than the land does
Thunderstorms form along the coastline

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Florida?
questions.e: She mentions Florida right after explaining that sea air can force warm air upward and 'set off afternoon thunderstorms'. It is an example of that effect. She does not discuss who first studied sea breezes or compare land breezes by climate.
o: To name the place where people first studied sea breezes
To show that land breezes are stronger in warm climates
To give an example of sea breezes setting off storms
To explain why beaches there are cooler than inland towns

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains buffers using blood, where carbonic acid and bicarbonate keep the pH within a narrow range so that it 'barely moves'. Exercise and the kidneys are parts of that explanation, not the main subject.
o: Why hard exercise makes people breathe more quickly
How the kidneys remove waste products from the blood
How a buffer system keeps the pH of blood stable
Which enzymes stop working when blood becomes too basic

questions.s: According to the professor, what does bicarbonate do when extra acid enters the blood?
questions.e: He says 'bicarbonate picks up the hydrogen ions and becomes carbonic acid'. Releasing hydrogen ions is what carbonic acid does when blood becomes too basic, so the first option reverses the roles. The kidneys hold on to bicarbonate rather than remove it.
o: It releases more hydrogen ions into the blood to balance it
It breaks down into water and oxygen
It is carried to the kidneys so that it can be removed quickly
It takes up hydrogen ions and forms carbonic acid

questions.s: Why does the professor mention hard exercise?
questions.e: When acid builds up 'during hard exercise, you breathe faster and get rid of more of it', meaning more carbon dioxide is breathed out. The example shows the lungs supporting the buffer. The point is that pH stays stable, not that it changes greatly.
o: To show that blood pH changes a great deal during sport
To illustrate how breathing helps remove excess acid
To explain why the kidneys work faster than the lungs
To warn that the body produces too much carbon dioxide

questions.s: What does the professor say about the kidneys compared with the lungs?
questions.e: He says the kidneys 'work over hours or days, while breathing adjusts within minutes'. The second option reverses the two organs. He also says 'the kidneys help too', so they do play a part.
o: They act more slowly in correcting the blood's pH
They react within minutes, while the lungs take days
They produce the carbonic acid that the lungs need
They play no real part in controlling blood acidity

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes mycorrhizae as a 'deal': the fungus passes nutrients to the plant, and 'in return' the plant gives it sugars. The move onto land is mentioned only as one researchers' idea about the history of this partnership.
o: How the roots of plants grow deep in search of water
Why some fungi are harmful to the plants they live on
How the earliest plants managed to move from the water onto land
A partnership in which plants and fungi exchange resources

questions.s: According to the professor, what does the plant give the fungus?
questions.e: She says 'the plant gives the fungus sugars it makes through photosynthesis'. Phosphorus and water go the other way, from the fungus to the plant, so those options reverse the exchange. The thin threads belong to the fungus itself.
o: Phosphorus that it collects from deep in the soil
Sugars that it produces through photosynthesis
Water that its roots take in after heavy rain
Thin threads that help the fungus spread further

questions.s: Why does the professor mention fossils that are about four hundred million years old?
questions.e: She introduces the fossils with 'This relationship is very old', and they 'already show fungi living in their tissues'. The fossils are evidence of the partnership's age. Nothing is said about dating methods or animals.
o: To show that the partnership began very long ago
To explain how scientists measure the age of fungi
To prove that early plants had no roots at all
To argue that fungi appeared on land before any animals did

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward some claims about the 'wood wide web'?
questions.e: She says 'fungal networks connecting trees do exist, but some of the bigger claims go beyond the evidence', and advises treating them 'with caution'. So she accepts the networks but doubts the larger claims, which rules out both the first and second options.
o: She thinks the fungal networks themselves do not exist
She fully accepts that trees warn each other through fungi
She is skeptical of claims that go beyond the evidence
She believes the phrase was invented to sell more books

questions.s: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.e: The professor follows paper money from merchants' receipts called jiaozi to government notes and later inflation. Distrust of the deposit shops is one step in this story, and Marco Polo is a closing detail, not the subject.
o: The early history of paper money in China
Why iron coins were more valuable than silk in Sichuan
How Marco Polo's travels changed the European economy
Why merchants in Sichuan stopped trusting deposit shops

questions.s: According to the professor, why did merchants in Sichuan begin using paper receipts?
questions.e: Iron coins 'were terribly heavy for large purchases', so a merchant might need 'a cart full of coins' to buy silk. The government became involved only later, after shops failed, so it did not start the use of receipts.
o: The government ordered them to stop using coins
Paper was much cheaper to make than iron in that region
Silk traders refused to accept payment in coins
Large amounts of iron coins were too heavy to carry

questions.s: According to the professor, why did the government take over issuing the notes?
questions.e: Some shops 'issued more receipts than they had coins to back them up', and people lost their savings, so 'the government stepped in'. Marco Polo visited two centuries later, so he could not have influenced the decision.
o: Merchants wanted to send money to Europe more easily
Some shops had issued receipts they could not repay
The price of silk had risen sharply in Sichuan
Marco Polo had advised officials to print their own notes

questions.s: What can be inferred about the paper money printed in later periods?
questions.e: The professor says later governments 'printed more and more notes, and their value fell sharply', calling it 'an early example of what we'd now call inflation'. The correct option links the large amount printed to the fall in value.
o: It was backed by more coins than the earlier notes
It was used mainly by merchants traveling to Europe
It lost value because too much of it was issued
It was printed only by private deposit shops again

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor explains Weber's 'ideal type of bureaucracy', lists its features and ends with his mixed opinion of it. The everyday complaints about bureaucracy are only an opening contrast, and family control of jobs is one comparison.
o: Why modern bureaucracies have become so inefficient
How families controlled government jobs in the past
Max Weber's model of bureaucracy and his view of it
The way written records were kept in early organizations

questions.s: According to the professor, what does Weber mean by an 'ideal' type?
questions.e: She says 'ideal here doesn't mean perfect or desirable. It means a simplified model' for comparing 'real organizations against it'. The option with 'perfect and desirable' uses the everyday meaning she explicitly rejects.
o: A simplified model used for comparison
An organization that every country should copy
The most perfect and desirable form of organization
A system that once existed in early twentieth-century Germany

questions.s: Why does the professor mention positions going to relatives or favorites?
questions.e: She says 'Compare that with older forms of organization, where positions often went to relatives or favorites', and Weber judged bureaucracy 'fairer than those systems'. The example describes the past, not today's bureaucracies, and the iron cage is a separate worry.
o: To show that bureaucracies still hire people unfairly today
To explain why Weber disliked his own government
To describe the main cause of the iron cage problem
To contrast bureaucracy with earlier forms of organization

questions.s: How does the professor describe Weber's attitude toward bureaucracy?
questions.e: Weber found bureaucracy 'more efficient, more predictable and fairer', but 'he was also worried' about an 'iron cage'. The professor sums up that he was 'neither simply a fan nor simply a critic'. Long lines and pointless forms are today's popular image, not Weber's view.
o: He saw it only as a source of long lines and pointless rules
He saw advantages in it but also serious dangers
He believed it would soon be replaced by older systems
He thought it was perfect and should spread everywhere

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks 'how has this dome stayed up' without steel, then explains the material and how builders 'managed weight'. Modern steel-reinforced concrete is only mentioned to explain the word 'unreinforced'.
o: How Hadrian chose the location of the Pantheon in Rome
How a huge dome was built to stand without steel
Why modern concrete needs steel bars to resist cracking
How sunlight entering the oculus was used to tell time

questions.s: According to the professor, how did the builders vary the concrete in the dome?
questions.e: He says 'as they went higher, they switched to lighter and lighter materials, ending with' pumice. The first option reverses this, since the heavy stone was 'near the bottom'. The dome is thicker, not thinner, at its base.
o: They placed heavier stone near the top for extra strength
They used the same heavy mixture all the way to the top
They used lighter materials higher up in the dome
They made the dome thinner at the base than at the crown

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the oculus?
questions.e: He calls leaving out the center, 'where extra weight would cause the most trouble', 'a smart structural choice'. So the opening helps the structure by removing weight. Pumice is used near the top, but the oculus itself has 'no concrete at all'.
o: It takes away weight from the top of the dome
It was added later to repair a crack in the concrete
It was made of pumice so that it would let in light
It makes the dome less stable but more beautiful

questions.s: How does the professor organize the explanation?
questions.e: He asks 'how has this dome stayed up for nearly nineteen hundred years?' and then answers it: first the material, then the varied concrete, the thickness, the coffers and the oculus. Only one emperor, Hadrian, is named, and no other domes are compared.
o: He lists the emperors who added parts to the building over time
He compares the Pantheon with several later domes in Europe
He describes the building's history from its first to its final version
He raises a question and then answers it in several steps

questions.s: What is the main idea of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says early sound films 'took a step backward' in some ways and calls sound 'a big leap forward that briefly made filmmaking lose skills'. Hidden microphones are one example of the problems, and she says studios switched to sound 'within just a few years'.
o: Al Jolson was the most popular actor of the late nineteen twenties
Silent films stayed more popular than sound films for many years
Microphones were first hidden inside objects such as lamps
The arrival of sound caused some temporary problems for film

questions.s: According to the professor, why were cameras placed inside soundproof booths?
questions.e: The cameras 'were noisy machines, and the new microphones picked up every whirring sound', so they were put in booths. The booths actually stopped cameras from moving, since 'a camera in a heavy box can barely move', so the third option reverses the effect.
o: To keep the microphones from recording their noise
To protect the cameras from damage during filming
To allow the cameras to move more smoothly around the set
To hide the camera operators from the actors on stage

questions.s: What does the professor say about many early talkies?
questions.e: She says 'a lot of early talkies feel stiff and stagey, almost like filmed plays'. That is a comparison, not a statement that they were filmed in theaters. Camera movement decreased, so the first option reverses the point.
o: They used more camera movement than silent films did
They were filmed in theaters in front of live audiences
They often seemed stiff, like recordings of stage plays
They were shorter than the silent films that came before them

questions.s: What point does the professor make at the end of the talk?
questions.e: She concludes that 'the story of sound isn't a straight line': a leap forward that 'briefly' cost filmmakers skills they had mastered. The change to sound took 'just a few years', not decades, and nothing is said about cost.
o: Sound films took decades to become common in Hollywood
Progress in film sometimes involves a temporary loss
Booms and camera cases made sound recording more expensive
Directors preferred to return to silent filmmaking afterward

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks 'What made it different?' and describes three features: the classroom, the materials and the teacher's role. Her medical training is only background, and the modern research mentioned is about the method as a whole, not furniture.
o: The training Montessori received as a medical doctor
Key features of an approach to early education
Why children in Rome had poor schools in nineteen oh seven
The results of modern studies on classroom furniture

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a wooden block with holes and cylinders?
questions.e: If a cylinder is in the wrong hole, one is 'left over at the end', so 'the child sees the error and tries again, without an adult pointing it out'. The third option reverses this point, since no adult is needed to check.
o: To show how children learned to count using wooden objects
To describe a toy that Montessori found in a Roman school
To explain why young children need an adult to check all of their work
To show a material that lets children spot their own errors

questions.s: According to the professor, what does the teacher do in a Montessori classroom?
questions.e: 'Instead of lecturing the whole class, the teacher observes, introduces materials to individual children, and lets them choose'. Children choose their own work, so the third option is wrong, and rows of fixed desks describe older classrooms.
o: Observes children and guides them one at a time
Gives lectures to the whole class from the front of the room
Chooses which activity each child must work on every day
Moves the furniture to keep the children in neat rows

questions.s: According to the professor, where did Montessori's ideas come from?
questions.e: He says 'Montessori based these ideas on careful observation. She watched how children actually behaved.' Modern research came much later and has 'produced mixed results', so it could not be the source. Her first school was in 'a poor neighborhood'.
o: Mainly from earlier books about education
From the results of modern classroom research
From watching what children actually did
From the needs of children in wealthy families

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains the law of superposition, 'the deeper a layer is, the older it is', and how archaeologists use it. She says it gives 'relative dates, not exact ones', so exact dating methods are not the topic.
o: A principle for working out the order of buried layers
How seventeenth-century geologists measured the age of rocks
Why animals that burrow cause damage to archaeological sites
The methods used to find exact dates for ancient objects

questions.s: According to the professor, what is one limitation of the law of superposition?
questions.e: She says it 'tells us that one layer is older than another, but not by how many years'. Long-occupied sites are her example of where it is 'extremely useful', and she says it applies to 'soil or rock', so the first two options contradict the talk.
o: It cannot be applied to sites where people lived for centuries
It works only for rock layers, not for layers of soil
It shows which layer is older but not by how many years
It was never accepted by geologists in Steno's time

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a pit dug in a later period?
questions.e: A later pit 'can carry newer objects deep down into older layers', which could lead you to 'badly misdate what you find'. It illustrates the 'catch' in the rule. The pit was dug by past people, not by archaeologists.
o: To describe how archaeologists reach the deepest layers
To show where people in the past stored their pots
To explain why layers form more quickly near houses
To show how newer objects can end up in older layers

questions.s: What can be inferred from the professor's statement that 'there's no going back to check'?
questions.e: She says 'excavation destroys the very layers we're studying', which is why excavators 'record every layer so carefully'. Once a site is dug, the records are the only evidence left. The first option contradicts her statement directly.
o: Most sites are dug a second time by other teams later on
Careful records are all that remain of the layers
Archaeologists should avoid digging below the top layer
Exact dates are more important than the order of layers

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how cold, nutrient-rich water 'rises up from below' and feeds a food chain, making these 'some of the richest fishing waters on Earth'. Earth's rotation turns the surface water, not winds over land, and it is one step in the explanation.
o: Why anchovies prefer warm water to cold water
How the rotation of Earth changes the direction of winds over land
How rising cold water makes some coastal seas rich in life
Why fishing communities in Peru moved to California

questions.s: According to the professor, why does surface water move away from the shore?
questions.e: The winds blow 'parallel to the shore', but 'because of Earth's rotation, the moving surface water is turned to one side' and flows out to sea. The winds do not blow straight out to sea, and the rising cold water is a result of the movement, not its cause.
o: Strong winds blow it directly out to sea
Earth's rotation turns the moving water to one side
Rivers push large amounts of fresh water into the ocean
Cold water rising from below pushes it outward

questions.s: Why does the professor mention phytoplankton?
questions.e: The nutrients 'feed huge blooms of tiny drifting plants called phytoplankton', which feed small animals and then fish 'up the food chain'. He says these blooms happen 'where there's sunlight', so the second option contradicts him.
o: To explain how deep nutrients support a large food chain
To show that tiny plants can grow without any sunlight
To describe the main food that people catch off Peru
To give an example of an organism that sinks and breaks down after it dies

questions.s: What can be inferred about El Nino events?
questions.e: During El Nino 'upwelling off Peru weakens, fewer nutrients reach the surface, and the anchovy catch can fall dramatically'. Fewer nutrients means less phytoplankton and so less food for fish. The first and third options reverse what happens.
o: They bring extra nutrients to the coast of Peru
They make the winds along the coast of California stronger
They cause cold water to rise faster near the surface
They reduce the food available to fish off South America

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains countercurrent heat exchange, in which arteries and veins run 'right alongside' each other so the duck loses little heat through its feet. Dolphins and fish are brief examples at the end, and the duck's feet 'have no feathers'.
o: Why ducks prefer to stand on ice rather than swim
How a blood vessel arrangement reduces heat loss
Why dolphins and fish have warmer muscles than birds
How feathers protect birds' bodies from freezing water

questions.s: According to the professor, what happens to the blood flowing down to the duck's feet?
questions.e: The warm blood 'passes its heat to the cold blood flowing up next to it', so it arrives at the feet 'already quite cool'. It is the returning blood that gets warmed, so the first option reverses the direction of the heat.
o: It is warmed by the veins before it reaches the toes
It stops flowing whenever the feet touch the ice
It flows in the same direction as the blood in the veins
It gives up much of its heat to the returning blood

questions.s: Why does the professor describe what would happen if both flows ran the same way?
questions.e: She says 'the key is the opposite direction': with flows in the same direction, temperatures would even out and 'the exchange would stop'. The imagined case shows why the countercurrent design matters. She does not say any real animal works this way.
o: To show that ducks sometimes lose too much heat
To describe how the system works in fast-swimming fish
To explain why the opposite direction is essential
To suggest that some birds have a less efficient system

questions.s: What can be inferred about the fast-swimming fish the professor mentions?
questions.e: The fish use the arrangement 'to keep their muscles warmer than the surrounding water', so heat is kept inside instead of being lost. Since they have 'the same arrangement', their vessels run side by side, not far apart.
o: They use the system to hold heat in their muscles
They lose more heat through their fins than ducks do
They swim only in water that is close to freezing
They have arteries and veins that run far apart

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor says 'here's how a hailstone grows' and follows it from a small ice particle to the moment it falls. Forecasters appear only at the end, and they watch updraft strength, not cloud temperatures.
o: Why hail is more dangerous than snow in winter
How forecasters measure temperatures inside clouds
The different shapes of ice crystals in the atmosphere
How hailstones form and grow inside storms

questions.s: According to the professor, what is supercooled water?
questions.e: He says temperatures are 'well below freezing, but many of the water droplets there are still liquid. We call that supercooled water.' The first option is tempting because the droplets freeze onto ice particles, but supercooled water itself is still liquid.
o: Water that has frozen into small particles of ice
Rain that falls from the bottom of a thunderstorm
Liquid water at a temperature below freezing
Water vapor rising quickly in the center of a cloud

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the rings inside a hailstone?
questions.e: The rings appear because the stone grew 'layer by layer' as it moved through different parts of the cloud. The onion is only a comparison for the rings inside, not the outer shape, and he does not say clear hail falls faster.
o: As evidence that the stone grew in separate layers
To show that hailstones are shaped like onions
To explain why clear hail falls faster than white hail
To compare hailstones with the rings in a tree trunk

questions.s: What can be inferred about a storm that produces very large hailstones?
questions.e: Stones 'the size of golf balls or larger need extremely strong updrafts', and the professor defines updrafts as 'currents of rising air'. Pea-sized hail is what forms in 'fairly ordinary storms', so the last option describes small hail.
o: It must have formed during the winter months
It has unusually strong rising air currents
It contains no supercooled water droplets
It is an ordinary storm with weak updrafts

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk explains the Maillard reaction, which produces 'brown colors and literally hundreds of new flavor and aroma molecules'. Maillard himself is mentioned only by name, and sugar breaking down alone is caramelization, which is a contrast.
o: A browning reaction that creates flavor in cooked food
Why boiled meat is healthier than meat fried in a hot pan
The life and career of the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard
How sugar breaks down when it is heated on its own

questions.s: According to the professor, which substances react in the Maillard reaction?
questions.e: The reaction 'happens between amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and certain sugars'. Sugar alone describes caramelization, which the professor says is 'not the same', and fats are never mentioned.
o: Water and sugar at the boiling point
Amino acids and certain sugars
Sugar alone, broken down by strong heat
Proteins and the fats used in frying

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that cooks pat meat dry before searing it?
questions.e: While water is present 'the surface can't get much hotter than a hundred degrees', so 'the surface moisture has to evaporate before browning can really begin'. Patting the meat dry removes that water. Drying does not change the amount of amino acids.
o: To show that dry meat contains more amino acids
To explain how caramelization begins on the surface of meat
To warn that wet meat can be dangerous to fry
To show that water must leave before browning starts

questions.s: How does the professor distinguish the Maillard reaction from caramelization?
questions.e: Caramelization is 'sugar alone breaking down under heat', while the Maillard reaction 'needs the building blocks of protein as well', meaning amino acids. The last option gives caramelization's feature to the Maillard reaction, so it reverses the contrast.
o: Caramelization happens only at low temperatures
The Maillard reaction produces no brown color
Caramelization does not need amino acids
The Maillard reaction involves sugar alone

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor says 'what's interesting is how scientists figured out the mechanism' of phototropism, then describes the Darwins' experiments and the later discovery of auxin. Darwin's theory of evolution is not discussed, and auxin's structure is never described.
o: Why plants on windowsills need more water than other plants
How Charles Darwin developed his theory of evolution
How scientists discovered why shoots bend toward light
The chemical structure of the plant hormone auxin

questions.s: According to the professor, what happened when the Darwins covered only the tip of a seedling?
questions.e: He says that with a cap over the tip, 'the seedling didn't bend'. Bending still happened in the other test, when the lower part was shaded instead, so the options about bending mix up the two experiments.
o: The seedling did not bend toward the light
The seedling bent more sharply than before
The lower part of the shoot grew much faster
The tip itself began to bend away from the light

questions.s: What did the Darwins' experiments suggest?
questions.e: Because 'the tip was sensing the light, but a lower region was doing the bending', the Darwins concluded that 'some kind of influence must travel down from the tip'. The first option reverses the roles of the tip and the lower region.
o: The lower part of the shoot senses the light directly
A signal travels from the tip to the bending region
Grass seedlings can grow only in direct sunlight
Auxin is produced in the shaded part of the roots

questions.s: What does the professor mean when he says the experiment opened up 'another' question?
questions.e: The Darwins showed that an influence travels from the tip, but 'they didn't know what that influence was'; that was the new question, answered later by the discovery of auxin. Their results were not shown to be wrong, and today the reason for bending is understood.
o: The Darwins' results were later shown to be wrong
Plants bend toward light for reasons nobody understands
Darwin wanted to study animals instead of plants
The nature of the signal from the tip was still unknown

questions.s: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains what the Hanseatic League was, 'a loose network of merchant groups and trading towns', how it held together, and why it was 'in decline' by the sixteenth century. She stresses that the Hansa 'wasn't a country', so Lubeck was not a capital.
o: Why pirates were a serious danger in the Baltic Sea
How a loose trading network worked and why it declined
The kinds of fish that were traded in northern Norway
How the city of Lubeck became the capital of a new country

questions.s: According to the professor, what was the main reason merchants joined together?
questions.e: Merchants 'traveling alone faced pirates' and other risks, but 'by acting together' they 'could win trading privileges' and 'protect each other'. An army, a currency and replacing kings are never mentioned.
o: To form an army that could defend their cities
To create a single currency for northern Europe
To gain privileges and protection they lacked alone
To replace the kings who ruled the towns on the Baltic coast

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Bergen?
questions.e: Bergen is introduced with 'for instance' after the trading posts abroad: there, merchants 'bought dried fish from the north and supplied grain in return'. Fish and grain are everyday bulk goods, 'not glamorous', so the luxury option is wrong.
o: To name the city where the League held its meetings
To show that the League traded mainly in luxury goods
To explain why Norway left the League in the sixteenth century
To illustrate how a foreign trading post exchanged goods

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the League's decline?
questions.e: Besides outside competition, she says 'a network built on shared interests was hard to hold together once those interests began to differ'. Earlier she stressed it had 'no permanent government', so its loose structure made it fragile. She names several causes, not a single event.
o: It was partly a result of the League's loose structure
It happened because merchants stopped trading in grain and fish
It was caused by a single defeat at sea
It began when Lubeck refused to host any more meetings

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes Burgess's concentric zone model and then the 'problems' critics found. Immigrants and plant communities are details used to explain the model, not the main subject.
o: Why many immigrants settled in Chicago in the nineteen twenties
How plant communities compete for space in a field
An early model of how cities are arranged and its limits
How railway lines were built around the edges of cities

questions.s: According to the professor, what was found in the zone in transition?
questions.e: The zone in transition had 'factories and older, crowded housing', often the first home of new immigrants. Offices and department stores belong to the business district at the center, so that option describes the wrong ring.
o: Offices, banks and large department stores
Factories and older, crowded housing
Middle-class homes with large gardens
Commuters traveling to the city center

questions.s: Why does the professor mention one plant community replacing another?
questions.e: Burgess 'borrowed ideas from ecology': as groups move outward, 'new groups take their place', which he compared to one plant community replacing another. The comparison explains his idea; the weaknesses come later, in the critics' points.
o: To show that Burgess was trained as an ecologist
To explain why growing cities need more parks and green spaces
To point out a weakness in Burgess's model
To show how Burgess pictured groups replacing each other

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the concentric zone model?
questions.e: He lists its problems but says 'even its critics used it as a starting point'. The model was 'hugely influential', so it was not ignored, and it 'was based on one city', which rules out the last option.
o: It remained useful even though it had flaws
It fit most cities better than it fit Chicago
It was ignored by sociologists after it was published
It was based on careful studies of many different cities

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how a windcatcher 'kept people cool long before air conditioning', with and without wind. Yazd is mentioned only as the place with famous examples, and thick walls are never discussed.
o: The history of the desert city of Yazd
How air conditioning replaced traditional buildings
Why houses in hot regions have very thick walls
How a traditional tower helps cool buildings

questions.s: According to the professor, why are a windcatcher's openings placed high up?
questions.e: She explains that 'wind near the ground is slowed down', while 'a few meters up, the air moves faster, and it's often cleaner and less dusty'. Evaporation is part of a different feature, the pool or underground channel.
o: Wind is faster and cleaner above the ground
Warm air from the street cannot reach that height
The towers need to be seen from far across the desert
Water evaporates more quickly at the top of a building

questions.s: According to the professor, how does a windcatcher work on a day with no wind?
questions.e: 'Even on a still day', the sun heats the air in the tower, it 'rises and escapes from the top, and that draws air through the house below', like a chimney. The last option contradicts her statement that 'the tower can work' without wind.
o: Water in a pool is pumped up to the top of the tower
Rising warm air draws air through the house
Its openings are closed to keep hot air outside
It stops working until the wind starts again

questions.s: Why does the professor mention modern architects?
questions.e: She says 'these ideas aren't just history' and that architects study windcatchers 'because they cool buildings without using any electricity'. The point is that the technique is useful today; electric fans are not mentioned.
o: To show that windcatchers are no longer used in Iran
To explain how electric fans improved the old designs
To suggest that the old technique is still relevant
To argue that windcatchers are more beautiful than modern towers

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk is about deep focus, where objects near, in the middle and far away 'are all sharp at the same time'. Blurred backgrounds are the usual approach that the professor contrasts it with, and Bazin appears only near the end.
o: A technique that keeps the whole image in sharp focus
How Orson Welles chose the actors and the locations for Citizen Kane
Why most films blur their backgrounds
The career of the French critic Andre Bazin

questions.s: According to the professor, how did Toland achieve deep focus?
questions.e: 'Toland used wide-angle lenses, very bright lighting and a small lens opening.' The correct option paraphrases this list. Deep focus works without cutting, as in the snow scene where 'nothing is cut', so the editing option is wrong.
o: By editing several separate shots together so they looked like one
By filming every scene outdoors in natural daylight
By using wide lenses, strong light and a small opening
By keeping the actors close to the camera at all times

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the scene with the young Charles Kane in the snow?
questions.e: The boy playing in the background and the adults signing papers in the foreground 'are both sharp, and nothing is cut', so the viewer connects the two actions 'all in one shot'. The scene has no editing, so the last option is wrong.
o: To show that Toland preferred to film outdoor scenes
To illustrate how one shot can show two actions clearly
To explain why the background in a film should be blurred
To show how editing changes the meaning of a scene

questions.s: What can be inferred about Bazin's view of editing?
questions.e: Bazin praised deep focus because 'instead of an editor deciding what you notice, you're free to look around the frame'. That implies editing takes this choice away from the viewer. He 'admired' deep focus, so he did not prefer editing.
o: He believed careful editing was essential to every good film
He thought it was too difficult for most directors
