He preferred it to deep focus in most situations
He felt it could limit the viewer's freedom to choose

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains how pollen in lake and bog layers lets researchers 'track how the plant life around the site changed over time'. Oak and pine are examples of identifiable pollen, and she notes pollen works 'even where no farm buildings have survived'.
o: Why oak and pine trees grew in ancient European forests
How preserved pollen reveals past landscapes
How insects carry pollen from one plant to another
The way archaeologists dig up the remains of old farm buildings

questions.s: According to the professor, why can pollen survive in lake mud and peat bogs?
questions.e: Pollen has 'an extremely tough outer wall', and 'in places where there's little oxygen' it 'can survive for thousands of years'. Wind does add pollen, but that explains why some plants are over-counted, not why grains survive.
o: These places are rich in insects that protect the grains
The pollen is buried too deep for plants to reach it
Wind keeps adding fresh pollen to the top layers each year
Its tough wall resists decay where oxygen is scarce

questions.s: Why does the professor mention tree pollen dropping while cereal pollen goes up?
questions.e: This pattern 'is usually read as people clearing forest to plant fields', so 'pollen can reveal the spread of farming'. The rise in cereal pollen reflects more fields, not cereals producing more pollen than trees.
o: To give an example of evidence for early farming
To show that cereal crops produce more pollen than trees
To explain why European forests were destroyed by insects
To describe how cores are drilled into a lake bed

questions.s: What does the professor imply about a simple count of pollen grains?
questions.e: Insect-pollinated plants 'release very little' pollen, so 'a simple count would exaggerate some plants and miss others'. That means insect-pollinated plants would seem rarer than they were. The count works for all plants but needs correcting, so the second option goes too far.
o: It is the most accurate way to date the layers of a core
It works only for plants that are pollinated by the wind
It would underestimate plants pollinated by insects
It can identify the exact year a forest was cleared

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks how a bee tells its nestmates 'where to go' and explains how the waggle dance codes direction and distance. Von Frisch's prize is background, and the smell idea is a doubt that later studies answered.
o: Why honeybees prefer certain kinds of flowers
How Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize
How bees communicate the location of food
How bees use the smell of flowers to find the hive

questions.s: According to the professor, what does the length of the waggling run indicate?
questions.e: He says distance is 'coded in how long the waggling run lasts. A longer run means the food is farther away.' Direction is shown by the angle of the run, not its length, so the second option mixes up the two codes.
o: How far away the food source is
Which direction the sun is shining from
How much nectar the flowers contain
How many bees should follow the dancer

questions.s: According to the professor, where is the food if a bee's straight run points straight up the comb?
questions.e: He explains that 'straight up on the comb stands for the direction of the sun', so 'if the bee runs straight up, the flowers are toward the sun'. Forty degrees to the right is his second example, for a run at an angle, not straight up.
o: Directly below the hive
Very close to the hive entrance
Forty degrees to the right of the sun
In the same direction as the sun

questions.s: Why does the professor mention studies that tracked bees with radar?
questions.e: Some scientists thought recruits 'just followed the smell of flowers', but radar studies 'showed that they really do fly in the direction the dance indicates'. The studies settle that doubt. They were 'later studies', so they are not how von Frisch made his discovery.
o: To show that bees can fly much farther than scientists believed
To answer the doubt that bees simply followed a scent
To explain how von Frisch first discovered the dance
To describe a new way of measuring the sun's position

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor opens with the question 'do adult human brains keep making new neurons?' and spends the talk on studies that disagree about it. The hippocampus is mentioned only as the place where new neurons might form, so the option about memory is true but too narrow.
o: A disagreement over whether adult humans form new neurons
Why the hippocampus is so important for learning and storing new memories
How research on songbirds changed the methods of brain surgery
Why early textbooks were wrong about the size of the human brain

questions.s: Why does the professor mention how long brain tissue waited before it was preserved?
questions.e: She asks how 'two careful teams' could disagree and answers that 'part of the answer seems to be method': the markers 'can fade quickly after death'. This is a possible technical cause, not an accusation of carelessness; she actually calls both teams careful.
o: To show that one of the two research teams made a careless mistake in its work
To explain why animal studies are more reliable than human ones
To suggest that a technical factor may explain the conflicting results
To argue that new neurons die soon after a person's death

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion about the debate?
questions.e: She says treating the question as closed is 'a bit premature' and that she would 'keep both possibilities on the table'. That means neither answer has been proven yet. The last option reverses her view: she disagrees with colleagues who think the matter is closed.
o: She is convinced that older adults produce many new neurons every day
She thinks it is too early to decide either way
She thinks the question is no longer worth studying
She agrees with colleagues who say recent studies have already settled the matter

questions.s: According to the professor, where were new neurons in adult brains first found?
questions.e: The professor says the old view 'began to crack' when researchers found new neurons 'in the hippocampus of adult rats, and later in songbirds and monkeys'. Songbirds came later, not first, and human tissue was studied only in the late nineteen nineties.
o: In tissue taken from healthy older humans
In songbirds, before any mammals were studied
In the brains of children with memory problems
In adult rats

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The talk presents an observation, outer stars 'didn't drop off' in speed, and then two explanations: dark matter and modified Newtonian dynamics. Neptune and Mercury are only an example, and the option about detecting particles reverses the script, which says experiments 'have found nothing so far'.
o: Why Neptune orbits the Sun more slowly than Mercury
How Vera Rubin built new telescopes to photograph distant galaxy clusters
Experiments that have recently detected dark matter particles
Two ways of accounting for the speed of outer stars in galaxies

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Neptune and Mercury?
questions.e: He says outer stars 'should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune moves around the Sun much more slowly than Mercury'. The planets show the expected pattern, which galaxies then failed to follow. Nothing is said about dark matter in the solar system.
o: To show that our own solar system contains a large amount of dark matter
To illustrate the pattern astronomers expected to find
To compare the masses of two very different planets
To explain how the modified theory of gravity was first tested

questions.s: What can be inferred about the professor's view of modified Newtonian dynamics?
questions.e: He says 'to be fair to that idea' and admits it predicts galaxy rotation 'remarkably well', which gives it partial credit. The second option is too extreme, because he says it 'struggles' with clusters and the early universe. The failed particle searches are a problem for dark matter, not for this idea.
o: He thinks it deserves credit for some of its predictions
He considers it better than dark matter on every scale
He believes direct searches for particles have disproven it
He thinks it is mainly a theory about clusters of galaxies

questions.s: According to the professor, what is one weakness of the dark matter explanation?
questions.e: He calls it 'the awkward part for dark matter' that experiments 'built to detect its particles directly have found nothing so far'. The first option reverses a detail: bending of light by clusters is something dark matter helps explain. He also says most astronomers do accept it.
o: It cannot explain why galaxy clusters bend light that passes them
It predicts that outer stars should move faster than they do
Its particles have not been directly detected
Most astronomers have recently stopped accepting it

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor introduces linguistic relativity, then rejects its 'strong form' and defends a 'weaker version'. The talk is about how much of the claim survives. Russian is only one example, and she never says it has the most color words.
o: Why Russian has more words for colors than any other language in the world
How Whorf learned to speak the Hopi language
How well a claim about language and thought holds up in two forms
Why children learn new words faster than adults do

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Russian words for blue?
questions.e: Right after saying the weaker version claims language can 'nudge thinking', she says 'Take color' and describes the Russian results. The second option goes too far: she says plainly that 'Russian speakers aren't seeing different colors'.
o: To give an example that supports the weaker version of the idea
To prove that speakers of different languages actually perceive colors differently
To show that Whorf's research on Hopi was correct
To explain how new color words enter a language

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the strong version of the claim?
questions.e: She says 'very few researchers accept that version' and that Whorf's evidence 'took a beating'. Her warning about 'dramatic' headlines suggests the strong version is popular for reasons other than evidence, so the first option reverses her point.
o: She thinks it is popular because the evidence for it is strong
She believes it explains the Russian results better than the weak version
She thinks it should be tested again with speakers of Hopi
She considers it poorly supported

questions.s: According to the professor, what did later linguists show about the Hopi language?
questions.e: Whorf claimed Hopi had 'no way of talking about time', but later linguists showed 'it has plenty of ways to do exactly that'. The last option repeats words from the talk but states the strong claim the professor rejects.
o: It has no basic words for colors such as blue
It does have ways of expressing time
It is no longer spoken by anyone today
It determines how its speakers think about time and space

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor gives 'Popper's answer', falsifiability, then says critics 'pointed out a problem' and ends by calling it 'harder to apply than it first sounds'. The planets are examples, and the Neptune case actually saved Newton's laws rather than disproving them.
o: To explain how nineteenth-century astronomers calculated planetary orbits
To present a definition of science and a difficulty in applying it
To compare the careers of Popper and Einstein
To argue that Newton's laws were disproven by the discovery of Neptune

questions.s: Why does the professor discuss the discovery of Neptune?
questions.e: Astronomers 'didn't throw out Newton'; they assumed an unseen planet and found Neptune, so 'rescuing a theory can be perfectly good science'. The first option reverses the case: Newton's theory was kept, not abandoned. Eclipses belong to the Einstein example.
o: To give an example of a theory that was abandoned after one failed observation
To explain why Popper admired Newton
To show how eclipses are used to test predictions
To show that protecting a theory from a failed prediction can be justified

questions.s: How does the professor organize the information?
questions.e: He states Popper's idea with the Einstein example, introduces the critics' objection, and then uses Uranus and Mercury as historical cases. The events are not in date order, since nineteen nineteen comes before the eighteen forties, so the first option does not fit.
o: He lists events in the history of astronomy from the oldest to the most recent
He compares two theories of gravity and chooses one
He states an idea, raises an objection, and gives historical cases
He describes one experiment and explains its result step by step

questions.s: What does the professor imply about Popper's idea?
questions.e: He calls it 'useful as a rule of thumb' but says as 'a strict test' it is 'harder to apply than it first sounds'. The Mercury case shows that rescuing a theory can fail; it does not prove Popper wrong, so the second option is too strong.
o: It is helpful but not reliable as a strict rule
It was shown to be false by the case of Mercury
It works well only for theories in physics
It is the clearest way anyone has found to separate science from non-science

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor introduces the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, gives its 'classic support', and then spends the rest of the talk on studies and arguments against it. Storms and seaweed are only examples, and conservation planning is mentioned once to show the idea's influence.
o: An influential idea about species diversity and doubts about it
How storms and fires damage the seaweed that grows along rocky coastlines
Why fast-growing species are always the strongest competitors
How conservation planners choose which areas to protect

questions.s: Why does the professor mention boulders on a rocky shore?
questions.e: She introduces the boulders as 'classic support': rocks overturned 'now and then' had more kinds of seaweed than rocks rarely or constantly moved. That is the middle-level pattern the hypothesis predicts. Boulders rolled 'all the time' are only one group in the study, so the last option misses the point.
o: To show that waves do the most damage to seaweed growing on the largest rocks
To explain how researchers combine the results of many studies
To describe evidence that was used to support the hypothesis
To give an example of a disturbance that happens constantly

questions.s: According to the professor, what did researchers find when they looked at hundreds of studies?
questions.e: She says the hump-shaped pattern 'showed up in only a minority of them', which means fewer than half. The first option reverses this finding. The last option is too extreme: diversity often 'rose' or 'fell', so disturbance did have effects.
o: Diversity was always highest at medium levels of disturbance
The predicted pattern appeared in fewer than half of them
Most of the studies had been carried out on coral reefs
Disturbance had no effect on any of the species that were studied

questions.s: What does the professor imply when she calls the hypothesis a local story rather than a law of nature?
questions.e: Just before this, she says 'a rule that holds only some of the time', so 'local story' means it fits particular places but not nature in general. The other options take the word 'local' literally or reverse her meaning.
o: It should be tested only in small areas
It is supported mainly by researchers who work near the coast
It is a law that applies to every kind of ecosystem
It cannot be relied on as a general rule

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The talk presents the efficient market hypothesis, that 'prices already reflect the information available', and then the behavioral economists' challenge. The first option reverses the hypothesis, which says by the time you read the news 'the opportunity is gone'.
o: How investors can use news reports to choose shares that will rise
The history of internet companies that grew around the year two thousand
Why professional fund managers charge high fees
A debate over how well market prices reflect available information

questions.s: Why does the professor mention internet company shares around the year two thousand?
questions.e: Behavioral economists 'point to bubbles, like the rise and crash of internet company shares', when prices 'drifted far above any sensible estimate of value'. The example challenges the idea that markets are rational. Nothing in the talk says anyone predicted the crash.
o: To show that professional fund managers predicted the crash in advance
To give an example that critics use against the hypothesis
To explain how funds that track the whole market were invented
To illustrate how quickly prices respond to good news

questions.s: What point do defenders of the hypothesis make about bubbles?
questions.e: Defenders say 'spotting a bubble afterward is easy' but spotting it 'in advance' is 'another matter entirely'. They do not deny that bubbles happen, so the last option goes too far.
o: They are hard to recognize while they are happening
They are caused mainly by the high fees that funds charge
They prove that investors act rationally in every market
They never actually happen in real markets

questions.s: What does the professor suggest by mentioning the Nobel Prize in two thousand thirteen?
questions.e: Because leading figures 'on both sides' shared the prize, he concludes that 'the profession hasn't quite made up its mind'. Honoring both sides does not show that one replaced the other or that they now agree.
o: Behavioral economics has now replaced the older hypothesis
The prize committee preferred the efficient market hypothesis to its critics
The question is still unsettled among economists
Both sides have finally agreed on a single theory

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor describes Hockney and Falco's idea that artists used 'optical devices' to explain 'a sudden jump in realism', and then the objections to it. Hockney's own career is not discussed, and fabric and metal are only examples of realistic details.
o: The life and career of David Hockney as a modern painter
How lenses were manufactured in the fourteen hundreds
A claim about how certain painters achieved realism
Why fabric and metal were popular subjects in early European paintings

questions.s: What is one objection that critics raised against the thesis?
questions.e: Critics noted that 'almost no written record from the period describes artists working this way'. The second option reverses a fact from the talk: 'lenses and mirrors did exist at the time'.
o: Written sources from the period say very little about such methods
Lenses and mirrors had not been invented when the paintings were made
The paintings contain no especially realistic details
Falco had no training as an art historian

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Hockney's statement that a projected image still has to be painted?
questions.e: Some critics felt the thesis made the painters' skill 'a kind of trick'. Hockney's answer, that painting a projected image 'takes enormous skill', is his reply to that criticism. He does not give up the thesis, and the critics, not Hockney, said early mirror images were 'dim and small'.
o: To prove that early mirrors produced bright, clear images that artists could easily copy
To explain why Falco came to disagree with Hockney
To show that Hockney later gave up his thesis
To present his reply to one criticism of the thesis

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the thesis?
questions.e: She says 'even if the thesis turns out to be wrong, it's made a lot of people look much harder' at how the paintings were made. She does not claim it is correct, and the view that it insults painters belongs to some critics, not to her.
o: She is certain that it is correct
She values it for the attention it has drawn to painting methods
She thinks it insults the painters and should be dismissed for that reason
She believes it should be taught as an established fact

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor presents the snowball Earth hypothesis and the rival slushball view, then discusses how they relate. The magnetic signals show the rocks' latitude, not their age, so the first option mixes up a detail.
o: To explain how magnetic signals in rocks reveal the age of ancient glaciers
To compare two accounts of an ancient period of extreme cold
To describe how volcanoes formed near the equator
To show how simple organisms first evolved in the oceans

questions.s: According to the snowball Earth hypothesis, how did the planet eventually warm up?
questions.e: Volcanoes 'kept releasing carbon dioxide', little was removed, and 'over millions of years it built up' until the greenhouse effect melted the ice. Reflected sunlight is the reason the cooling 'feeds on itself', so the first option reverses its role.
o: Ice reflected more and more sunlight back into space over millions of years
Simple organisms in the oceans released large amounts of heat
The continents moved away from the equator
Volcanic gas gradually accumulated in the air

questions.s: Why does the professor mention organisms that needed sunlight?
questions.e: He says the critics' 'main argument is biological': these organisms survived, which is hard to explain 'if every ocean was sealed under thick ice'. The carbonate rocks are the snowball supporters' evidence, not the critics'.
o: To explain why carbonate rocks formed on top of the glacial deposits
To show that life began only after the ice had melted
To present the main evidence for the competing view
To describe how the oceans first froze

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the debate?
questions.e: He notes that each answer from snowball supporters 'moves the snowball a little closer to the slushball' and that the camps 'may end up meeting somewhere in the middle'. Supporters are adjusting their claims, so the last option is the reverse of what he says.
o: The two positions may become harder to tell apart
Geologists have completely abandoned the snowball hypothesis
The slushball view has no real evidence behind it
Snowball supporters refuse to change any of their claims

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor presents two models of where modern humans 'came from' and shows how genetic findings 'partly resolved' the argument. The first option mixes up two details: it was living Africans, not Neanderthals, who show the most genetic variety.
o: Why Neanderthals had more genetic variety than any other group of early humans
How genetic studies of living people are carried out
How new evidence reshaped a debate about modern human origins
Why early humans left Africa in search of food

questions.s: According to the professor, why did early genetic studies seem to support the Out of Africa model?
questions.e: She says 'living Africans show more genetic variety than any other population', as expected of 'the oldest population'. The first option reverses a later finding: Neanderthal DNA is found in people whose ancestors come from outside Africa.
o: Neanderthal DNA was found only in people living in Africa today
Fossils of the oldest modern humans were found in Asia
Modern humans appeared to have evolved in several regions at once
People in Africa today show the greatest genetic diversity

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the Neanderthal genome?
questions.e: The genome showed a small share of Neanderthal DNA in many people, so 'there was mixing after all' and 'neither side got exactly what it predicted'. The second option is too extreme; the mixing was 'not much', and most researchers still describe 'a mostly African origin'.
o: To introduce a finding that neither model fully predicted
To show that the multiregional model had been right about everything from the start
To explain how DNA is taken from ancient fossils
To prove that Neanderthals first evolved in Africa

questions.s: What does the professor imply about debates that are framed as either-or?
questions.e: She says such a debate 'sometimes ends with a messier answer', as here, where the result is mainly African origin plus 'a little interbreeding', an idea from the other camp. The talk covers decades of argument, so the last option does not fit.
o: They are always won by the side with genetic evidence
Their final answer may combine parts of both positions
They should be avoided in anthropology
They are usually settled within a few years

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor asks 'what did the Romans know' and then gives two explanations for the long life of Roman concrete: volcanic ash with seawater, and self-healing lime lumps. He never says modern engineers have copied these methods.
o: How modern engineers have copied Roman methods in harbor walls and bridges
Explanations for why some Roman concrete has lasted so long
Why Vitruvius wrote about building materials
How quicklime is produced from volcanic ash

questions.s: According to the professor, what did researchers in the twenty tens discover about Roman harbor concrete?
questions.e: Seawater seeping through it 'had caused rare minerals to grow in its cracks and pores', so it 'kept strengthening over time'. The second option reverses this. The view that the lumps showed careless mixing is the old idea that the two thousand twenty-three team rejected.
o: Seawater had helped new minerals form inside it
Seawater had slowly weakened it from the outside in
It contained no volcanic ash at all
Its white lumps came from careless mixing

questions.s: How does the professor describe the relationship between the two explanations?
questions.e: He says they 'aren't really competitors': 'one is about structures in seawater, the other about cracks in general. They could both be true.' Nothing suggests either explanation disproves the other.
o: The newer explanation proves that the older one was based on faulty samples
The older explanation has now replaced the newer one
They contradict each other about the role of seawater
They concern different situations and may both be correct

questions.s: Why does the professor mention that the white lumps were once seen as careless mixing?
questions.e: He says what experts 'had written off as sloppy work might turn out to be deliberate technique', which is 'worth remembering whenever we judge old methods by modern standards'. The first option repeats the old view that he is questioning.
o: To show that Roman builders often made mistakes that weakened their structures over time
To explain why the lumps dissolve so quickly in seawater
To warn against assuming that unfamiliar old methods were mistakes
To suggest that modern concrete is better made than Roman concrete

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The professor describes the discovery of mirror neurons and then questions the 'big theories built on top of them'. The second option reverses a point: scans show 'whole regions, not individual cells', so they are less precise.
o: How monkeys learn to grasp objects by imitating other members of their group
Why brain scans are more precise than recordings from single cells
The history of DNA research in biology
A discovery about the brain and the claims later made about it

questions.s: Why does the professor mention a prediction comparing mirror neurons to DNA?
questions.e: The prediction comes right after 'the excitement was enormous' and a list of grand roles proposed for the cells. It shows how much people hoped for. The rest of the talk suggests these hopes are 'still waiting for their evidence', so the prediction has not come true.
o: To explain how genes control the development of neurons in motor areas of the brain
To argue that the prediction has largely come true
To show how high expectations for the discovery became
To compare two methods of studying the brain

questions.s: What is one criticism that the professor describes?
questions.e: Critics say 'a cell responding to an action doesn't mean it causes understanding of that action'. The first option contradicts the talk, since the cells were found in monkeys. The last option reverses the comparison: monkeys 'imitate very little compared with human children'.
o: Mirror neurons have never been found in monkeys or in any other animal species
Activity in a cell does not prove that it causes understanding
Brain scans show single cells too clearly to be useful
Children imitate less than monkeys do

questions.s: What is the professor's view of mirror neurons?
questions.e: She separates 'the cells, which are well documented' from 'the big theories', which are 'still waiting for their evidence'. She also says the discovery was 'real or important. It was.', so the second option is wrong.
o: The cells are real, but the larger theories are unproven
The discovery was a mistake caused by poor recording methods
They explain empathy and language in humans
Research on them should stop because of the criticism

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: Most of the talk explains the giant impact hypothesis and then 'a new puzzle': the Moon and Earth are chemically 'almost identical'. The Apollo samples are only one step in the story, and the Moon's dryness is a single detail.
o: The leading explanation of the Moon's origin and a problem it faces
How the Apollo astronauts collected and analyzed rock samples on the Moon
Why the Moon has almost no water
How the planet Mars was formed

questions.s: According to the professor, why did the Apollo samples cause problems for the earlier ideas?
questions.e: The Moon was 'very dry' with 'only a small iron core', and 'none of the old ideas explained that combination well'. Mars appears only as a comparison for the size of the impactor, so the first option mixes up details.
o: The samples showed that the Moon had once been a part of the planet Mars
None of the ideas explained a dry Moon with little iron
The rocks turned out to be older than Earth itself
The samples were too small to analyze properly

questions.s: Why does the professor mention isotopes of oxygen and titanium?
questions.e: Simulations suggested the Moon should look 'chemically different' from Earth, but the isotope measurements show the two are 'almost identical'. The isotopes create the puzzle; they say nothing about capture or about how water was lost.
o: To explain how the heat of the impact drove water out of the Moon's rocks
To show that the Moon was most likely captured by Earth
To present evidence that conflicts with early impact simulations
To describe what the impactor was made of

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the giant impact hypothesis?
questions.e: He calls it 'the best story we have' and says 'don't throw it out', but adds that it 'has needed some revisions' and 'may need more'. The first option is too strong, because researchers responded with variations rather than giving it up.
o: He thinks measurements of isotopes in lunar rocks have disproven it
He considers it less likely than the capture idea
He believes it needs no further changes
He supports it while accepting that it is incomplete

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor sets Chomsky's poverty of the stimulus argument against the 'rival view', usage-based learning, and weighs evidence for each. Chomsky's career is not described, and the made-up syllables are only part of one experiment.
o: Why babies learn made-up languages faster than the real languages spoken by adults
How parents correct their children's grammar
The life and early career of Noam Chomsky
Competing views of how children acquire grammar

questions.s: Why does the professor describe the experiment with eight-month-old babies?
questions.e: He introduces the study by saying it 'supports' the view that children are 'extraordinary pattern detectors'; the babies began 'to find word boundaries on their own'. The second option states the opposite position, the nativist one.
o: To give evidence that infants learn from patterns in what they hear
To prove that knowledge of grammar is present from birth in every child
To show that babies cannot learn language without being corrected
To explain how made-up words are created for experiments

questions.s: According to the professor, what is the main claim of the poverty of the stimulus argument?
questions.e: Chomsky said the language children hear is 'too limited and too messy to teach them all the rules they end up knowing'. The second option reverses a detail, since he said children are 'seldom corrected'.
o: Children who hear more words at home learn to speak much earlier than other children
Children are corrected too often by the adults around them
The language children hear is too limited to explain what they come to know
Babies are unable to find the boundaries between words

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the nativist position?
questions.e: He says the research 'doesn't prove nothing is built in, but it does shrink how much needs to be'. He also admits 'the baby study doesn't settle the grammar question', so the first option is too strong.
o: It has been completely disproven by the study of babies and syllables
Less inborn knowledge may be needed than it once claimed
Every recent study of children supports it
It is mainly a theory about word boundaries

questions.s: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.e: The professor asks whether 'the things it describes are real' when a theory works, then gives the realists' argument, the anti-realists' reply and a realist response. Electrons and genes are only examples; she never claims they don't exist.
o: To explain how nineteenth-century physicists measured the speed of light through the ether
To argue that electrons and genes do not really exist
To present a debate about what successful theories tell us
To describe how scientific theories make predictions

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the theory of the ether?
questions.e: The ether is the anti-realists' example of a theory that 'made excellent predictions' and yet 'there's no ether'. The talk says many of the equations for light waves 'were kept', so the last option reverses a detail.
o: To show that the no miracles argument was first developed by physicists who studied light
To illustrate a successful theory that was later abandoned
To prove that light does not travel in waves
To explain why the equations for light were changed

questions.s: According to the professor, how have some realists responded to the pessimistic induction?
questions.e: Some realists 'argue that what survives from old theories is their mathematical structure'. They accept that some old theories were wrong about their objects, so the first option cannot be right.
o: By arguing that every successful theory in the past turned out to be completely true
By denying that the ether theory made good predictions
By giving up the no miracles argument entirely
By claiming that the structure of old theories often survives

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the realists' response?
questions.e: She calls the move 'clever' but says 'it gives up quite a bit': the realist ends up 'believing less than she started out believing'. Calling it clever shows she takes it seriously, so the third option is wrong.
o: It leaves them with a weaker form of realism
It completely defeats the historical argument against realism
It is too complicated to be taken seriously
It was first suggested by the anti-realists

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor tells 'one of the most famous stories in ecology' and then explains how 'more recent research' has made it 'more complicated'. He mentions that wolves were absent for seventy years but never explains why they disappeared.
o: Why wolves disappeared from Yellowstone National Park early in the twentieth century
How a well-known ecological story has been questioned
How beavers build dams across rivers
The way elk choose their food in winter

questions.s: What did the studies that tracked elk with collars find?
questions.e: The collar studies found that elk 'didn't avoid risky places nearly as strongly as the original accounts suggested'. The first option is the extreme version of the popular story that these studies called into question.
o: Elk stopped visiting riverbanks completely once the wolves had returned to the park
Elk numbers rose sharply after the wolves returned
Elk preferred aspen to willow
Elk avoided risky areas less than earlier accounts claimed

questions.s: Why does the professor mention bears, cougars and dry years?
questions.e: He introduces them with 'other things were changing at the same time', meaning the changes may not be due to wolves alone. The third option is too extreme: he says wolves 'almost certainly' mattered.
o: To point out other possible causes of the changes
To explain how wolves learned to hunt elk calves in the open valleys of the park
To show that wolves had no effect at all
To describe animals that also returned in nineteen ninety-five

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion of the popular version of the story?
questions.e: He says the 'tidy version' 'probably gives the wolves more credit than any single species deserves'. The second option reverses this. He still thinks wolves mattered, so he does not reject the story completely.
o: It is accurate in every detail and supported by all recent field studies
It gives too little credit to the wolves
It exaggerates the role of a single species
It should no longer be taught at all

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The talk follows the Phillips curve from its discovery through the challenge by Friedman and Phelps, stagflation, and the rebuilt version, ending with 'a theory being repaired'. British data is only where the story starts.
o: How an economic relationship was challenged and revised
Why British workers in the nineteenth century earned higher wages than workers elsewhere
How central banks decide on interest rates
The causes of high unemployment in the nineteen fifties

questions.s: According to Friedman and Phelps, why would the trade-off not last?
questions.e: Their point 'was about expectations': people 'build it into wages and prices', so extra inflation 'stops buying any extra jobs'. Nothing suggests workers refused wage increases or that Phillips's data was wrong.
o: Unemployment would rise because workers refused to accept any wage increases
Inflation would disappear on its own after a few years
People would come to expect inflation and adjust for it
Phillips had used incorrect British data

questions.s: Why does the professor mention stagflation in the nineteen seventies?
questions.e: Stagflation meant 'high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, something the simple curve said shouldn't happen'. It supported Friedman and Phelps against the original curve, so the first option reverses its role.
o: To show that the original curve correctly predicted the economy of the nineteen seventies
To give an example of events the simple curve could not explain
To describe a new type of unemployment insurance
To explain how Phillips collected his data

questions.s: What does the professor imply about the history of the Phillips curve?
questions.e: She says economists 'didn't throw the curve away' but 'rebuilt it', and calls the history 'a theory being repaired, more than once'. The first option contradicts her final sentence, which says it 'isn't really a theory being refuted'.
o: It shows that the curve was proven false and has been rejected by most economists
It came to an end with the work of Friedman and Phelps
It proves that inflation and unemployment are unrelated
The idea has been adjusted rather than abandoned

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains that many Greek statues 'were originally painted', discusses color reconstructions and ends with people's 'reaction' to them. Ultraviolet light is used to 'detect colors', not to clean statues, so the first option changes a detail.
o: How museums use ultraviolet light to clean ancient statues and restore their surfaces
The original colors of ancient statues and reactions to them
Why Greek sculptors preferred marble to bronze
The life and writings of Johann Winckelmann

questions.s: What is the main criticism of the full-color reconstructions?
questions.e: The traces show 'which pigment was used' but 'not how it was blended or shaded', so reconstructions use 'flat, solid colors' while 'the originals may have been far subtler'. The reconstructions are based on the surviving traces, so the second option is the reverse.
o: They use pigments that were not available in ancient Greece
They ignore the traces of paint that survive on the statues
Their colors may be simpler than the originals were
They are based only on what ancient writers said

questions.s: Why does the professor mention Johann Winckelmann?
questions.e: Winckelmann 'praised the whiteness of classical statues', and 'later sculptors copied that look on purpose'. He helped spread the white-marble ideal. He lived in the seventeen hundreds and is not one of the 'ancient writers' or the modern scholars who made reconstructions.
o: To show that ancient writers described the colors of statues in great detail
To give an example of a scholar who made full-color reconstructions
To criticize sculptors who painted their work
To show how the ideal of white sculpture was promoted

questions.s: What does the professor imply about people who find the painted versions tasteless?
questions.e: She says they judge by 'a standard of white marble that was itself, in large part, a later invention'. In other words, their taste comes from a later period, not from ancient Greece. She says the coloring 'isn't really in doubt', so the third option is wrong.
o: Their judgment rests on a later idea of beauty
They have studied the pigment traces more carefully than the scholars who made the reconstructions
They are right that the statues were never painted
They usually prefer bright colors in modern art

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor explains why geologists 'rejected the idea for decades' and what 'changed things' in the nineteen fifties and sixties. The coastlines and glaciers are pieces of Wegener's evidence, not the topic of the talk.
o: Why an idea about moving continents was rejected, then accepted
How the coastlines of South America and Africa were mapped by early explorers
How ancient glaciers shaped the continents
Why physicists and geologists often disagree

questions.s: According to the professor, what was the main objection to Wegener's idea?
questions.e: He says 'the main objection was the mechanism': Wegener 'couldn't explain what force could push whole continents'. The fossils were of 'land animals and plants', and the coastlines did fit 'like puzzle pieces', so the first two options contradict the talk.
o: His fossils came from animals that had lived only in the oceans
The coastlines of the continents did not really fit together
Pangaea was too large to have existed
He could not explain what moved the continents

questions.s: What is the professor's attitude toward the geologists who rejected Wegener's idea?
questions.e: He says 'it's tempting to call the critics stubborn, but put yourself in their place', and concludes 'skepticism wasn't unreasonable'. The first option is the view he warns against. The physicists actually supported the critics, so the second option does not fit.
o: He considers them stubborn and unwilling to look at evidence they disliked
He thinks they should have trusted the physicists less
He thinks their doubts were understandable
He believes they were right that the continents never moved

questions.s: What can be inferred about plate tectonics from the talk?
questions.e: Plate tectonics 'kept his conclusion while throwing out his explanation': continents do move, but they 'ride along on moving plates'. The third option reverses this, since continents 'don't plow through the ocean floor'.
o: It was developed by Wegener himself after new surveys of the ocean floor
It kept Wegener's conclusion but not his explanation
It shows that continents push through the ocean floor
It was rejected because of the magnetic stripes

questions.s: What is the main topic of the talk?
questions.e: The talk opens with 'Why did people start farming?' and then reviews several answers: the oasis theory, population pressure and the idea suggested by Gobekli Tepe. The pillars were not homes; they are discussed as evidence of gatherings for ceremonies.
o: Why hunter-gatherers in southeastern Turkey built stone pillars for their homes
How the climate changed after the last ice age
The career of Gordon Childe in the nineteen twenties
Possible reasons that people began to farm

questions.s: Why does the professor mention evidence from the skeletons of early farmers?
questions.e: Early farmers were 'shorter and had more dental problems', so farming was not an obvious improvement, and she asks 'what pushed people into it?' The first option reverses the comparison: the farmers, not the hunter-gatherers, seem to have been less healthy.
o: To prove that hunter-gatherers lived much shorter lives than the farmers after them
To show why the shift to farming needs explaining
To describe the diet of the people at Gobekli Tepe
To support Childe's oasis theory

questions.s: According to the professor, what did the excavators of Gobekli Tepe suggest?
questions.e: They suggested that 'large gatherings for ceremonies came first' and that feeding the crowds 'encouraged people to cultivate wild grains'. The builders were 'still hunting and gathering', not farmers, so the second option mixes in the oasis theory.
o: Ceremonial gatherings may have led to cultivation
Farmers built the site after moving there from oases in drier areas
The climate near the site became wetter
Population pressure caused the pillars to be built

questions.s: What is the professor's opinion about the explanation suggested by Gobekli Tepe?
questions.e: She calls it 'an exciting idea' but says 'one site, however remarkable, can't carry the whole explanation'. She also stresses that farming 'began independently in several parts of the world', which rules out the last option.
o: It has replaced all earlier theories and is accepted by nearly every archaeologist
It is less likely to be true than the oasis theory
It is interesting but cannot explain everything alone
It proves that farming began in one single place

questions.s: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.e: The professor says researchers agree ramps were used and 'the argument is about what kind', then compares straight, outside and inside ramps. The alabaster quarry is mentioned only as evidence about steep ramps.
o: How Egyptian architects decided on the shape and height of the Great Pyramid
Why alabaster was chosen as the main stone at Giza
Competing ideas about how the pyramid's blocks were raised
The tools that were used to cut stone in quarries

questions.s: According to the professor, what is the problem with a ramp around the outside of the pyramid?
questions.e: An outside spiral 'would have covered the corners and edges, which the builders needed to see'. The second option repeats the problem with the straight ramp, and the post holes belong to the quarry ramp.
o: It would have hidden parts the builders needed to see
It would have contained almost as much material as the pyramid itself
It would have been too steep for the workers
It would have needed holes for wooden posts

questions.s: Why does the professor mention the ramp found at a quarry?
questions.e: The quarry ramp shows blocks were hauled up 'slopes much steeper than people had assumed', which 'changes the geometry argument' against a simple ramp. It says nothing in favor of the inside ramp, which still has 'little direct physical evidence'.
o: To prove that the inside ramp idea is correct and the pyramid was built from within
To show that an assumption behind one objection may be wrong
To describe where the stone for the pyramid came from
To show that the Egyptians did not use ramps

questions.s: What does the professor mean when he says progress can come from questioning an assumption hidden inside the old objections?
questions.e: The objection to a straight ramp assumed that ramps had to be gentle. The quarry evidence questioned that belief, not the ramp idea itself. The first option reverses his point that progress here came 'not from a new theory'.
o: New theories are always more useful than looking again at older evidence
Egyptologists should stop criticizing one another's ideas
The inside ramp was hidden from earlier researchers
Criticism of an idea may rely on beliefs that need checking
